item.title: The WHATWG: eight for, eleven against
item.description: In June 2004 a straw poll at a W3C workshop declined to extend HTML, and two days later the people who had asked opened a mailing list and did it themselves.
item.content:encoded:
The group that writes HTML announced itself in June 2004, two days after a workshop in San Jose was asked whether HTML should get any new features and mostly did not raise its hand.

Dean Jackson (W3C): For 8, against 11.

Jackson was co-chairing the W3C's Workshop on Web Applications and Compound Documents, held at Adobe's offices on 1 and 2 June 2004, and the line is how the minutes of the second day record the count. The question had been put by an engineer from Opera Software whom the minutes call Ian Hixson. Ian Hickson went on to edit HTML for more than a decade, and the minute-taker, who had a full room to keep up with, can be forgiven the spelling.

Six years after HTML was dead

By 2004 the W3C had spent about six years treating HTML as finished. What came after it was a family of XML languages, XHTML for documents, XForms for forms, SVG for graphics and SMIL for timing, and much of the two days in San Jose went on how to combine them.

The difficulty was the browser most people had. Alex Hopmann of Microsoft told the workshop on its first day that the Internet Explorer team "has been very focused on security work", and that the coming service pack would not bring new features. Hickson's notes from that day add that the Internet Explorer due with Longhorn, the next Windows, would not support XHTML or SVG.

Hickson had been circling this for a while. In January 2004 a post on their blog, "Void filling: Web Applications Language", said that the web had no language for writing things like Bugzilla or eBay's auctions, and that the only party doing anything about it was Microsoft, with proprietary technology that looked designed for lock-in. The post ends with a promise and a hedge: "I intend to do something about this (hopefully within a W3C context, although that will depend on the politics of the situation)."

The something was a forms draft begun at Opera in 2003, which by that summer was called Web Forms 2.0 and extended the forms chapter of HTML 4.01 instead of replacing it.

Seven principles and a game of Lemmings

Opera and the Mozilla Foundation sent the workshop a joint position paper. It warned of "a rising threat of single-vendor solutions" and then listed seven principles. New features should be usable in IE6 through scripting, so that authors had a way across. Every feature had to be justified by a use case, preferably from real sites that had worked around the gap badly. Development should happen on public lists with public drafts. And error handling had to be specified down to the last case:

Error handling should for the most part be defined in terms of graceful error recovery (as in CSS), rather than obvious and catastrophic failure (as in XML).

On the afternoon of the first day Håkon Lie of Opera opened the joint presentation with a game of Lemmings written in HTML and JavaScript. Lie conceded, by the minutes, that it was scary inside. Hickson followed with the case for building on what browsers already ran: Flash ships and people use it, SVG ships and people don't. The day had opened with Bert Bos of the W3C telling the audience that "JavaScript is the worst invention ever."

Hickson wrote the day up that night, a Tuesday, in a post on the same blog. The only sustained, spontaneous applause of the day, it says, came when someone answered Hickson's case for backwards compatibility by suggesting it was time to drop HTML and Windows IE6 from the roadmap. Then the post asks what Opera and Mozilla should do, and lists three options: work in public and submit the result to the W3C or another standards body once there were implementations; work alone and forget about standards; or join whatever group the W3C set up and implement its output years later, knowing few would use it. Hickson was leaning towards the first, with the poll not yet taken.

The straw poll on extending HTML

The second day ended with straw polls. The first two went through without trouble. Should the W3C write a specification combining profiles of its newer languages, aimed at mobile phones? Nineteen to none. Should it charter a group to work out the use cases for web applications and a roadmap? Twenty-three to two. Then Jackson put up Hickson's question:

Develop declarative extension to HTML and CSS and imperative extensions to DOM, to address medium level Web Application requirements, as opposed to sophisticated, fully-fledged OS-level application APIs.

It went badly before anyone counted. Jackson remarked that it sounded like a matter for the use-case group the room had just voted for. Tantek Çelik of Microsoft said the questions were not good enough for half the room. Hopmann did some arithmetic on the polls so far: about 46 people in the room, about half of them not voting, which was "not an overwhelming interest". Hopmann then leaves, by the minutes, and Jackson reads the question again and announces the count this essay opened with.

Only then did somebody ask what it meant. Kelvin Lawrence of IBM said one word, "Example?", and Hickson pointed to Web Forms 2: "One example would be to add a required attribute to the input element."

<input name="email" required>

The tag is my illustration, not a line from the minutes, but it is the size of the thing the room had just declined. Çelik objected that the proposal mixed things people wanted with things they didn't, and the question came back without its clause about the DOM. Before the hands went up T. V. Raman of IBM reminded the room that six years earlier a hundred people had agreed HTML was dead and started XHTML. If the question was being put again now, Raman asked, "what will we be asking six years from now?" The second count was 8 for, 14 against. Taking the scripting out had won no new supporters and found three more opponents.

The minutes do not say who voted which way. Hickson's account, written two days later, is that every browser vendor present favoured some variant of the idea and that they "were easily out-numbered by the non-browser members". It also records their reply to the six-years-ago point, which was that six years ago they were in school.

The W3C's summary of the workshop is careful to say that the polls only indicated what participants felt and bound nobody. It also says the W3C would probably charter work on the two topics that passed, and that it "does not intend to put any resources into the third", beyond what its existing working groups were already chartered to do.

The WHATWG announcement

Hickson flew back to Europe and posted again on Friday 4 June. The post argues with the workshop for a while and then stops arguing. "The issues have been discussed, the positions have been given, everyone knows where everyone else stands, now it's time to get down and actually start doing work." Its last line, with the first three words in italics, is "What working group is going to work on extending HTML..."

About two hours later, at 17:28 Pacific time, the first message arrived on a new public mailing list. It announced the Web Hypertext Applications Technology Working Group, "a loose, unofficial, and open collaboration of Web browser manufacturers and interested parties", writing specifications for mass-market browsers, of which it named Safari, Mozilla and Opera. There would be three documents to begin with: Web Forms 2.0, Web Apps 1.0 and Web Controls 1.0. The results were to be submitted to a standards organisation in due course, as in the first of Tuesday night's three options.

One sentence in the announcement matters more than the rest. The forum, it says, "follows from several months of work by private e-mail". The poll did not cause the WHATWG, then. My reading is that it decided only where work already months old would continue, and Tuesday's post suggests even that was mostly decided.

Mozilla said so the same day. Brendan Eich's post of that Friday regretted having "missed the chance to hear JavaScript praised as the worst invention of all time" and announced that Mozilla was joining Opera to work on incremental improvements to HTML.

By 29 June the list had carried some 600 messages, by Hickson's count, and the first call for comments on Web Forms 2.0 was out. Hickson's report of that day explains how the group worked. The members, who were Mozilla and Opera employees and a couple of people from Apple's Safari team, were an oversight committee, and "the specs are actually edited by me". The same post claims the first public demonstration of a Web Forms 2.0 control, in front of an audience that had no idea: a small slider at the top right of Safari's RSS view, shown during Steve Jobs's keynote at Apple's developer conference, which Hickson says was an <input type="range">.

Why the workshop said no

The membership is Hickson's explanation. The W3C had many more server-side people than client-side people, "and most of the client-side people are plug-in vendors, not browser vendors." David Baron of Mozilla, who had presented alongside Hickson, said the same thing less kindly a week later: a consortium does what its members want, and its members were mostly building for intranets, phones and other places where one company controls both ends.

Microsoft made the browser that mattered and did not want it extended this way. Hopmann's presentation on the first day said that "Standards for APIs and Object Models are not going to be successful," because they make a fragile platform, and urged the W3C to stay with declarative formats. Hickson agreed about the large case, writing that night that standardising an API for sophisticated applications was a non-starter, and the question's "medium level" marks the difference. As I read it, the compromise pleased neither side: too little for the people who wanted a new platform, too much script for Microsoft.

The opponents also had an argument. Robin Berjon of Expway, who had been at the workshop, made it in the comments under Eich's post: "people don't switch for small incremental improvements, they switch for stuff that is an order of magnitude better". Nobody could show that was wrong in June 2004. The WHATWG was betting the other way, that authors would use whatever worked in the browser their visitors already had.

The W3C adopts the WHATWG draft

The reversal came from the top. In late October 2006 Tim Berners-Lee published a post called "Reinventing HTML", quoted that week by Daniel Lemire and Anne van Kesteren: "It is necessary to evolve HTML incrementally." The attempt to move the world to XML all at once, it said, had not worked. A new HTML Working Group would be chartered, and its charter names the WHATWG and promises to "actively pursue convergence" with it.

Convergence turned out to mean taking the document. On 9 April 2007 Maciej Stachowiak of Apple posted a "Proposal to Adopt HTML5" signed by two people each from Apple, Mozilla and Opera, with Baron, Eich and Lie among them. It asked for three things: that the group start from the WHATWG's text, that the result be called "HTML 5", and that Hickson be its editor.

Chris Wilson was both a co-chair of the group and Microsoft's representative on it. Wilson wrote of having no problem with taking the WHATWG's specification as the basis, provided the intellectual property was in order and the working group owned the text from then on, and gave the response to the name as "well, duh." The objection was to a single editor, which "sets up a dictatorship, benevolent though it might seem".

Hickson answered within the hour, and stated terms. Editing the WHATWG specification was a full-time job that would continue, so the offer stood only if the two groups' specifications were "the same actual document". Nor would Hickson work as an editor who waits for a formal decision before each change, a model the message estimates would move the finish from fifteen years away to fifty.

The chairs put the three questions to a survey, and 102 people answered. On 9 May 2007 Dan Connolly reported "a critical mass of support for all 3 parts of the proposal, though not quite consensus", and resolved the matter anyway: the name would be HTML 5, the review would start from the WHATWG's text, and the editors would be Hickson and Dave Hyatt of Apple. Within hours Hickson checked revision 785 into the W3C's repository and brought it up to revision 800. Web Forms 2.0 was already there. Opera and Mozilla had submitted it to the W3C in April 2005, and another working group had published it as a draft in August 2006. Three years after the workshop, the W3C had the rest of the extension in its own version control, written by the person who had asked.

Who ended up writing HTML

From 2011 to 2019 there were two HTMLs. In January 2011 Hickson announced that the WHATWG's copy would drop its version number and keep changing as a "living standard", while the W3C worked towards a finished one and published HTML5 as a Recommendation on 28 October 2014.

Microsoft joined, and the editor got an appeals court. In December 2017 the WHATWG announced a patent policy and a Steering Group drawn from Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla, admitting that without every browser engine's maker it "was only partially meeting its goals". The post says there is now a formal path of appeal when a participant disagrees with an editor's judgment of what browsers will support, which I take to be Wilson's objection of 2007 answered ten years late. Opera, where the first draft was written, is not one of the four.

The W3C stopped publishing its own HTML. On 28 May 2019 its chief executive, Jeff Jaffe, announced an agreement to that effect, on the grounds that two documents each claiming to be the normative one did the community harm. The memorandum says where the work happens: "HTML and DOM shall be developed principally in the WHATWG".

The winners wrote the history, and tidied it. The history section of the HTML Standard says of the 2004 workshop that "the W3C staff and membership voted to continue developing XML-based replacements instead." The outcome was as it says. What the minutes show is narrower: a non-binding straw poll in which twenty-two people raised a hand.

The takeaway

A lost vote did not start the WHATWG. The work was months old, its editor had weighed leaving the night before, and the count settled only the venue, which mattered less than having three browsers willing to ship what the list agreed on. The objection from those years that has aged best is Wilson's: a specification edited by one person with opinions is a kind of dictatorship, and the WHATWG took thirteen years to build a way to appeal.

The minutes that record "For 8, against 11" spell the proposer's name Hixson throughout. The example Hickson gave when someone finally asked for one is section 4.10.5.3.4 of the HTML Standard: "The required attribute is a boolean attribute. When specified, the element is required."

item.title: The 1998 CSS wish list: item 28 and the fifteen-year wait
item.description: In December 1998 the CSS working group published a numbered list of 67 features people kept asking for; the list's own editor wanted item 28, symbolic constants, left to outside tools and said so at length in 2008, and it shipped in 2014 as custom properties, a design neither side had proposed.
item.content:encoded:
In December 1998 the working group behind CSS published a numbered list of the features people kept asking it for, so that nobody would have to ask twice, and people went on asking for item 28 for another fifteen years.

@define orange = #faa;

H1 {color: orange}
H2 {color: orange}
H3 {color: orange}

That is item 28, Symbolic constants, in the List of suggested extensions to CSS, a W3C Note dated 10 December 1998 and edited by Bert Bos. You have typed its descendant many times, as --orange: #faa near the top of a style sheet and var(--orange) below. (The value #faa works out to rgb(255, 170, 170), which is pink. Whether that is a point for named constants or against them, I leave to you.)

I knew CSS variables had arrived late. What I hadn't understood until I read the Note and the mailing list around it was how early they were written down, beside columns, gradients and rgba(). Nor had I known that the Note's own editor, who had worked on CSS since its first draft, was pointing people who wanted macros toward outside tools a week after announcing the list, and said the same of plain constants ten years later, or that the feature shipped in a form neither side had proposed.

A list to stop the asking

Bos had been part of CSS almost from its first draft. The history chapter of the book Bos wrote with Håkon Wium Lie says Bos was among those who responded to that draft. Bos's W3C home page adds a thesis about graphical user interfaces, which matters later.

CSS2 became a Recommendation in May 1998, and requests for what it lacked kept arriving on the public mailing list, www-style. One Note about them already existed. CSS: Potential Enhancements, edited in August 1997 by Mike Wexler of Adobe, proposed constants and environment variables: 2em << $WIDTH/10 >> 20em meant a tenth of the window's width, kept between 2em and 20em. I read that as clamp(2em, 10vw, 20em) in an earlier spelling.

The 1998 Note names that document as its previous version, but it is a catalogue: every suggestion that was not in CSS2. Its abstract gives the reason in one sentence.

The purpose of the list is to make sure suggestions are neither forgotten nor suggested over and over again.

There are 67 numbered sections. The acknowledgements thank one person, Ian Hickson, "for suggesting this document, and maintaining one independently".

Reading the Note as a list of refusals would be a mistake. The abstract warns that being listed promises nothing, and many items appear without comment. I searched the text for a suggestion marked as rejected and found none. The firmest language is the status paragraph's, which asks that nothing be implemented except as a labelled experiment, and adds that an implementation "will by itself not be an argument to adopt the feature in CSS". That sentence comes back in 2008.

The Note also asked for votes. Every item ends with a row of options from 1, strongly opposed, to 5, strongly in favor, open until 5 February 1999. Bos announced it on www-style on Christmas Eve. The form submitted by mailto:, and that evening George Lund reported filling it in and being unable to send it, called this extremely annoying, and wished the list a merry Christmas. I could not find the results anywhere.

What the 1998 Note asked for

Read now, the Note is like a changelog that leaked a decade or two early. Item 1 is columns. Item 26 wants transparency in colours and writes rgba(40%, 40%, 100%,70%), "for a 70% opaque light blue". Item 27 asks for line-height: max(10pt, width/12). Item 24 wonders whether a gradient might be a primitive in CSS, item 43 suggests rounded corners, and item 55 is display: inline-block. Here are three lines from items 12, 18 and 23:

:target { color: red }
A.local {transition-style: fade}
IMG {float: left contour}

The first is the :target pseudo-class. The second is a page transition. The third wraps text around the outline of a floated image, and the Note traces it to a July 1996 working draft of CSS1, where the line can still be read. CSS got there in the end with shape-outside.

Item 28 in its first week

The argument over symbolic constants started two days after the announcement, with a question from Jelks Cabaniss. Chris Lilley of the W3C explained what @define was for: change a colour in one place and be sure of hitting every use. Cabaniss came back with a bigger idea: a constant holding a whole bundle of declarations, a theme.

Bos answered on New Year's Eve. The language could do that, and could even take parameters; the reply sketches @define myTheme(x,y) = "color: $x; background: $y;" on the spot. Then it doubts that this would help: many people would be bewildered, and those able to use such a thing had other options.

My preference is make CSS powerful in its stylistic capabilities, but simple in its language. Separate tools for separate tasks: people that would know how to use macros like those above are probably also knowledgeable enough to apply external tools, such as cpp, m4, editor macros, databases, server-side includes or scripts/programs of their own making to maintain complex style sheets.

That was a week after the announcement. It answers Cabaniss's macros and not the plain constant in the Note, but its two reasons, bewildered readers and outside tools, are the ones Bos would turn on plain constants in 2008. Even Cabaniss drew a line: "Making CSS a programming language raises the hair on the back of my neck." One who wanted more was Daniel Glazman, who asked for named bundles of declarations, with an example called edf-style.

The list did not stop the asking. In December 2001 Christoph Päper proposed an @var block with names like $fore, and added a postscript that is the reason the Note existed: being new to the list, "maybe this has been discussed here before". Glazman, by then at Netscape, replied with one line, a link into a newer copy of the list, which turned out to be for working group members only. Bos said there was no objection to updating the public Note. The request came again in 2005 and in 2007.

April 2008: a proposal and a refusal

On 8 April 2008 Glazman and David Hyatt of Apple posted a proposal to www-style called CSS Variables. The working group had given Glazman the job at its last meeting, and the message called variables "an oooooold request from the web authors' community". The first example in the specification:

@variables {
  CorporateLogoBGColor: #fe8d12;
}

div.logoContainer {
  background-color: var(CorporateLogoBGColor);
}

That is var() arriving, and it never left. The proposal also said script should be able to change a variable's value, which as I read it already went beyond what a tool run ahead of time can do.

Bos replied a little over three and a half hours later. The reply sets out three principles: a smaller CSS is better, what can be done outside CSS should be, and every indirection loses readers. Then the verdict.

Variables in CSS are wrong for the above three reasons. They make the language bigger and more difficult to learn, they make other people's style sheets more difficult to understand and re-use. They can instead be done with a generic macro processor and would then be useful for other languages, too (HTML, SVG, Javascript, Atom, etc.). They introduce extra indirections.

Glazman answered about twelve hours after that, and not gently. CSS 2.1 ran to 405 pages, the reply pointed out, and an author still couldn't add 10px to 50%. Then: "Bert, you have to accept that (1) you are not a web designer that fights on a daily basis with site management or corporate image". Bos had written that normal people don't program their video recorders. Glazman reported programming a set-top box all the time and finding it trivial.

On 23 June Hyatt announced an experimental implementation in WebKit's nightly builds. One week later Bos gave the refusal a page of its own, Why "variables" in CSS are harmful. On 25 July Hyatt added the rival spellings people had proposed, so that for a while WebKit accepted -webkit-var(foo), =foo= and $foo side by side. And on 24 September Hyatt wrote: "WebKit no longer supports CSS variables. I disabled the feature."

Why Bos refused and Hyatt backed out

The essay is a better argument than its title suggests. It concedes that constants can be built, since WebKit had just built them. Its subject is who CSS is for: it welcomes extensions that add typography and refuses ones that move CSS toward a programming language.

The first reason is the reader. People learn CSS by opening someone else's style sheet, the habit this collection has an essay about. A style sheet full of names its author made up has to be read in two places at once, and a beginner may give up. Bos is candid about the evidence for this: "Of course, this is a conjecture."

The second is size. The essay reports a count of the style sheets on the W3C's own site: 25,725 of them, the non-empty ones averaging 54 lines, too short, the essay says, to need named abstractions. It allows that the people writing more than a hundred lines seemed to be professional designers. I'd argue that is where the case was weakest, because the professionals were the ones asking. Simon Willison made the objection that August: "I personally think that the problem with CSS isn't the learning curve, it's how difficult it is to maintain later".

The third is modularity. Substituting constants is a job a separate tool can do before the browser sees the file, and the essay links six recipes for doing it with PHP or server-side includes. Bos's thesis was on graphical interfaces. The Note's remark on item 27 worries that an expression is hard to specify in a direct-manipulation editor, and the 2008 email says normal people use such interfaces where programmers use text editors. My reading is that Bos spent those ten years defending an author who never opens a text editor.

None of that is what stopped WebKit. Hyatt gave a different reason the day the feature was switched off: "The problem with leaving CSS variables turned on in WebKit is that if the feature ships, it is going to be hugely popular." Whatever shipped would have to be supported forever, and the design was still moving. L. David Baron had asked on day one what a browser should do when a variable holding a colour is used as a font size. Glazman's summary four years later was that the group could not reach an agreement. Hyatt had built a labelled experiment, as the Note's status paragraph asked, and declined to treat its existence as a reason to ship. As I read the record, the refusal that counted in 2008 came from the implementer who liked the idea.

Sass, LESS and a line of PHP

Authors, meanwhile, did what Bos had been telling them to do since 1998 and used a separate tool. Some generated style sheets from PHP, and others adopted preprocessors. Sass's changelog shows the same drift in vocabulary: the notes for version 2.2.0 rename constants to variables, and those for 3.0.0 change the prefix from ! to $, as in $width: 13px. LESS spelled the same thing @width: 10px;.

The essay had offered the PHP approach as a way for authors to find out for themselves whether constants were useful. They found out. By February 2011 Tab Atkins Jr., writing from the Chrome team, was telling www-style that the failure to agree "sucks for authors, particularly as the rise of preprocessing frameworks like SASS have shown just how popular and useful variables are". My reading is that Bos's modular answer worked as designed, and in working it measured the demand.

How constants became custom properties

Atkins's proposal that month, @var $foo red;, was one more run at the old design: global names, substituted into values. The change that mattered came on 24 October 2011, when Atkins proposed replacing that draft with an idea credited to Roland Steiner. Add no construct for variables at all. Let authors make up properties, and let those cascade and inherit like any others:

:root {
  data-main-color: #06c;
  data-accent-color: #006;
}
h1 {
  color: data(main-color);
  border-left: thick solid data(accent-color);
}

"As far as I can tell, there's not a single downside", Atkins wrote. A value set this way could differ from one part of a page to another. By my reading that finished off one of Bos's three reasons, which the scripting in the 2008 proposal had only strained. A macro processor runs before there is a document, so it cannot know which element inherits what. The feature that could be done outside CSS had turned into one that couldn't.

What remained was the name. The earliest Working Draft in the W3C's history of the module is dated 10 April 2012. That August the working group resolved on var-foo and var(foo), and gave three members the job of explaining why not the dollar sign.

Then, in March 2014, with Firefox about to ship var-, Atkins reopened the question. People saw the prefix and thought only of variables, and tying the name to var() had been Atkins's own argument: "I'm very aware of how much I've hoisted myself by my own petard." The suggested replacement was an underscore.

Within a day Brian Kardell offered another. A dash and a vendor's name already marked a browser's own properties, so two dashes could mean custom, with no vendor. That evening Zack Weinberg pointed out that the CSS grammar did not allow an identifier to start with two dashes, and Atkins conceded: "Well, -- is ruled out then." Six days after Kardell's message, the working group resolved to use it. The announcement doesn't say how the grammar objection was settled.

MDN's compatibility data gives Firefox 31 as the first release with custom properties. Its release notes record the prefix changing from var- to -- and date the release 22 July 2014: six years and three months after the 2008 proposal, and more than fifteen years after the Note. WebKit followed in the autumn of 2015, and Chrome's arrived in a beta in February 2016. Glazman approved of custom properties and called the double dash "our ugliest syntactic decision in 20 years". From Bos I found no message about custom properties. The essay is still at its address, and Bos's home page still says, in a line with no date, that symbolic constants in CSS are a bad idea.

Where the other sixty-six went

About two in five of the 67 items have shipped in browsers in some form. That is my count and not the W3C's, and it is rough. From the specifications' publication histories and MDN's compatibility data I can document 28 that arrived in a recognisable form, item 28 among them. Four print items and one about constraints went to other software, as described below. Two, scripted behaviours and // comments, stayed out of CSS as far as I can tell. Another 21 I believe never arrived but cannot prove it, and 11 I did not check. Some moved fast. Hickson quoted item 24 on the list in January 1999, and by 17 February had posted a definition of background-size, crediting the idea to Sjoerd Visscher.

The page transitions shipped twice. Item 18 imagines the change from one page to the next dressed up with slide-show effects, "wipes, fades, checkerboards". Microsoft's documentation of filters and transitions, which it says came with Internet Explorer 4.0 and above, describes just that, switched on by a Page-Enter meta tag. The standard version is the View Transitions API, which Chrome 111 shipped in March 2023, more than 24 years after the Note.

The print items and the constraint solver went to other software. Running headers, cross-references, footnotes and leaders have been specified since 2006 in a module that is still a working draft, and where I found them documented as working is in print formatters like WeasyPrint and Prince. Item 32 wanted a constraint solver to work out property values. A 1999 paper describes a prototype in the W3C's Amaya browser, built on a solver called Cassowary, and Cassowary's project page records where the solver went: in July 2011, into the layout engine of Apple's Lion release of the Mac operating system.

The list itself was never updated. The Note's header gives a "latest version" address, and what it serves is the 1998 text, byte for byte. The newer copy Glazman linked by accident in 2001 sits behind the W3C's member login. The document meant to keep suggestions from being forgotten stopped recording them after one edition.

The takeaway

The list kept the first promise in its abstract better than the second. Parts of it were remembered for a very long time: Chrome shipped what I read as a version of item 45 in February 2025. But the asking never stopped, and item 28 shows why. A refusal from a standards group lasts as long as its reasons do. Bos gave real reasons and held them for ten years, and constants as the Note wrote them, fixed values swapped in before the browser sees the file, really could be done by an outside tool. Then the workaround became the evidence. Once people were writing $width in Sass it was hard to say authors had no use for names, and once the design turned into properties that inherit, no preprocessor could do the job. The worry about the person reading a stranger's style sheet was never answered. I'd say it was outvoted.

What shipped was the thing neither camp had asked for. Custom properties are neither the macro Bos refused nor the global variable Glazman and Hyatt proposed, and they wear a prefix one of those proposers called the group's ugliest syntax in twenty years. Item 28 is still on the W3C's server, with its row of options from 1 to 5 and a form that closed on 5 February 1999. In a style sheet it now reads --orange: #faa. It is still pink.

Sources and further reading

  • Proposal for background-size, Ian Hickson, www-style, 1999 (archived)
  • Proposal for @var, Christoph Päper, www-style, 2001, and Bert Bos on updating the Note, 2001 (archived)

  • css constants, Daniel Brumbaugh Keeney, www-style, 2007 (archived)

  • Why "variables" in CSS are harmful, link and comment, Simon Willison, 2008 (archived)

  • Minutes on CSS Variables from the working group's August 2012 meeting, posted to www-style by fantasai, 29 August 2012 (archived)

item.title: The pop-up ad: a separate window for good intentions
item.description: Around 1997 Ethan Zuckerman moved an ad into its own window at Tripod to keep a car company off a user's page; the trick spread when ad prices collapsed, a Mozilla bug report about porn sites worked out the rule that tamed it, Microsoft adopted the same rule in 2004, and ten years later the apology arrived as an aside.
item.content:encoded:
The pop-up ad was invented to keep an advertisement off a web page, and the programmer who wrote it eventually apologised in print, in an aside.

I wrote the code to launch the window and run an ad in it. I'm sorry. Our intentions were good.

That is Ethan Zuckerman in "The Internet's Original Sin", an essay The Atlantic published in August 2014. In the 1990s Zuckerman worked at Tripod, which gave people free home pages and paid for them with advertising, and the essay owns up to what Tripod made along the way: "one of the most hated tools in the advertiser's toolkit: the pop-up ad." The Atlantic's site would not open for me, so I'm quoting the passage as First Things and several news sites reproduced it that month.

The apology is famous; forty news outlets saw to that. What I hadn't understood was nearly everything around it. The pop-up was built to put distance between an ad and a page, because an advertiser asked. The cure was argued out in a bug report about porn sites, and the rule that finally worked was suggested in that report's fifth reply, four years before Internet Explorer adopted it. And the apology sat inside an essay about something larger, which its author spent the following month trying to get people to read.

A banner on the wrong page

Zuckerman's own biography page says he left graduate school in 1994 to join friends building Tripod in Williamstown, Massachusetts, as the only one of them who knew HTML. The site was meant to offer "tools for life" to people in their twenties. What caught on was the free home page, and somebody had to pay for it. In a talk he posted in September 2014, Zuckerman explains the choice plainly: most people didn't yet know why they would want a home page, so they were not going to pay for one, and "we ended up with the only business model we could think of", the one broadcast television used. Tripod put banners on its users' pages.

The weakness of that arrangement is that the advertiser buys space on pages nobody at the company has read. The Atlantic passage says Tripod came up with the pop-up "when a major car company freaked out that they'd bought a banner ad on a page that celebrated anal sex." So the ad moved into a small window of its own, beside the page instead of on it.

How much of this was Zuckerman's? Engadget quoted what he told Wired that week: he had deployed what was "probably" the first pop-up, and had written both the JavaScript and the server-side Perl that launched it. The hedge is his. The biography page is more careful still, and it gives a date and a second motive:

I designed a vertically-oriented popup window that included navigation tools and an ad for inclusion on webpages at some point in late 1996 or early 1997. It was intended to be less intrusive than inserting an ad into the middle of a user's homepage.

The same paragraph declines the title of inventor and ends "the fault is at least in part mine, and I'm sorry. :-)" The page carries a 2013 date and has been edited since, so I can't tell when that was written. Put the two accounts together and the window was a partition serving both sides: the car company stayed off the page, and the page stayed clear of the car company. I'd call that brand safety, done with a second window.

The JavaScript was the easy part. Netscape's reference for the window object lists the open method as "Implemented in JavaScript 1.0", and the 1999 edition of its JavaScript guide teaches it in one line, then adds the options that made a window small and bare:

msgWindow=window.open("sesame.html")

msgWindow=window.open
   ("sesame.html","displayWindow","toolbar=no,scrollbars=yes")

Nothing in either statement consults the person at the keyboard. A script could call open as a page loaded or as it closed: the same reference documents onLoad and onUnload handlers, and those two events are where the rest of this story happens. I found no copy of Tripod's own script, so I can't show the original.

Why the windows multiplied

The pop-up spread when the money went. A Fox News report from 2001 has Kipp Cheng, an editor at Adweek, putting the price of a thousand ad views at about $85 in 2000 and $1 to $1.50 a year later. That is one editor's estimate, but a publisher facing anything like it sells whatever still pays. In the first half of 2001 a company called X10 bought "pop-under" ads, which opened behind the page, for a small video camera. Fox reported that x10.com was the fifth most visited site on the internet that May, with nearly 30 million visitors, "or, rather, the site went to 30 million unique visitors." In June InternetNews reported that New York Times Digital was adding the pop-under to its regular offering.

The first force, then, was desperation, and the trade said so: "Part of it is the industry got a little bit desperate", an advertising researcher told InternetNews in December 2002. X10's own defence was that this kind of advertising pays the running costs of the sites you visit for free, which is Tripod's bargain restated by a camera company.

The second was that the format seemed to work. In the same article Orbitz, which Nielsen//NetRatings ranked the second most frequent user of pop-ups, said people who clicked its pop-unders bought at a rate "extremely high compared to other forms of advertising", and NYTimes.com said it had raised its pop-up rates for 2003. Both capped how often a reader saw one. Orbitz answered complaints by recommending a free pop-up blocker, which is sporting of the number two advertiser in the format.

The third was the platform. window.open had no idea who was asking and, as Jesse Ruderman put it in a Mozilla bug, "is not standardized anywhere". Unless you installed a filter or had a browser with a setting for windows, the switch you were left with was the one that turned JavaScript off altogether.

A bug report about porn

Mozilla had been asked before. A request from July 1999 says its author had read that Opera could already refuse new windows, and another that November complains of advertisements that kept popping up after being closed. Both were later folded into the report that drew the votes, whose author was thinking about the same kind of page as the car company. On 26 February 2000 Jesse Ruderman opened bug 29346, "Prevent repeating pop-up windows", like this:

Since netscape has been established as the leading porn browser (because of its handy "close all" feature, which is now called "quit"), it should also be set up to easily disallow a porn site from opening lots of new windows, each of which has javascript to open more windows (on open and/or on close events), etc.

Ruderman added that such a site could be impossible to leave, and proposed an allowance of two pop-ups per site. A month later Warren Harris filed a companion bug about windows that reopened as you closed them, and later explained its priority: "when you're surfing porn, this is the number one bug you want to have fixed." The pop-up was written to get an advertiser away from this sort of page. Three years on, this sort of page was where it had become unbearable.

Four days into Ruderman's bug, a commenter offered something simpler than an allowance: restrict open() to calls that user input had triggered. Ruderman saw the hole at once, which was that moving the mouse counts as input, and the commenter tightened the wording to "events that require explicit user action to visible elements of a page."

Nobody built it. The thread ran for a year, and it is a good record of how a sensible request fails to ship. In August 2000 someone writing from a Netscape address filed it under "Future" as a "cool feature that tiny percentage of power users would love"; in fairness, the same comment says Netscape had no resources for enhancements before its release. Mitchell Stoltz, the engineer the bug was assigned to, pointed out repeatedly that a per-site block already existed in the preferences file. It had no screen, and for months its documented syntax was wrong. Blocking by event, Stoltz said, would be a large addition to the security model. In March 2001, by which time one commenter had counted 56 votes and 11 duplicates, Stoltz closed the bug, saying its purpose had become "utterly confused".

Good enough, in a month

The pop-under changed the answer. On 31 July 2001 Robert Ginda opened bug 92955, citing the looming threat of pop-unders. Once every site carries these ads, Ginda argued, a list of banned sites is useless, so block by occasion instead: refuse window.open while a page is loading or unloading. Ginda called this a "good enough" solution and listed its holes in the same message, among them that a site could dodge it with setTimeout. A patch followed within two hours, and a better one that also covered timers under four hours after that.

Two days later Stoltz reviewed the idea and forecast the next several years:

This will probably block the majority of popups/popunders right now, until the advertisers get wise to it and/or we regain enough market share to make it worth their while. Then, they will open popups on mouseover, on focus, etc. In the meantime, I think this is a good idea. We'll need to make this controllable by pref, because Netscape will probably want it off.

Stoltz took the patch over at the end of August and added the preference, and the last argument was about its name. The patch called it privacy.block_open_during_load. Mike Shaver objected that privacy should keep meaning personal information. Stoltz answered that pop-up ads were "a violation of my privacy (in that they are annoying, not that they steal personal info)", then gave way and renamed it dom.disable_open_during_load. Here is the heart of the change as Johnny Stenback posted it in review, with the diff's plus signs removed and the missing closing brace as posted:

  /* If we're in a commonly abused state (top level script, running a
   * timeout, or onload/onunload), and the preference is enabled, block
   * the window.open().
   */
  if (CheckForAbusePoint()) {
    nsCOMPtr<nsIPref> prefs(do_GetService(kPrefServiceCID));

    if (prefs) {
      PRBool blockOpenOnLoad = PR_FALSE;
      prefs->GetBoolPref("privacy.block_open_during_load", &blockOpenOnLoad);

      if (blockOpenOnLoad) {
#ifdef DEBUG
        printf ("*** Blocking window.open.\n");
#endif

        *_retval = nsnull;

        return NS_OK;
    }
  }

Stenback flagged the *_retval = nsnull line as important. As I read the code, it is why a blocked window.open() hands the calling script a null where it expected a window. The fix was checked in on 31 August, a month to the day after the report. There was no checkbox. You opened prefs.js and typed:

user_pref("dom.disable_open_during_load", true);

It broke things, as honest fixes do. A month after check-in, a user who spent all day in Outlook Web Access reported that with the preference set, Reply closed the message and opened nothing. The bug was closed as invalid, which I read as Mozilla calling it the site's problem. By February 2002 the setting had a checkbox, and a new bug opened with a user who had unticked it and found that "Somehow, NYTIMES.COM has managed to get around this." The bug's title names the trick: an onload handler on an image, which the check didn't cover.

Microsoft turns the blocker on

Mozilla's fix did not slow the format down. When Netscape 7.01 arrived with pop-up blocking options in December 2002, InternetNews put Netscape's share of the market that August at 3.4 percent. In July 2003, by Nielsen//NetRatings' count, 7.3 billion pop-up ads were served, up 189 percent on the July before.

Internet Explorer had nothing built in, and its users got their first relief from outside. EarthLink bundled a blocker with its software in August 2002. In June 2003 Google added one to a beta of its toolbar, which InternetNews called "the first one-click option" for the browser. It blocked every pop-up whatever its purpose and played a sound effect when it did.

Microsoft's own blocker came with Windows XP Service Pack 2, and in the first SP2 release it was not switched on. On 17 March 2004 Microsoft said it would ship switched on after all, a complete reversal that the company put down to significant customer feedback. Five days later an Internet Explorer developer who blogged as jeffdav described the design. The team had started by blocking everything, then met the legitimate uses, such as a shop's sizing chart, and needed a rule to tell them apart: "if the user clicks a link that wants to open a new window, we allow it to open one new window." That is the commenter's idea from bug 29346, four years on. I have no evidence anyone at Microsoft had read it. My guess is that it's simply where you end up once the other rules have failed.

Microsoft's guidance for site builders that July turned the rule into documentation: a window opened as the direct result of a user's action is allowed, and a blocked call returns null. In the comments under jeffdav's post, the developer of a web chat client that opened a window whenever a friend's message arrived wrote that the new default made the product impossible. A reply there, apparently from jeffdav, advised checking what window.open() returned, "which all good scripts should be doing already :)".

The apology in parentheses

Ten years later Zuckerman, by then director of MIT's Center for Civic Media, wrote his Atlantic essay to argue that advertising was "the original sin of the web": that paying for everything with ads had led, a step at a time, to keeping everyone under watch. The pop-up was his own exhibit. By his account in that September talk, the admission was hidden in a parenthetical comment, and his editor, Adrienne LaFrance, saw that readers would care about it far more than about three thousand words on surveillance. LaFrance interviewed him and ran a separate 300-word item.

That item, Zuckerman writes, "lightly rewritten, appeared in about forty news outlets over the next 24 hours". Jimmy Fallon and Conan O'Brien made jokes. Abuse arrived in several languages, and he spent a week offline until only one email in five was a death threat. He is careful to call the threats tongue in cheek, and mild beside what women who write online put up with routinely. On NPR, Robert Siegel accepted the apology personally, and Zuckerman spent most of his five minutes explaining that the pop-up had not been the point.

The reply he singled out was a tweet, which he gives approximately: "I do not accept your apology. This is your Frankenstein monster. You made it, you should kill it." He liked it enough to name the idea behind it the rat bastard theory of history, in which one person is to blame for whatever is broken, and to concede half of it: people like him should be trying to fix things.

His own theory of the web is less satisfying and, I think, better supported by everything above. It "was built by idiots like me, doing the best we could at the time."

Where the pop-up went

The rule moved into the definition of the function. MDN's page for window.open() now states that pop-ups "must be opened in direct response to user input", with a separate user gesture for each call, and that the method returns null when a blocker refuses. Every example in the 1999 guide assumes the window opens. The current page tells you what you get when it doesn't.

The preference kept the name from the argument. Firefox's default settings file still contains, under a comment reading "Scripts & Windows prefs", a line that sets dom.disable_open_during_load to true. It is on by default in Firefox now, and it is still not called privacy.

The pop-under moved to the click. Stoltz expected mouseover and focus events. The present-day pop-under, as Wikipedia describes it (the only source I have for this), uses the one event the rule lets through: a click listener on the whole document, so that selecting a word of text counts as asking for a window.

The ad moved into the page. Two weeks after Microsoft's about-face, a commenter on jeffdav's blog predicted: "The marketing people will just cover up the content the user wants to see with DHTML instead." A blocker that watches window.open has no opinion about a positioned layer. In August 2014 Peter Leithart began his First Things piece on Zuckerman's essay by reporting that the first thing on his screen when he clicked through to The Atlantic was a pop-up. The page where I read that lists, in its cookie notice, four cookies belonging to a plugin called Popup Maker.

The takeaway

The pop-up took one line of documented JavaScript and a business short of better ideas, and it was written by someone trying to be considerate to two parties at once: the advertiser who didn't want to be on the page, and the user whose page it was. What turned it into a plague was that window.open couldn't tell who was asking. The cure was to teach it one question, whether the person at the keyboard had just done something, and that took four years, a bug nobody could close cleanly, a patch its author called "good enough" and a change of mind at Microsoft.

The window got its rule. The business that wanted the window did not, which was Zuckerman's point, and I think it has aged better than the jokes about him. In August 2001 Stoltz and Shaver argued for two hours over whether an ad you can't get away from is a privacy problem or only an annoyance, and settled it with a neutral name. Zuckerman's argument, thirteen years later, was that a web paid for by advertising had got everyone used to being watched. If that is right, I'd say the two were one problem the whole time. The preference they named is still in Firefox, set to true. The sentence that explains how it got there is still "Our intentions were good."

Sources and further reading

  • "The Internet's Original Sin", Ethan Zuckerman, The Atlantic, August 2014: not opened, and quoted from the reproductions below
  • AdWorld Wide Web, Peter J. Leithart, First Things, 2014
  • About Me, Ethan Zuckerman, dated 2013 and since revised
  • A public apology – on screwing up by not questioning assumptions – my talk at #BIF10, Ethan Zuckerman, 2014
  • Pop-Up Ad Man 'Fesses To An Internet 'Sin' — But Hopes To Fix It, Robert Siegel with Ethan Zuckerman, NPR, 2014
  • The man responsible for pop-up ads reveals why he cursed us, Chris Velazco, Engadget, 2014
  • Pop-Up Ads Creator Ethan Zuckerman: 'I'm Sorry', Devin Coldewey, NBC News, 2014
  • Client-Side JavaScript Reference: window, Netscape, 1999, hosted by Oracle
  • Client-Side JavaScript Guide, chapter 12: Using Windows and Frames, Netscape, 1999, hosted by Oracle
  • 'Pop-Under' Ads Click Off Web Surfers, Fox News, 2001
  • Pop-Under Ads Catching On, as More Advertisers Take the Bait, Christopher Saunders, InternetNews, 2001
  • Are Pop-Ups Doomed?, Brian Morrissey, InternetNews, 2002
  • Pop-Ups Under Siege, Brian Morrissey, InternetNews, 2003
  • Google's New Toolbar Blocks Pop-Ups, Ryan Naraine, InternetNews, 2003
  • Windows XP SP2 Turns 'On' Pop-up Blocking, Ryan Naraine, InternetNews, 2004
  • Bug 9307: [RFE] ability to say no to window.open, Chris Booton and others, Mozilla, 1999
  • Bug 18441: Switch to turn off spawning of additional windows, Mozilla, 1999
  • Bug 29346: Prevent repeating pop-up windows, Jesse Ruderman and others, Mozilla, 2000
  • Bug 33448: disable 'new window' when close box clicked, Warren Harris and others, Mozilla, 2000
  • Bug 92955: Disable window.open from onload and onunload, Robert Ginda, Mitchell Stoltz and others, Mozilla, 2001
  • Bug 102481: Outlook Web Access - "reply" breaks after disabling pop-ups, David Gerard and others, Mozilla, 2001
  • Bug 126224: (NY Times) Web sites can create pop-up windows using img onload even if unrequested window is blocked, Mozilla, 2002
  • XP SP2 RC1, jeffdav, Microsoft, 2004
  • Fine-Tune Your Web Site for Windows XP Service Pack 2, Microsoft, 2004
  • Window: open() method, MDN
  • firefox.js, the default preferences of the Firefox browser, Mozilla
  • Pop-up ad, Wikipedia

item.title: YUI: the toolkit Yahoo gave away, and the notice that ended it
item.description: In 2006 Yahoo gave away the toolkit its own pages ran on, with a CSS reset, a grid, a browser policy and a lecture series attached. In 2014 it stopped, and the engineer who signed the notice wrote the next day that the announcement should have come sooner, maybe a year sooner.
item.content:encoded:
For eight years Yahoo gave away the JavaScript library its own pages ran on, and the documentation is still online, with a notice across the top.

IMPORTANT: The YUI library is no longer actively maintained. Please see this announcement for more information.

That banner sits on the home page of the YUI documentation. Under it the page carries on as though nothing had happened, still offering to get you started with YUI 3.18.1 in two easy steps, and a little further down: "Pull requests welcome!"

I knew YUI as the big one, where fetching an element was spelled YAHOO.util.Dom.get. What I had not understood until I read the archive was how much shipped under those three letters (a CSS reset, a grid system, a browser support policy, a minifier, a lecture series), or how the rewrite meant to modernise the library left its users running two of them. I also had the ending wrong. The announcement behind that banner says development stops immediately. The engineer who signed it wrote on a mailing list the next day that it should have come much sooner, perhaps a year sooner.

The toolkit behind My Yahoo!

YUI went public in February 2006, in two posts on a new blog. The first, dated the 12th and signed by Nate Koechley, Bill Scott and Eric Miraglia, announced two libraries at once: JavaScript components under a BSD licence, and a Design Pattern Library under Creative Commons. The second, a day later and signed by Thomas Sha, Koechley and Miraglia, described the code: five utilities and three widgets, shaped by more than 100 of Yahoo's web engineers and already running under My Yahoo!. These were, the welcome post said, "the exact same things that power Yahoo! today."

Other libraries already existed, and Miraglia explained why Yahoo had built its own four days later, in "Developing a JavaScript Library for Yahoo!". The word doing the work is heterogeneity. Yahoo was many products, built by different teams with different technologies, and by an internal estimate more than 10,000 different client configurations turned up at them regularly. A library for that company could not ask a team to rebuild its pages around a framework. In Miraglia's words the library "had to impose few constraints and live happily in a lot of different ecosystems."

Under the code sat a policy. Koechley had spent years on what Yahoo called Graded Browser Support, and made it public alongside the library. It sorted every desktop browser into one of three grades, so that each got an answer and QA had a fixed list to test. The chart was revised quarterly, and by that August it was warning that IE 5.5 was next to lose its A.

One global, in capitals

Everything in the library hung off a single name. In June 2006 Douglas Crockford of JSLint, who worked at Yahoo and taught its engineers the language, wrote a short post called "Global Domination" that turns on one short paragraph: "Global variables are evil." A page that mixes components from many authors is safest, Crockford reasoned, when each claims exactly one global. Yahoo's was YAHOO, in capitals so that nobody would make one by accident.

The price was length, and Crockford's answer to anyone who minded YAHOO.util.Dom.get is my favourite line in the archive: "if you don't like the length, you only have to type it once." Here is what typing it looked like. Nicholas Zakas used this function in a 2008 post on the same blog:

function toggle(element){
    if (YAHOO.util.Dom.hasClass(element, "selected")){
        YAHOO.util.Dom.removeClass(element, "selected");
    } else {
        YAHOO.util.Dom.addClass(element, "selected");
    }
}

The post is about helping the minifier. Julien Lecomte's YUI Compressor, released the previous August, shortened local variable names but could do nothing with a global or a dotted path. Zakas's fix was, I'd say, Crockford's advice in practice: type it once, as var YUD = YAHOO.util.Dom;.

What the typing bought was a browser problem you never had to meet. In the last YUI 2 source, Dom.get doesn't simply trust document.getElementById. It checks that the element that came back really carries the id that was asked for, and the comment beside the check says why: // IE: avoid false match on "name" attribute. Somebody had already found that bug for you, which, multiplied by every method, was the case for the library.

A reset, a grid and a lecture hall

In the summer of 2006 YUI began shipping stylesheets that the blog credits to Koechley. Reset flattened every browser's default styling: margins and padding to zero, list bullets gone, headings the size and weight of body text. Grids built page layouts out of ids and class names, which Koechley walked through in an article for 24 ways that December:

<div id="doc3" class="yui-t3">
  <div id="yui-main">
    <div class="yui-b"></div>
  </div>
  <div class="yui-b"></div>
</div>

The id doc3 meant a fluid page at full width. The class yui-t3 put a 300-pixel secondary column on the left, whichever order the two blocks came in the source. By Miraglia's count that October the one Grids file could produce "more than 130 different wireframes", and Reset, Fonts and Grids together weighed 1.3KB on the wire.

The part I had underrated is the blog. The archive of YUIBlog holds 1,002 posts by 87 contributors, by its own count, and they range well beyond YUI. Joe Hewitt came to Yahoo in May 2006 to show Firebug, then about five months old, and the video went up on the blog. Tenni Theurer's measurements of where page-load time goes were published there that November, the work of the performance team whose leader wrote YSlow. Crockford's classes on the language were filmed and posted, in a series that became YUI Theater and later carried talks by John Resig, the creator of jQuery.

I'd argue this was the larger gift. The library was one company's answer to scripting across browsers. The blog was that company teaching its working habits in public (grade your browsers, stay out of the global scope, minify and gzip, measure the page), and the habits travelled further than YAHOO.util did.

YUI 3 and the sandbox

By 2008 the team wanted to start again. YUI 3.0 Preview Release 1, announced by Miraglia and Matt Sweeney on 13 August, set five goals: lighter, faster, more consistent, more powerful, and one I didn't expect, more securable, glossed as "safer and easier to expose to multiple developers working in the same environment". That is the heterogeneity problem of 2006 again: many teams, one page. The answer this time was to stop sharing an object at all. This is how the first production release, 3.0.0 on 29 September 2009, told you to make something draggable:

<div id="demo">I'm draggable.</div>
<script type="text/javascript" src="http://yui.yahooapis.com/3.0.0/build/yui/yui-min.js"></script>
<script>
YUI().use('dd-plugin', function(Y) {
    Y.one('#demo').plug(Y.Plugin.Drag);
});
</script>

One small seed file went on the page, 6.2KB gzipped. You named the modules you wanted. The seed worked out what they depended on, fetched the lot from Yahoo's CDN in what was usually a single combined request, and called your function with a private instance of the library, named Y. The post bills this as three easy steps, and the third reads: "Step 3: There is no step 3."

The YUI documentation calls the pattern a sandbox and describes it as "the most important concept to understand about YUI." Modules attached to one instance were out of reach of another, and the only global left was the function YUI. Three years after "Global Domination", the library had gone from one global object that held everything to one global function that handed out private copies.

The bill was stated up front. The preview's FAQ asks whether YUI 3.0 is backward compatible with YUI 2.x, and the answer begins with one word: "No." Migrating would take real effort, it went on, though a limited compatibility layer was promised and the two libraries could share a page. The schedule slipped, too: the preview expected a beta in December 2008, and by the dates in the blog's archive the beta arrived in June 2009.

In November 2010 Miraglia published "A Status Check on the YUI 2-to-3 Transition". The old library was a giant: downloaded more than 2 million times, with Yahoo's CDN serving about 15 billion YUI files a month. The new one had the better utilities, but at the widget level it was, in Miraglia's words, "still catching up." The DataTable, Editor, Menu, Button and Calendar that had made YUI 2 popular were still the YUI 2 versions, and anyone who needed them from YUI 3 was pointed to a bridge called YUI 2-in-3, which loaded both libraries. Miraglia's own verdict was upbeat: counting community modules, YUI 3 already offered more widget options than YUI 2 had shipped with. The post also concedes that switching between two APIs was less than ideal, and I'd argue that was the part a YUI shop felt, with the library it was supposed to be leaving still doing the heavy lifting.

Two months earlier the team had announced SimpleYUI, a build that skipped the instantiation and bound everything to "a global Y variable", so that Y.one("#foo").addClass("highlight"); worked straight after the script tag. I read it as an answer to jQuery, though the post never names it: the most important concept in YUI now came with an off switch.

The notice of August 2014

There were signs. On 16 June 2014 Lecomte, the author of the Compressor, announced that the YUI Gallery, by then more than 600 community modules served from Yahoo's CDN, would get its last build on 31 July. Anyone publishing a module to npm or bower was asked to tag it yui-module.

On Monday 25 August a post signed "Administrator" appeared under the title "We've Moved to Tumblr!". The blog would become read-only, and announcements would now come from the Yahoo Engineering Tumblr. On the Friday one did. "Important Announcement Regarding YUI", signed by Lecomte as Director of Engineering, walks through everything that had changed in front-end development (Node, npm and bower, Grunt and Gulp, Backbone and React and Angular, browsers that update themselves) and arrives at one sentence: "we have made the difficult decision to immediately stop all new development on YUI". Future releases would be rare, and confined to fixes Yahoo's own sites could not do without.

The same text went to the yui-support mailing list, opening with "Howdy!", and the thread under it is uncomfortable reading. The first reply quoted a July comment on the blog, about cool things happening that could not be discussed yet, and counted a month wasted since then on more legacy YUI code. One poster objected to the greeting. Lecomte answered on the Saturday, and the first point of the answer is the thing I had not known:

I agree that the announcement should have come a long time ago. Maybe a year ago, when all new development on YUI effectively ceased. There is nothing else I can say about this besides apologizing to the community.

That is one person's estimate, hedged with "Maybe", and it concerns new development, not releases. From outside the library had looked alive: the blog's archive lists 3.15.0 in February 2014, 3.16.0 in April and 3.17 in May and June. The rest of the reply is blunter than the official notice, and I think fairer. Yahoo depended on YUI more than anyone and could not rewrite millions of lines overnight either. The code was open, so fork it. It was written on a weekend, and at least one poster wrote back with thanks.

Not everyone was surprised. Liferay, which had built its AlloyUI components on YUI 3, posted the same day. The news was no news there, Nate Cavanaugh wrote, pointing to the Gallery notice and other public hints, and Liferay, being close to the YUI team, had been discussing its options for a couple of months. The hints were there for anyone to read. The plain statement came on the Friday.

Why Yahoo stopped

The notice gives its own reasons, and its most candid sentence concedes that many developers had come to see large libraries "as walled gardens they don't want to be locked into." One word is missing from its list of tools, frameworks, standards and browsers: jQuery.

The first force is the one the notice ends its list on: the browsers converged. YUI existed because of those 10,000 client configurations, and by 2014 browsers updated themselves. John Lindal, who had worked at Yahoo, put it plainly in the thread: for most of the company YUI had "mostly been a browser-independence layer", and with old Internet Explorer on the way out a thick one was no longer needed.

The second is the package manager. Put YUI 3's loader, CDN and Gallery together and you have a private one: ask for a module by name, and something resolves its dependencies and delivers it. Getting a module into it meant signing a contributor agreement, sending a pull request and waiting for the next push to the CDN, about every two weeks. Then npm (which has an essay of its own) and bower did that job for any JavaScript at all.

There is a detail here that stopped me. Isaac Schlueter's résumé lists four years at Yahoo, from January 2006 to January 2010, ending as lead front-end architect on the Yahoo! Application Platform. The changelog for YUI Compressor 2.0 includes the line "Integrated Isaac Schlueter's CSS compressor", and Schlueter spoke at YUIConf 2009 on solving problems with YUI 3. In an interview with Increment, Schlueter dates the first version of npm to September 2009, the month YUI 3.0.0 shipped, and describes it as automating a habit picked up at Yahoo, of working with a package manager. Nothing I read connects these facts to each other, and I am not suggesting npm was an answer to YUI. But the first package manager the notice names was started by a Yahoo front-end engineer, in the same month Yahoo shipped a loader of its own.

The third force, I'd argue, was the rewrite. YUI 3 asked every user to move while the widgets they depended on stayed behind. The archive's own tally shows posts to the blog falling from 194 in 2010 to 94 in 2011, which may mean many things, and the notice describes most core modules as having no active maintainer. One poster, Simon Gilligan, called the technical explanation "a diversion" and asked the question the notice doesn't: how the project lost its momentum in the first place.

The fourth is the sponsor. YUI was Yahoo's toolkit before it was anyone else's, which in 2006 was the selling point and in 2014 was the exit: the code would now change only when a Yahoo property needed it to. Gilligan drew the moral in two words, "Buyer beware", and thanked Yahoo for the library all the same. What was decided inside Yahoo, and by whom, I have no source for. The notice carries one signature.

Where YUI's pieces went

The reset had a descendant within a year. When Eric Meyer published "Reset Reloaded" in May 2007, commenters asked how it compared with Yahoo's. Meyer answered that the work had started from Yahoo's styles, and could be considered "a variant on theirs, or a fork, or a sequel, or maybe just an alternative." I had always thought of the two resets as rivals.

A stranger's extension became a company. In August 2006 a developer named Jack Slocum began publishing extensions to YUI under the namespace YAHOO.ext, and by October the YUI Blog was interviewing Slocum about a Grid component that had the blogs talking. Asked what YUI itself should build next, Slocum replied: "Definitely not a Grid component. :-)" According to Jay Garcia's history of the project, the namespace was shortened to Ext in January 2007 and Ext JS 1.0 followed that April. Six days after Yahoo's notice, the company that Ext JS turned into, Sencha, published "A Fond Farewell to YUI". It says that big enterprise frameworks remain the right idea, as a company selling one would.

One large outside user tried every exit. On the day of the notice Cavanaugh listed Liferay's options: take over stewardship of YUI, migrate off it, or fork a cleaned-up "YUI4". By mid-September the plan was AlloyUI 4, rebuilt as jQuery plugins, and in October AlloyUI 3.0.0 shipped as the last release on YUI. Then, in 2016, Cavanaugh reported that the jQuery version had been dropped, because putting a different API under the same name "would lead to a very confusing situation", and that AlloyUI itself was deprecated as of Liferay 7. The YUI4 fork does not come up again in those posts.

The blog and the docs were kept. The "Moved to Tumblr" post promised that the blog would be archived, and an archive exists, on the same domain as this collection. The documentation stops at version 3.18.1, which Wikipedia dates to 22 October 2014, under two months after development officially ended.

The takeaway

YUI was built for a web of ten thousand client configurations and a company of many teams, where the most valuable thing a library could offer was one tested, documented answer to everything: one global, one reset, one grid, one loader, one list of browsers that mattered. For a few years that completeness was the product. Then the browsers converged, a package manager made it cheap to assemble your own answer from small parts, and the completeness started to look like a wall. The rewrite had already asked YUI's users to cross over once, and the sponsor that made the library trustworthy was the only party who could decide it was finished. The avoidable mistake, I'd argue, was the silence: by Lecomte's own estimate the announcement came perhaps a year late.

The code is the part that lasted least. The habits the blog taught lasted longer (graded browsers, clean globals, minified files), and so did the descendants, in a reset here and an enterprise framework there. The documentation is still up, banner and all, and "Pull requests welcome!" is the line I keep returning to. It was true in the way it is true of any open repository, and Lecomte's notice says exactly why it had stopped being true in the way that counts: few reviewers still had the time to look at them.

Sources and further reading
