item.title: FormMail: the contact form that mailed anyone
item.description: Matt Wright wrote FormMail in high school in 1995 and it became the web's default contact form; it took its recipient from the page, spammers turned it into a mail relay, and the author ended up offering the London Perl Mongers' replacement from the same download site.
item.content:encoded:
From 1995 the contact form on a great many small websites was one free Perl script, and the script sent its mail to whatever address the web page told it to.

<input type=hidden
  name="recipient"
  value="email@your.host.com">

That tag comes from the Readme of FormMail, which prints it on one line; I have broken it to fit. "There is only one form field that you must have in your form, for FormMail to work correctly," the Readme says, and names this one. You put your address in a hidden input, pointed the form at FormMail.pl, and whatever a visitor typed arrived in your inbox.

FormMail was written by Matt Wright and given away at Matt's Script Archive. I knew it the way most people now do, as the script spammers abused and Perl programmers warned you off. What I had not understood until I read its change log, the security advisory written against it and its author's own account was how the trouble was built into the selling point, how hard the author was to find when it mattered, and that the people who wrote the replacement ended up with their download links on the author's own site.

A mail gateway for people without a cgi-bin

Wright tells the beginning on a page of the archive. The scripts went up from 1995, when Wright was still in high school and had no formal training in programming: "I released the code as I learned, hoping others would find it useful." The history at the end of the Readme dates version 1.0 of FormMail to June 11, 1995. The header of the script itself says June 9.

A form needs a program on the server to receive it, and the Readme's list of possible uses describes who had trouble with that: people who wanted a form mailed to them and did not know how to write the program, and webmasters who wanted their users to have forms without giving each of them a cgi-bin directory. FormMail's answer was one script, installed once, that every form on the server could be aimed at, with its options set in hidden fields of the form itself. Wright's page for the script calls this "the perfect system-wide solution for allowing users form-based user feedback capabilities without the risks of allowing freedom of CGI access." So FormMail was offered to administrators partly as a safety measure.

It had security fixes almost at once. Version 1.1, on August 3, 1995, closed a hole that let users run commands under the server's user ID, with thanks to a Paul Phillips who noticed it. Version 1.3, in January 1996, closed the door on strangers' forms, and its history entry is my favourite line in the file: "Security hole, which allowed any user on any system to bum off of your formmail script, has been plugged up with the @referers variable." You listed your own domains, and the script checked that the browser's Referer header named one of them. That decided whose forms could use your copy. It put no limit on where the mail could go.

Then came version 1.6, on May 2, 1997, and after it nothing for more than four years. Wright's page about the archive says most of its scripts stopped being updated after 1996, apart from major security flaws and bugs. The downloads did not stop. Wright's page for the script claims FormMail was "downloaded over 2,000,000 times since 1997" and may be the most used CGI program on the internet. Those are Wright's own figures, and I have no second source for them.

How FormMail 1.6 became a mail relay

The best account of what went wrong is an advisory posted to the Bugtraq mailing list on January 23, 2002, by Ronald F. Guilmette and Justin Mason, who is identified in it as the maintainer of SpamAssassin. Abuse, it says, "was rendered trivial by the script's total reliance on information transmitted by the web client to the web server", both to decide whether a request was allowed and to decide where the mail went.

This is the referer check, from the 2009 release of the script; the advisory quotes the same lines from the version current in 2002.

if ($ENV{'HTTP_REFERER'}) {
    foreach $referer (@referers) {
        if ($ENV{'HTTP_REFERER'} =~ m|https?://([^/]*)$referer|i) {
            $check_referer = 1;
            last;
        }
    }
}
else {
    $check_referer = 1;
}

Read the else. A request with no Referer header at all is waved through. The advisory expects most attackers to do exactly that, and adds in a footnote that the Lynx browser had a -noreferer switch for the purpose. If you could not drop the header, the pattern would still pass any URL that had an allowed domain somewhere in it, such as http://www.attacker.tld/myform.html?http://www.victim.com/. That mattered to anyone attacking from a browser: the authors note that JavaScript's submit() always sent a Referer and they had found no way to stop it. Guilmette's covering note points to a working demonstration, written entirely in client-side JavaScript, of an exploit for FormMail 1.6. I have not seen that page.

Once past that check, in the version that had spread, there was no second one. The Readme's history shows no list of permitted recipients until version 1.7, in 2001. Until then the address in the hidden field was simply believed, and a stranger needed only the URL of your FormMail.pl and a request that set recipient to anyone they liked. The script piped the message to the mail program on the same machine, which treated it as a trusted local user, and the advisory points out that a recipient could trace such a message "only as far as the web server that hosts the FormMail script."

The advisory dates the discovery loosely, to some time between the release of 1.6 and March 2001, by when spammers were using installed copies as what it calls the functional equivalent of anonymising open mail relays. In September 2001, on the Security Incidents list, Jay D. Dyson answered a report of probes for the script by saying that many had succeeded at one agency Dyson advised, and offered a theory: "spammers have tired of simply looking for open relays and are now looking for other avenues by which they can abuse third-party mail systems".

FormMail did have one accidental defence. Every message it sent began with its own line, "Below is the result of your feedback form." The advisory's authors assume, with what reads like some pleasure, that this habit annoyed spammers enough to explain why they had generally preferred ordinary open relays. Even a spammer has brand standards.

Three patches in a week, then silence

The Readme's history shows Wright coming back to the script in the summer of 2001, and it shows the chase. Version 1.7, on July 27, added @recipients, a list kept in the script on the server of where mail was allowed to go, and the entry says outright that it was there to defeat spamming. Version 1.8 followed on August 2, because "under certain cases in v1.7, spam could still get through by appending a legit recipient to the list of intended spam victims." Version 1.9 came the next day, with a check against newline characters in the subject field. That is three releases in a week, each fixing what the one before had missed.

The January 2002 advisory was about 1.9, and it found that the job was not finished. It goes further than the Readme does, and says versions before 1.9 did no checking of the recipient at all; I have not seen the 1.7 or 1.8 code, so I can only report that the two disagree. On 1.9 itself the advisory is specific. The referer check was unchanged. The recipient check compared only the end of the address against the allowed list, so if you had allowed your whole domain, an address such as user%somewhere.tld@ourdomain.tld passed. That is what the advisory calls the old Sendmail percent hack, a form of address that the mail server next to FormMail would, the authors explain, almost certainly accept and send on to user@somewhere.tld. And the newline check covered the subject only. The sender's address and name went into the header through this line, unfiltered:

print MAIL "From: $Config{'email'} ($Config{'realname'})\n";

Put a newline in the email field and you were writing mail headers of your own. The advisory's example sets it to IGNORED\nCc: user@somewhere.tld,..., where \n stands for a real newline, and then shows the same trick supplying a subject and an opening line of body text, which pushes FormMail's tell-tale sentence down the page. The sample text is "MAKE MONEY FAST!!!".

The part I did not know is in the section headed "Notification". Both authors wrote to the address on the FormMail home page more than five working days before publishing and got no answer, and had no more luck by telephone. Guilmette posted a patched copy, labelled 1.9s, warned in capitals that nobody had reviewed or even tested it, and explained why: "I have been totally unable to even get into contact with the original FormMail author, so you may be sure that he has not even seen this (1.9s) version of his script." A script its author thought might be the most used CGI program on the internet had, as far as two security researchers could tell that month, nobody at the other end. I have only their side of this. Nothing I read gives Wright's.

The answer came just under three months later. The history's entry for version 1.91, dated April 19, 2002, concedes the point in its first sentence: "The same vulnerability that was patched in 1.9 with the subject field still existed in the email and realname fields." The same release tightened the default recipient patterns against the percent hack, and the Readme's overview says it addresses the worst problems made public in an advisory it cites by URL, a PDF on Guilmette's site that I could not open and that looks to be this one. The script's page still carries the banner from that week, a security update dated April 19, 2002, telling everyone on an earlier version, 1.6 included, to upgrade immediately.

Why one script sat on so many servers

The first force was convenience, and I'd argue it cannot be separated from the flaw. A script that takes its settings from the HTML can be used by someone who cannot edit a script. A form handler configured by the page has to trust the page, and the page comes from the browser.

The second was that popularity fed itself. Dave Cross laid this out in "Finding CGI Scripts", an article the copy on the Perl Hacks site says first ran on perl.com in January 2002. Searching for CGI scripts put Matt's Script Archive in the first two results, and the people searching were not programmers who could judge the Perl they downloaded. So the best-known archive got the links, the links got it the ranking, and, as Cross put it, "at no point does any kind of quality control enter into the process."

The third was time. Perl changed a great deal after 1995, and the script mostly did not. Cross's checklist for a trustworthy script (warnings, use strict, taint mode, the standard CGI.pm module, recent updates) is a list of things FormMail lacked, and the nms project's own site, which I'll come to, was blunter about the archive's code. Wright's page does not really argue. "My interests and activies have moved on", it says, typo and all, and it adds that there has been no time to update the scripts. A person who wrote something useful in high school is allowed to grow up and do other things. The web had no arrangement for what happens to two million downloads when they do. Dyson's theory supplies the trigger: if spammers came to form scripts because the lists that tracked open relays had shut or started charging, the hole sat in plain sight for years and became valuable only when the easier doors closed. That is one administrator's reading, from one mailing-list post.

The London Perl Mongers' drop-in replacement

The fix that lasted did not come from the archive. Cross's article says that in the summer of 2001 a group of London Perl Mongers began to wonder what it would take to write replacements for the CGI programs in common use. The article says "we" throughout, so I take Cross to have been one of them. They called the project nms and chose Wright's scripts as the target, for a reason Cross was careful about: "This wasn't because Matt Wright's scripts were the worst out there, but simply that they were the most commonly used."

What I admire is the constraint they set themselves. The scripts had to be drop-in replacements, so that anyone using one of Wright's could put the new one in its place and carry on, and the nms site is clear that the audience was webmasters who might not know much Perl at all. And they could use no modules beyond those that ship with Perl, even though that meant the form mailer ended up "talking directly to sendmail" where good practice would have used a mail module. Cross's reasoning was that the audience was on hosted servers, often without shell access. A secure script nobody could install would protect nobody.

The other rule was about readers of the code. The nms site complains that "one of the worst legacies of Matt's scripts is that people use them to learn Perl", so every replacement had to run clean under use strict with warnings and taint checking on. Free scripts were the View Source of the server side: people opened them to change a colour and copied the habits.

It was not a clean victory, and the sources say so themselves. Cross admitted in January 2002 that "the one advantage that Matt's scripts have over ours is that they've had many years of testing on a large number of Web sites." The Bugtraq advisory, the same month, names nms as one of two fixed versions of FormMail in circulation and says neither dealt with every problem it raised. The name was a small embarrassment too. By Cross's account it began as a disparaging remark about one of the existing archives, and by the time the group thought better of that, the initials had stuck. Officially they stand for nothing.

For everyone else, coping meant the advice Dyson gave that September: don't run a web-to-mail gateway "unless you've got your script configured to allow only specific recipients." The nms news page records how far that advice had to travel. It says SecurityFocus put attacks on Wright's FormMail third in its list of top attacks for the first quarter of 2002. I could not open SecurityFocus's own list, so that is nms's report of it.

What survives of FormMail

The author recommended the replacement, and hosts it. The nms site says that in May 2002 Wright redesigned the archive and added a page about the project. That page is still there, and it is not grudging. It recommends the nms versions to anyone who wants to learn CGI programming, and says of the archive's own code that it is "not representative of how even I would code these days." Below that, the archive offers the nms files for download from its own server, fourteen of them, each listed against the script of Wright's that it replaces. The originals stay up, Wright explains, because they still work for many people.

The nms site quotes Wright's page and adds one line of its own: "I call that a good result :)".

The referer check is still in the script, with a label on it. The last release I could find is 1.93, dated July 14, 2009, two months after three researchers at ush.it reported cross-site scripting and response-splitting holes in 1.92; the script's header credits them by name. The code I quoted earlier is from that release, else branch included. What changed is the documentation around it. The Readme now describes the check as a remnant of the days when it was used for security, and says: "This is not a security check. Referer headers can EASILY be faked."

FormMail turned into a service. The archive's pages advertise FormMail.com, a hosted form processor for people who would rather not install anything, with plans "at less than $1 per month". The script's first pitch was that one copy could serve every form on a server. The hosted version is that idea with the server moved to the author's side.

And old copies were still in service long afterwards. Under Cross's article there is a comment from March 2017 by a reader who mentions having used the archive's scripts as a teacher, and who had "hundreds of scripts that send email using the old formmail.pl code" and server logs showing thousands of messages going out. The comment does not say how the mail was being sent, or whether those scripts were Wright's FormMail or things built on it. Cross replied within minutes and told the reader to start by taking the compromised program off the server. That was more than fifteen years after the first anti-spam patch.

The takeaway

FormMail believed what the browser sent, which is how a great deal of the early web went wrong. The design that let anyone use it without touching a script, with the destination written in the page, was the design that let any stranger use it too, and the patches of 2001 and 2002 were attempts to keep the convenience while taking back the trust. What I find worth remembering is how the ending went. The people who wrote the replacement were rude about the code and careful about the users, they built it to be swapped in by people who could not read it, and the author put it on the front counter next to the original and said plainly that it was the one to learn from.

The hidden field is still in the Readme, and a form written for FormMail would still need it. The difference is one sentence further up the same file: "@recipients is the most important variable you need to configure." The page still says where the mail should go. The script no longer takes its word for it.

item.title: Cookies: the standard said off, the browsers said on
item.description: In 1997 the cookie's own standard said third-party cookies should be off by default. Lou Montulli, who invented the cookie at Netscape and co-wrote that standard, was the one who left them on, and his reasoning was still winning in 2025.
item.content:encoded:
In 1997 the web cookie got a standard that said a cookie from a site you never chose to visit should be off until you switched it on, and one of its two authors is the engineer who, by his own account, decided to leave it on.

Cookie: CUSTOMER=WILE_E_COYOTE

That is a browser introducing itself to a shop, in the worked example from Netscape's own cookie specification, a page headed "Preliminary Specification - Use with caution". Over the next few requests the customer puts ROCKET_LAUNCHER_0001 in the basket and chooses SHIPPING=FEDEX. The page's overview explains the name of the thing in one clause: "The state object is called a cookie, for no compelling reason."

I knew the short version of this history: the cookie was a shopping-cart hack that advertisers turned into a tracking device while nobody was looking. The reading says people were looking. Cookies were first argued over in public as the more private of the options on offer. A standards group found the advertising hole in the winter of 1995 to 1996, when its members had barely heard of an advertising network, and wrote a rule to close it. The rule was published and the browsers ignored it, and the person who made that call at Netscape, by his own account, was Lou Montulli, who had invented the cookie and whose name is on the rule.

A server with no memory

HTTP forgets you between requests. A server in 1994 answered a request for a page and hung up, and the next request from the same person was a stranger's. That is fine for documents and useless for a shop.

Montulli told the origin story himself in 2013, in "The reasoning behind Web Cookies". One fix that kept coming up in the web's design groups was to give every browser a unique identifier. Montulli was against it, "because the unique identifier could be used to track a user at every website." Then, around July 1994 by his account, he went to a meeting about a shopping server another group at Netscape was building. They needed a cart and had no reasonable way to make one. Within a week he had the idea: let a single site hand the browser a token that the browser gives back only to that site. He widened the token into a general payload, and took the name from "magic cookie", a term from an operating systems course. It shipped in the browser Netscape released that autumn.

It shipped quietly. David Kristol, who comes into this story as a rival and leaves it as Montulli's co-author, wrote the long insider account, "HTTP Cookies: Standards, Privacy, and Politics", in 2001. Kristol says the first public Navigator supported cookies "although that fact was not well known at the time", and gives a slightly different origin, a request from one of Netscape's customers. Both could be true, and I can't settle it.

Sites that could not wait for a mechanism made their own, and it was worse. Here is what Time Warner's Pathfinder did to its visitors in July 1995, as recorded on the www-talk mailing list by Robert Thau, writing from an ai.mit.edu address:

http://www.pathfinder.com/@@VFNihgAAAAAAQDIL/pathfinder/Quick_Navigator.html

The part after @@ is you. Brian Behlendorf, who had built the access system at HotWired, had opened a thread called "Session tracking" on that list on the evening of 17 April 1995 to say that schemes like this were "fatally flawed". Bookmark such a URL, or mail it to your friends, and they all arrive wearing your session. And because every visitor gets a different address for the same page, the caches fill up with copies.

Three proposals by lunchtime

Behlendorf's own proposal was the gentlest one of the year. The browser, not the server, would make up a Session-ID of 32 random characters and change it at every restart, or whenever the user liked, on the principle that any solution had to protect the user's anonymity. The next day brought two answers. Kristol, writing from an AT&T address, proposed a single opaque value that the server would issue and the browser would hand back. Less than an hour and a half after that, Montulli replied: "We have been doing some work along these lines."

Set-Cookie: NAME=OPAQUE_STRING \
            [; expires= ] \
            [; path=] \
            [; domain=] \
            [; secure]

Cookie: NAME=OPAQUE_STRING *[; NAME=OPAQUE_STRING]

"Some work" was a modest way to describe a feature that had been in a shipping browser for months. And the two optional parts that would cause all the later trouble are already there. expires lets a cookie outlive the session, so the server can know you next month. domain lets one machine set a cookie that its sibling machines receive. Larry Masinter, at Xerox PARC, pressed on that within two days: what stops a malicious site A telling the browser to send its cookies to site B? Montulli's answer was the rule already in the proposal, that only a host inside a domain may set a cookie for it.

Worse than a cardboard box

Asked what all this was for, Montulli named the shopping basket, and the back button as the reason it could not live anywhere else. State kept in a URL or a hidden form field goes wrong the moment the shopper navigates out of order. A cookie is tied to neither the URL nor the document.

Paul Burchard was not charmed. The objection, preserved in Montulli's reply of 21 April, was about who gets to see the basket:

As I feared. A cookie hidden in the HTTP headers is not the way to implement this! Just think about it from the customer's point of view: With a real shopping basket, I can see at all times what I've collected so far.

Burchard added: "Your solution compares poorly with a cardboard box :-)". Then Marc Andreessen turned up in the thread to make the commercial case: the server can draw the basket page whenever the customer asks, so the web gets to use HTML and forms as they are and no browser needs new machinery. That approach had worked before, when Andreessen shipped the image tag past a list full of more general designs.

The argument came back in July, and this time Burchard said of cookies something much closer to what everyone would be saying a year later: "'Shopping basket' information may even be invisibly transported to a completely different server without any visual hint to the naive user." Burchard's alternative was a cookie as a real linked document that the browser could show you.

What I did not expect is who was on the other side of the privacy argument. Thau's Pathfinder message comes down, tentatively, on the side of cookies, and on privacy grounds. With a session ID in a URL, whatever the server keeps about you is invisible. A cookie at least sits on your own machine, where the browser could show it to you, and Thau wished aloud for a menu entry that did. Thau closed with a prediction worth holding on to: refusing to bless a mechanism would not stop tracking, it would "force people to create forms of session-id which you can't regulate".

The rival who wrote the standard

By December 1995 there were three proposals in circulation (Behlendorf's, Kristol's and Montulli's) and an HTTP working group at the IETF with more urgent things to do. Its co-chair, Masinter, asked the interested parties to go away and come back with one. Kristol agreed to lead the group, which grew from three people to eight, Montulli among them.

Kristol is candid about what Kristol wanted: "frankly, I hoped my State-Info proposal would prevail." It did not survive the first weeks. Netscape's mechanism was already deployed, in browsers and in servers, and anything new would have to coexist with it, so the group gave up on simpler designs and took on the job of tightening up Montulli's specification, which Kristol found fuzzy.

The hole behind the inline image

On a conference call late that December, the group started talking about cookies that arrive with inline images. A page from one site can pull its pictures from another, and the second server can set and read cookies of its own. If the same second server supplies pictures to a thousand sites, it sees you on all of them. Kristol's phrase for it is that they "had stumbled onto" third-party cookies.

The person who saw where it led was Koen Holtman, a Dutch participant whose comments had already pushed Kristol into adding privacy sections to the State-Info drafts. Holtman worked out that third-party cookies could be used to build profiles, and persuaded the group that Europeans, at least, would be very troubled by it: an EU directive of October 1995 already called for informed consent before personal data was collected. Here is the part that changed my picture. The group's motive, Kristol writes, "was not advertising networks (which at best we were only dimly aware of at that time)". DoubleClick was incorporated in January 1996 and, by Kristol's footnote, did not come up in the group's discussions until June. The rule was written against a theory.

The February 1996 draft took Holtman's wording nearly verbatim, and it survived into RFC 2109. A request the user did not choose and could not have checked first, such as an image the browser fetches on its own, is an "unverifiable transaction", and on one of those a browser must neither send nor accept cookies unless the other server falls inside a domain that the page the user asked for has already exchanged a cookie for. Then comes the sentence the fight was about:

User agents may offer configurable options that allow the user agent, or any autonomous programs that the user agent executes, to ignore the above rule, so long as these override options default to "off".

That same month, on 12 February 1996, the Financial Times ran the story that Kesan and Shah, in a 2004 law-journal study, credit with telling the public that cookies existed. I could not open it, and nothing I read says whether the newspaper and the committee knew about each other.

Montulli was in the room for all of it, and on the cautious side. In June 1996, when someone argued for a new feature that would let cookies spread more widely, on the grounds that privacy could be subverted by other means anyway, he told the working group he was with Holtman. Privacy might be subverted in other ways, but "I do not want to be a party to making it trivially easy." The IETF's steering group thought the draft too soft, if anything: it relied on a sophisticated user reading the page's HTML to see where requests would go, and the steering group would accept View Source as a privacy control only as the bare minimum. It approved the document on 2 December 1996. RFC 2109 came out in February 1997, by D. Kristol of Bell Laboratories and L. Montulli of Netscape Communications.

Ninety-nine percent of the population

The RFC was announced on 18 February 1997, and two things went wrong with it at once.

The first was a bug. The new standard reused Netscape's header names and added attributes, on the assumption that old browsers would skip what they did not understand. The previous October, Holtman had tested that assumption. A server sent this:

Set-cookie: xx="1=2\&3-4";
Comment="blah";
Version=1; Max-Age=15552000; Path=/;
Expires=Sun, 27 Apr 1997 01:16:23 GMT

Navigator 3 sent back Cookie: xx="1=2\&3-4". Internet Explorer 3 sent back Cookie: Max-Age=15552000, which is an attribute and not the cookie. The two major browsers could not be sent the same standard cookie. Kristol was circulating a corrected draft on 17 February, hoping to swap it for the one in the publication queue, when "events overtook our plan" and the flawed one was published the next day.

The second was that the theory now had an industry living inside it. On 13 March, Dwight Merriman of DoubleClick told the working group that the default was the whole game: switching the feature off by default "is basically equivalent to not allowing them at all, because 99% of the population will see no reason to change the default". Others replied, in Kristol's summary, that the default would by no means disable advertising networks, only the business models that depended on third-party cookies. Sixty-nine messages later, inside a week, Masinter called a halt so that HTTP/1.1 could get some attention.

Then the browsers answered, by doing nothing. Netscape's own documentation for its networking library, a page signed by Judson Valeski in 1998, says that version 4 and later let a user refuse what it calls "foreign cookies", and that none of Netscape's browsers complied with RFC 2109. The option existed. Kristol records which way it pointed: the vendors left third-party cookies enabled by default.

Kristol's paper does not say who decided that. Montulli's 2013 post does:

In the end the decision to disable 3rd party cookies or keep them on was left to me. I agonized about the decision for weeks and in the end I chose to keep them.

Why the default lost

The calendar did a lot of it. Kristol's reckoning is that the document was essentially complete seven months after the group began and then took seven more to be published. When they started, in December 1995, Navigator dominated, Internet Explorer barely existed and advertising networks scarcely did. Fourteen months later Internet Explorer was a serious competitor, e-commerce was blossoming and the networks were common, and a rule drafted against a theory arrived as what the networks felt, in Kristol's phrase, was "a dagger aimed at the heart of their business".

Money did the rest, in Kristol's opinion, and I think it's a fair one. Both browser makers were giving the browser away and selling servers. The people buying servers wanted advertising, and the networks wanted targeting. Vendors were going to listen to "their paying customers, not the people who got programs for free."

And Montulli had a reason that was not about money. A company able to track people across a large part of the web would have to be large and visible, and cookies can be seen, so the public would have a way to push back. Take third-party cookies away and the advertisers would switch to something with less visibility and control: "We would be trading out one problem for another." It is Thau's 1995 prediction, made by the person who says the switch was his.

My own view is that the first half of that bet failed and the second half has never been disproved. People could look at their cookies, and in time could refuse the foreign ones, and almost nobody did: a 2001 study Kristol cites found users rejecting fewer than 1% of cookies across more than a billion page views. Merriman's arithmetic worked in both directions: whichever way the default pointed, that is where 99% of the population would stay.

What the cookie default cost

The standard was the thing that got withdrawn. Kristol and Montulli fixed the compatibility bug with new headers, Set-Cookie2 and Cookie2, in RFC 2965, which sat with the steering group for two years and came out in October 2000. In April 2011 RFC 6265, by A. Barth, said so officially: of the Netscape page and the two RFCs, "none of these documents describe how the Cookie and Set-Cookie headers are actually used on the Internet." It asked for both RFCs to be marked Historic, deprecated the 2 headers, and wrote down what browsers did. On third-party cookies it declined to endorse any policy at all.

Something close to the default the RFC asked for reached a mainstream browser twenty-three years later. On 24 March 2020 WebKit announced that Safari, after three years of tightening restrictions, now blocked cross-site cookies by default "across the board". By WebKit's own account only the Tor Browser had done it fully before.

Chrome set out to follow, and stopped. Two months before Safari's move, its engineers said they would phase third-party cookies out within two years, though not by simply blocking them, because "blunt approaches to cookies encourage the use of opaque techniques such as fingerprinting". That is the argument Montulli says he made to himself in the 1990s. In July 2024 Google proposed asking users to choose instead. In April 2025 it dropped the prompt too and kept things as they were, and that October it retired most of the replacement technologies it had built for the purpose.

The standard that replaced RFC 2109 concedes the other side's point. Blocking third-party cookies often fails, RFC 6265 says, because two cooperating servers can track a user with no cookies at all, "by injecting identifying information into dynamic URLs." I'd call that Pathfinder's trick, sixteen years on.

The takeaway

The cookie beat its rivals because it was already in the browser when the argument started, and the rule against third-party cookies lost for the same reason: third-party cookies were already in the browser too. In between sat fourteen months in which a committee that found the problem before it had properly heard of the advertisers was overtaken by them. I came away thinking the standard was right and that it hardly matters. On the web the default is set by whoever ships, at the moment they ship, and a document written afterwards can only describe it or be ignored.

Nobody in this story was careless. Montulli refused a browser-wide identifier in 1994 because it could track people, sided with Holtman in 1996, signed the rule in 1997, and somewhere in those years weighed it against an advertising-funded web and something worse than cookies, and kept the hole open on purpose. You can think that was the wrong call and still see that it was a call. Cookie: CUSTOMER=WILE_E_COYOTE still fits the grammar in RFC 6265, and the shop it is sent to is still not the difficulty. Mr Coyote's trouble was always the thing arriving from somewhere he wasn't looking.

Sources and further reading

  • Persistent Client State: HTTP Cookies, Preliminary Specification, Netscape, undated, in the copy kept by the curl project (archived)
  • The reasoning behind Web Cookies, Lou Montulli, 2013 (archived)
  • Why blocking 3rd party cookies could be a bad thing, Lou Montulli, 2013 (archived)
  • HTTP Cookies: Standards, Privacy, and Politics, David M. Kristol, 2001 (archived)
  • Session tracking, Brian Behlendorf, www-talk, 17 April 1995
  • Re: Session tracking, Dave Kristol, www-talk, 18 April 1995
  • Re: Session tracking, Lou Montulli, www-talk, 18 April 1995 (the cookie proposal)
  • Re: Session tracking, Lou Montulli, www-talk, 19 April 1995 (the shopping basket)
  • Re: Session tracking, Lou Montulli answering Larry Masinter, www-talk, 20 April 1995
  • Re: Shopping baskets (was: Session tracking), Lou Montulli answering Paul Burchard, www-talk, 21 April 1995
  • Re: Shopping baskets (was: Session tracking), Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 22 April 1995
  • Session-Id vs. Cookies, Paul Burchard, www-talk, 26 July 1995 (archived)
  • session-ids here now, with *all* the problems., Robert S. Thau, www-talk, 26 July 1995
  • Re: "1:n domain cookies" issue status, Lou Montulli, ietf-http-wg, 17 June 1996 (archived)
  • RFC 2109: HTTP State Management Mechanism, D. Kristol and L. Montulli, 1997 (archived)
  • RFC 2965: HTTP State Management Mechanism, D. Kristol and L. Montulli, 2000 (archived)
  • RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism, A. Barth, 2011 (archived)
  • Deconstructing Code, Jay P. Kesan and Rajiv C. Shah, Yale Journal of Law and Technology, 2004 (archived)
  • netlib Cookies, Judson Valeski, Mozilla, 1998 (archived)
  • Full Third-Party Cookie Blocking and More, John Wilander, WebKit, 2020 (archived)
  • Building a more private web: A path towards making third party cookies obsolete, Justin Schuh, Chromium Blog, 2020 (archived)

  • "This Bug in Your PC is a Smart Cookie", Tim Jackson, Financial Times, 12 February 1996: cited by Kesan and Shah, not opened and not linked

item.title: IMG: the tag that shipped mid-argument
item.description: In February 1993 Marc Andreessen proposed an image tag that already worked in Mosaic; Tim Berners-Lee and others answered with more general designs, Mosaic 0.10 shipped IMG seventeen days later, and the losing ideas came back as ALT, ISMAP and the wording of the standard.
item.content:encoded:
The web's picture tag was proposed late on a Thursday in February 1993, in a mailing-list message that mentioned near the bottom that the thing already worked.

I'd like to propose a new, optional HTML tag:

IMG

Required argument is SRC="url".

That is the top of "proposed new tag: IMG", sent to the www-talk list by Marc Andreessen of the National Center for Supercomputing Applications, with a header dated February 25, 1993, 21:09 Pacific time. Further down comes the sentence that settles most of what follows: "This is required functionality for X Mosaic; we have this working, and we'll at least be using it internally." It is followed at once by an invitation to anyone with a better idea to say so.

People did. I knew the outline, as most web developers do: Andreessen proposed, Tim Berners-Lee would have preferred something else, Mosaic shipped, the end. What I had not understood until I read the thread is how many better ideas arrived, how quickly, and from whom. Two other browsers already had picture markup of their own. Berners-Lee's alternative was specific enough to type in. And within a week the tag's own author was wondering on the list whether the real answer was something else entirely.

Pictures in a separate window

HTML had no picture element to argue about. The list of tags preserved in the W3C's copy of the project's pages from November 1992 has titles, anchors, headings and lists, and in the copy I opened the words "image" and "IMG" do not appear.

That did not mean a browser could not show you a GIF. The release notes for Mosaic 0.9, posted a week after the IMG proposal, show how it was done at the time. They list ten kinds of file as recognised automatically, GIF, JPEG, MPEG and PostScript among them, and give the mechanism in four words: "Pipe to external viewers". There is a setting called gifViewerCommand, and its default is xv. You followed a link, and a different program opened a different window with the picture in it.

The same notes call that arrangement a temporary hack and promise "inlined" multimedia later. The word doing the work is "inlined". Putting the picture in the middle of the text, where the author wanted it, was the missing piece, and it needed markup that HTML did not have.

Three browsers, three picture tags

Andreessen's proposal is short and practical. It gives one example:

<IMG SRC="file://foobar.com/foo/bar/blargh.xbm">

There is no closing tag. Put the tag inside an anchor and it becomes a clickable icon, which means the clickable image is as old as the image. On formats the message shrugs: browsers get to choose, with XBM and XPM, the X Window System's bitmap and pixmap files, suggested as good ones to support. GIF is not mentioned. Andreessen knew this was a hole and said the only course was to "wait for the perfect solution to come along (MIME, someday, maybe)."

The first reply is the one that surprised me. About two hours later, if its header's "PDT" is a slip for Pacific time, Tony Johnson of SLAC wrote that much the same thing existed in another browser, Midas 2.0, which was in use at SLAC and "due for public release any week now". Midas spelled it like this:

<ICON name="NoEntry" href="http://note/foo/bar/NoEntry.xbm">

The extra name let a browser use a built-in picture instead of fetching one, and Johnson thought it could also hint to a line-mode browser what symbol to print in the picture's place. That is a first sketch of a problem nobody would properly pick up for almost seven months. Johnson mildly preferred the name ICON and cared more about agreement: "it would be sensible if we used the same things."

The same message carries a second idea. Johnson also wanted an <INCLUDE HREF="..."> tag for Midas, to drop one document into another, pictures of any size included, and offered a variant written as an ordinary anchor with an extra word in it, so that browsers that didn't understand would simply show the link.

The next evening Pei Wei reported that Viola was in a similar position: it had "a number of bitmap tags, but for a DTD other than HTML", kept apart so as not to make a mess of HTML. So three browser authors had each arrived at picture markup, one inside NCSA, one unreleased at SLAC, one outside HTML, and the question in front of the list was whose spelling everybody would use.

Berners-Lee's link that embeds

Tim Berners-Lee answered just under eight hours after the proposal, and the answer was that no new tag was needed. A figure was a kind of link:

<a name=fig1 href="fghjkdfghj"  REL="EMBED, PRESENT">Figure </a>

EMBED meant put the thing here when showing it. PRESENT meant fetch it without waiting to be asked. A browser that understood neither word would show an ordinary link reading "Figure", and nothing broke, which is the advantage Johnson's anchor variant had pointed to the night before. The message spots its own weakness, that a clickable icon would mean one anchor nested inside another, and ends that thought with "Hmmm. But I hadn't wanted a special tag."

A second message later that day makes a case I found more interesting than I expected. The reader, not the author, might want to choose which figures open inline and which in a separate window, and a link with switches leaves that choice open. It also imagines anchors carrying x,y coordinates inside a picture, which is the image map, described before the image had shipped. And it closes with the objection that was really about procedure: "I don't want to change HTML now if I can help it, until it has gone to RFC track".

Andreessen's reply agrees, "in all cases", and then explains why it would happen anyway: browsers were going to implement inline pictures whether or not they were standard, so it would be better to agree on one form first.

A second objection came from the other direction. Jay Weber of Enterprise Integration Technologies had no quarrel with pictures but did not want "idiosyncratic hooks for media one at a time", and asked what had become of the plan to use MIME types. Dave Raggett of HP Labs seconded that message on March 1. Weber, in a follow-up, predicted where one-off tags would lead: next week, somebody would propose an AUD tag for audio.

Then Berners-Lee moved. On February 27 a message conceded that HTML2 should have something for inclusion, and saw no reason to limit it to images. On March 2, in a single sentence, the no-special-tag position was gone: "Let the IMG tag be INCLUDE and let it refer to an arbitrary document type." Five days in, the inventor of HTML had accepted a dedicated tag, under the name Johnson had floated, and was asking only that it be general. Andreessen, meanwhile, was wondering aloud whether the list should instead be designing a graphics language with links in it, something between PostScript and CGM. The author of IMG was not, at that moment, its strongest advocate.

The decision and Mosaic 0.10

The thread went quiet for ten days. Then, on the night of March 12, Andreessen came back to it with a release nearly ready and three decisions made.

We're not prepared to support INCLUDE/EMBED at this point; it raises a number of nasty issues that are quite separate from the idea of inlined images. For example, what happens if one EMBEDS a document that in turn EMBEDS the first document? Oops.

That disposed of generality. The name went next, and the reason was Andreessen's own: it would be IMG and not ICON, because not every inlined image could sensibly be called an icon. The format question was answered by the code. Inlined images would carry no content type for now, and it did not matter, because Mosaic's image routines worked out the format by reading the file.

The loop objection lasted a few hours. Guido van Rossum, writing from CWI in Amsterdam, called it an author's error that a browser should detect, at the cost of keeping a stack of nested embeds. Andreessen's answer fell back to performance and to principle, and contains the most candid parenthesis in the thread. A document pieced together from other documents, it says, "essentially throws the single-hop principle of WWW out the door (well, IMG does that too, but for a very specific reason and in a very limited sense)". My gloss on "single-hop" is that a page had been one fetch. Andreessen conceded that IMG already bent that, and held that the bend was small.

Within a day the argument was over, because the software was out. Mosaic 0.10 was announced on March 14, 1993, seventeen days after the proposal by the calendar, in notes signed "Marc & Eric" for Andreessen and Eric Bina. The first item is support for the IMG tag, which "Handles X bitmap and GIF formats so far". So GIF, which the proposal never mentioned, was in, and XPM, which it recommended, is not on the list. A new setting, colorsPerInlinedImage, capped the colours a picture could use at a default of 50. Three days later version 0.11 fixed bitmaps showing in the wrong colours on X servers that weren't SGI's.

Why the general answer lost

The first force is the plain one: working code on a short cycle. Mosaic put out three releases in under two weeks, on March 4, 14 and 17. The list took five days to converge on the principle of inclusion and had not started on its syntax.

The second is that every general design leaned on things that were not there yet. Johnson's plan for typing images was to use the file extension until "HTTP2 comes along". Wei wanted MIME identifiers. And in the middle of March van Rossum could still ask, in a postscript, whether there was any consensus on how the web should use MIME, and get the answer from Andreessen that Mosaic handed files ending in .mime to an external program and that beyond that nobody was sure. The general tag needed a way to say what a thing was. The specific tag needed code that could tell a GIF from a bitmap by looking at it.

The third is that there was no process to lose to. Berners-Lee did not want HTML changed until it was on the RFC track, and Wei agreed that "HTML should stay stable". Nobody declared a freeze, and on March 10 Berners-Lee told the list the specs were headed towards an Internet Draft. But I'd argue the wish had an unintended effect: while the document was being held steady, and with no procedure for amending it that I can find in the thread, the only place a new feature could happen that month was inside a browser.

The fourth is the one I think gets left out of the usual telling: the rivals didn't fight. Johnson didn't much care about tag names. Wei had no particular preference either. Jim Davis of Cornell summed up the mood: "I am indifferent to the syntax, so long as we get a standard." The people who might have defended ICON or a Viola tag wanted one answer more than they wanted theirs. In fairness to both sides, Andreessen asked before shipping, and the worry about pages assembled from many fetches was not a silly one. Equally, van Rossum was right that the loop was cheap to catch, and Weber's worry would be echoed years later in the HTML specification itself.

ISMAP, ALT and the text browsers

Two months later the pattern repeated, and this time its author described it better than I can. On May 18, 1993, Andreessen pre-announced that Mosaic 1.1 would support ISMAP, an attribute credited to Tony Sanders that, going by a description quoted on the list that June, sent the coordinates of a click on an image to the server:

I realize that this is another unplanned change that I'm making without getting a consensus or having it added to the spec or whatever. I also realize that, as with the IMG tag, it may be used fairly widely in documents on the net even though it's not part of the HTML spec, possibly making those documents not as friendly to other browsers (although I hear the next Midas will support this, and really, it's not that complex to add to an existing image-capable browser).

One of the three reasons given is that there was no other way to get the effect, for want of a "CGM-style hypermedia graphics description language". The grand idea from March had become the excuse for the small attribute in May.

Note the qualifier in that parenthesis: easy for an image-capable browser. The ones with no graphics at all had to wait. In June, Lou Montulli of Lynx, the text browser, described how Lynx might ask a server for a text description in place of a picture, and admitted there had been no time yet to make Lynx aware of images. The fix reached the list on September 21, 1993, almost seven months after the proposal, when frans van hoesel described an attribute used "as suggested to me by Lou", which I take to mean Montulli:

<img src="some_url" alt="some title">

The text would appear on line-mode browsers in place of the default, which was the word IMAGE in square brackets. Van hoesel had already put it on a page and asked the list three questions at once: "can I use this tag, should I, will it be part of HTML+". Raggett offered something more ambitious, an IMG with an end tag whose contents were the description, links and all. The attribute won anyway, for the reason IMG had: by October 15, Dale Dougherty of O'Reilly's Global Network Navigator could report that Lynx supported it and that GNN was using it on its navigation icons.

The same message shows how far things had moved in under eight months. Dougherty had complaints from users of older text browsers and had to tell them the documents would not be changed to suit. The remedy Dougherty proposed, and it was only one publisher's proposal, was to grade browsers. Level 0 was original HTML, and Level 1 "Supports HTML extensions introduced by Mosaic such as the IMG tag." The optional tag had become the first rung.

What survives of the 1993 arguments

The standard, when it came, described the tag in Berners-Lee's terms. HTML 2.0, RFC 1866, is dated November 1995 and says of itself that it roughly corresponds to HTML "in common use prior to June 1994", which is a polite way of saying it wrote down what browsers did. But look at how it words the element: IMG "refers to an image or icon via a hyperlink", and a later section lets such hyperlinks be followed without the user asking and their results embedded where the tag stands. That is EMBED and PRESENT in a specification's vocabulary. My reading is that the people who lost the syntax kept the model. There is even a note advising that an essential graphic be referenced from an anchor and not from IMG.

Raggett's end tag came back twice, and the person who proposed it also wrote a spec that entrenched its rival. Raggett's HTML+ paper has a FIG element whose contents are shown only on non-graphical displays. The HTML 4.01 specification has OBJECT, with fallback text inside it, and a sentence Weber could have written: IMG and APPLET "fail to solve the more general problem of how to include new and future media types." Between the two came HTML 3.2, a W3C Recommendation of January 14, 1997 with Raggett named as author, in which IMG goes from the four attributes of HTML 2.0 to ten. The general element was specified; the specific one is what pages kept using, as far as I can judge.

ALT stayed optional through two versions of the standard. In the HTML 2.0 definition SRC is required and ALT is not. HTML 3.2 calls ALT "vital for interoperability with speech-based and text only user agents" and, a few lines away, leaves it optional in exactly the same way. Only in the HTML 4.01 definition is it marked required. The current HTML standard has since caught up with Raggett in its wording if not its syntax: the alt text "is the img element's fallback content".

And the one required argument is no longer strictly required. The proposal's third line made SRC mandatory. The current standard says: "At least one of the src and srcset attributes must be present." Somewhere in the three decades since, the tag gained a second attribute for offering several files to suit different screens, with the browser doing the choosing. I read that as a modest cousin of the format negotiation Raggett asked for on March 1, 1993.

The takeaway

IMG won because it was the smallest thing that worked and it was in a release seventeen days after it was proposed. In the thread the careful designers get their hearing: their objections were mostly correct, and the person shipping the hack agreed with a fair number of them. Several of them, Andreessen included, wrote as though something more general was on its way. General solutions did arrive, and the stopgap absorbed them instead: the fallback text became an attribute, the hypergraphics became an attribute, the link model became a paragraph in the RFC.

My own conclusion is narrower than "shipping beats talking", and it is a judgment, not something any message says. I think the argument was lost while HTML was being held steady for the RFC track with no procedure yet in sight, because that left a browser release as the only ballot. The example from that Thursday night would still be recognised as an image element now: no closing tag, one source, pointing at a bitmap called blargh on a host called foobar.com that was, I assume, never expected to answer.

Sources and further reading

  • proposed new tag: IMG, Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 1993 (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Tony Johnson, www-talk, 1993 (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Tim Berners-Lee, www-talk, 1993 (the EMBED, PRESENT reply) (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Jim Davis, www-talk, 1993 (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Tim Berners-Lee, www-talk, 1993 (the longer reply) (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Jay C. Weber, www-talk, 1993 (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 1993
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Jay C. Weber, www-talk, 1993 (the AUD prediction) (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Pei Y. Wei, www-talk, 1993 (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Tim Berners-Lee, www-talk, 1993 ("something for inclusion") (archived)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Dave Raggett, www-talk, 1993
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 1993 (PostScript and CGM)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Tim Berners-Lee, www-talk, 1993 ("Let the IMG tag be INCLUDE")
  • NCSA Mosaic for X 0.9 released, Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, www-talk, 1993
  • World-Wide Web documentation in paper form, Tim Berners-Lee, www-talk, 1993
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 1993 (the decision)
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Guido van Rossum, www-talk, 1993
  • Re: proposed new tag: IMG, Marc Andreessen, www-talk, 1993 (the single-hop principle)

item.title: X-UA-Compatible: the default that lasted 42 days
item.description: In January 2008 Microsoft, with help from web standards advocates, proposed that IE8 should render like IE7 unless a page opted in with a meta tag; the standards world turned on itself, Microsoft reversed the default 42 days later, and the tag's discouraged value, IE=edge, ended up in the templates anyway.
item.content:encoded:
On December 3, 2014, the HTML specification finally acknowledged a line that had been turning up at the top of web pages since 2008, and the check-in comment on the change ran to six words.

With great reluctance, admit X-UA-Compatible exists.

That is revision r8870 of the WHATWG's HTML spec, as recorded in the bug that asked for it. The thing being admitted is a meta tag, and the admission was as narrow as the comment sounds: about four weeks earlier the validator had been changed to accept the tag with one value, IE=edge, and to reject any other.

You may know the line as furniture: it came with the template and told Internet Explorer something. What I had not understood until I did the reading is that it is what's left of a row that ran for forty-two days in early 2008, after Microsoft proposed that IE8 should go on behaving like IE7 unless a page asked for better. The proposal was written with the help of web standards advocates, and the people who attacked it hardest were other web standards advocates. And the value that ended up in the templates was the one the tag's first write-up had marked "strongly discouraged".

What IE7 broke

Since about 2000, browsers had offered two rendering modes and chosen between them by reading the top of the page. In "Beyond DOCTYPE", Aaron Gustafson credits the idea to Todd Fahrner in 1998 and its first implementation to IE5 for the Mac two years later. A complete, current DOCTYPE got a page standards mode. Anything else got quirks mode, laid out the way IE5 for Windows had done it. The switch worked because, at first, only people who cared about standards wrote a DOCTYPE at all.

Chris Wilson, IE's platform architect, later put a number on that. In a post on the IE team's blog, Wilson says that when IE6 shipped in 2001 the team ran a report on the top 200 websites and found less than 1% of them in standards mode. Gustafson names what changed. IE6's rendering went five years without an update, so developers came to treat it as fixed, and the makers of authoring tools began putting complete DOCTYPEs into everything they generated, "egged on by A List Apart and The Web Standards Project". That was the first thing I did not expect: the standards campaign's own success helped wear out the switch it relied on, and the admission ran in A List Apart.

By the time IE7 shipped in late 2006, Wilson writes, roughly half of the top 200 US sites were in standards mode, opted in by a tool or by people trying to do the right thing, who had then worked around IE6's faults until the page looked correct. IE7 fixed a good many of those faults, in standards mode only, on the theory that the switch would contain the damage. It didn't, to the team's surprise, and the pages adjusted to fit the faults broke. The team's rule, through six major versions by Wilson's count, had been "Don't Break the Web". The post rewrites it as a longer and sadder one: don't change what developers expect IE to do for pages that are already deployed.

IE8 was going to be a much bigger change. On December 19, 2007, the general manager of Internet Explorer, Dean Hachamovitch, announced that a week earlier IE8 had correctly rendered Acid2, the Web Standards Project's test page. The same post set the goal of getting there "without breaking the existing web". Gustafson's article says how Microsoft set about having both: it asked the Web Standards Project, and a few other standards-minded developers, for help.

The opt-in for IE8

The answer came out on January 21, 2008, in two places at once. Wilson's post, "Compatibility and IE8", gave the summary in three bullets: quirks mode stays as it is; standards mode "remains the same as IE7"; and a developer who really wants the best IE8 can do may ask for it. Gustafson's article, in issue 251 of A List Apart, showed how to ask:

<meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=8" />

The tag had to sit near the top of the head, and a server could send the same thing as an HTTP header for a whole site. The task force called the idea version targeting: a page names the browser version it was tested in, and every later version of that browser undertakes to behave like it. A page that named nothing would be treated as tested in IE7, and Gustafson later spelled out for how long: it would render as IE7 "even if the site was being viewed on IE8, IE9, or IE1000."

Two details matter later. The syntax was built for more than one browser, with an example value of IE=8;FF=3;OtherUA=4, and Gustafson hoped other vendors would join in. And under "Extra credit" there was a keyword, IE=edge, which asked for whatever the newest engine happened to be. The article discourages it for anything but experimental sites, since "even Eric Meyer can't predict layout or scripting bugs that may be accidentally introduced by a new browser version."

Gustafson's own reason was not quite Microsoft's, and I find it the most sympathetic way in. The article describes a panel on digital preservation and asks whether reading a page built for IE6 will one day mean keeping a copy of IE6. Seen from there, the tag is an archivist's tool.

Standardistas against standardistas

The same issue carried a second piece, by Eric Meyer, called "From Switches to Targets: A Standardista's Journey". It opens with Meyer's first reaction, that the mechanism was "just wrong, completely backwards, the exact opposite of what we ought to be doing", and looked like browser sniffing coming back with a vendor's blessing. Then the piece argues itself round: sniffing asks a page to guess at future browsers, targeting asks a browser to remember a past one, and the past is easier to predict.

Meyer's own site carried a less settled note that day. Meyer had come round only after arguing with Gustafson on the magazine's editorial board, and had also argued against the IE7 default with a member of the IE team, and lost: "I couldn't make what I wanted square with their requirements, and came to see that I couldn't, and was deeply saddened by it."

So the proposal arrived with its doubts attached, and more came within a day. The Web Standards Project published a note by Drew McLellan saying that not every member backed the proposal. At the W3C, Karl Dubost's list of responses grew to seventeen links, one of them titled <META HTTP-EQUIV="X-BALL-CHAIN">. John Resig, of jQuery, went after the multi-browser syntax in "Meta Madness". No other vendor had helped design the tag, Resig wrote, and none could adopt it without hauling its old engines around. Resig's summary: "A shiv for jamming standards support into future versions of Internet Explorer."

The sharpest objection was also the politest. Jeremy Keith had no quarrel with the tag, only with what happened in its absence, and made the case a month later in A List Apart, in "They Shoot Browsers, Don't They?" Keith had asked Wilson directly what IE8 would do with a valid page under a strict DOCTYPE, and was told it would behave exactly like its predecessor. The article's opening has the line I'd keep from the whole row: "the only way to opt out of using the technology is, perversely, to use it."

Meanwhile anyone who just wanted IE8's engine already had a recipe. Dubost's list credits Sam Ruby with two lines of Apache configuration that put the discouraged keyword on every response sent to IE:

BrowserMatch MSIE best-standards-support
Header set X-UA-Compatible IE=edge env=best-standards-support

The case for acting like IE7

It would be easy to tell this as a company protecting its old mistakes. The defenders deserve better, and they had four arguments.

The first was about who pays. A site that breaks in a new browser gets fixed by its developer, but the person who meets the broken page is a reader with no way to know whose fault it is. Wilson's post speaks of half a billion users and says the team could not break existing sites "for users like my mom", however good the reason.

The second was that some pages have nobody left to fix them: pages burned onto a CD, as an unsigned reply in the comments under Wilson's post pointed out, and above all the company intranet, built for one browser and never opened in another. When three Web Standards Project members held a call with Wilson on February 16, one idea on the table was a patch to IIS that would mark every site it served as an IE7 site, to spare the intranets.

The third was script, and for anyone who has this filed as a quarrel about CSS, it changes the picture. In "Version Targeting: Threat or Menace?", which ran opposite Keith's piece, Jeffrey Zeldman, A List Apart's publisher, pointed out that IE8 was also due to overhaul its DOM support and drop conflicting JScript behaviour:

While the CSS changes in IE7 may have "broken" a site's layout, IE8's JavaScript improvements could easily render a site useless.

The fourth was one nobody at Microsoft said in public. Zeldman had defended the default that first week, arguing that if IE8 broke enough sites, the complaints might, "in the hands of the wrong director of marketing", cost the standards-minded engineers on the IE team their jobs. That is Zeldman's fear, and I have seen nothing that reports it as fact. But it explains why standards campaigners were defending a default that ignored them: they thought the alternative was an IE that gave up.

Keith's reply to the whole case was to ask for evidence. What was at stake, the article says, was "some websites" displaying differently in one browser, and how much that mattered was a matter of faith until somebody measured. So measure: ship a beta of IE8 with the new engine on by default and see what breaks. If the damage turned out to be real, Keith promised to back the IE7 default.

Forty-two days

On March 3, 2008, forty-two days after Wilson's post, Hachamovitch published a new one. It began:

We've decided that IE8 will, by default, interpret web content in the most standards compliant way it can. This decision is a change from what we've posted previously.

The tag survived with its meaning turned over. Pages in standards mode would get IE8's engine, and a site that needed IE7's would have to ask. Zeldman reported the next day that developers from Microsoft had phoned round before the announcement, and listed the readings on offer: Microsoft had caved, or had listened, or meant what it said.

What it said is the second thing I did not expect. The post credits feedback from the community, but its headline reason is a set of Interoperability Principles the company had recently published (Meyer dates them to February 21). Then comes a sentence of a kind a browser team's blog rarely carries: "While we do not believe any current legal requirements would dictate which rendering mode a browser must use, this step clearly removes this question as a potential legal and regulatory issue."

InformationWeek pointed out that the reversal followed an 899 million euro antitrust fine, and that Microsoft's press release gave nearly the same sentence to Brad Smith, the company's general counsel. Meyer's reading that day was that the IE team "seems to have used recent Microsoft PR efforts to their, and our, advantage", and in the comments Meyer added that the IE7 default had never been the team's first choice. My best guess is that six weeks of argument made the case and the lawyers' sentence made it winnable, but it is a guess.

Meyer was glad, and worried that once a public beta showed how many sites broke, the default would flip back.

The beta and the button

Two days later, at Microsoft's MIX conference, IE8 Beta 1 went out to developers, with the new engine as the default. That was the experiment Keith had asked for, and Joel Spolsky wrote up a result. "Martian Headsets", published on March 17, declines to take a side, on the grounds that the IE team had been asked to walk "a line of negative width". But Spolsky had installed the beta:

Almost every web site I visited with IE8 is broken in some way. Websites that use a lot of JavaScript are generally completely dead.

One person's browsing is a long way from a survey, but it is Zeldman's script argument observed in the wild. Spolsky predicted that Microsoft would run a long beta, find that too little of the web rendered properly, apologise and go back to the IE7 default before shipping.

Microsoft did something more interesting. Beta 1 had an Emulate IE7 button. On August 27, 2008, writing about Beta 2, Scott Dickens of the IE team introduced its replacement, Compatibility View: a button beside the address bar that redrew the current site the way IE7 would have, and remembered the choice for that domain. The team later used telemetry on where the beta's users pressed it, among other feedback, to build a list of sites to show that way unprompted. The list was offered to each user as a choice when the browser first ran.

The Beta 2 post also contains this, under a heading about the enterprise: by default, public sites display in IE8's standards mode "and all intranet websites display in Internet Explorer 7 Standards mode". The January proposal had moved indoors. On office networks, IE8 acted like IE7 unless told otherwise, which is how Wilson's January proposal had worked for every page. A site's owner could overrule all of it with the tag, whose presence, the same post says, also hid the button.

IE8 shipped on March 19, 2009, at the following year's MIX, with its own standards mode as the default for the public web. Spolsky's prediction had missed, and so had Meyer's worry. I'd argue the line turned out to have some width after all, once the default could differ by zone, by site and by user.

Where the meta tag went

The discouraged value became the standard one. Microsoft's own IE8 documentation said that Edge mode "actually breaks the 'lock-in' paradigm" and recommended keeping it to test pages. But the intranet rule and the button gave careful developers a reason to reach for it: without the tag, a page they had tested in IE8 could still be shown as IE7. Version 1.0 of HTML5 Boilerplate, which the project's changelog dates to March 21, 2011, says so in a comment:

  <!-- Always force latest IE rendering engine (even in intranet) & Chrome Frame
       Remove this if you use the .htaccess -->
  <meta http-equiv="X-UA-Compatible" content="IE=edge,chrome=1">

Microsoft's later documentation concedes the point: developers had used the tag to hide the Compatibility View button, and from IE11 the mode IE=edge selects is "the preferred document mode", having been treated as experimental before.

Google borrowed the header. The second half of that Boilerplate line, chrome=1, belongs to Chrome Frame, the plug-in Google released on September 22, 2009 to run Chrome's engine inside Internet Explorer (it has a part in the IE6 funeral). Resig had said no other vendor could usefully adopt Microsoft's tag. Google used it as the switch for a plug-in that swapped out IE's engine. Google announced the plug-in's retirement in June 2013, and Boilerplate 4.3.0 removed the code that September.

The HTML spec held out until 2014. One of the three names on the Chrome Frame announcement was Alex Russell, who wrote to the WHATWG's mailing list that October asking for X- headers to be allowed in http-equiv. Ian Hickson, the spec's editor, answered a few days later: "This would make X-UA-Compatible conforming, which is not desireable." So the line failed validation, as Boilerplate's own documentation warned. In October 2014 Michael[tm] Smith filed the bug this essay opened with, titled "deal with the reality of meta@http-equiv=x-ua-compatible", and about three weeks later changed the validator. The spec followed.

And the DOCTYPE got its old job back. Meyer's January 2008 piece had mentioned, late in the piece, that an HTML5 DOCTYPE might be targeted by default to some later version of IE. Microsoft's documentation from the IE11 years says that document modes are deprecated, recommends the HTML5 DOCTYPE for nearly everything, and describes IE=edge as "functionally equivalent" to it. The switch that Gustafson's article had declared broken was back in service.

The takeaway

The row over IE8 was an argument about who should pay when a browser gets better, and every answer to it was a default. Microsoft's first answer charged the developers who had followed the standards: one line on every page, for ever. The reversal charged everyone else for the length of a beta, then refunded the people least able to pay, with the IE7 default for office networks, a list for popular sites and a button for users. I think both camps were right. A browser that won't use its own engine unless asked has things backwards, as Keith said. And a great many pages that claimed to follow the standards were really following IE, as Wilson said and Spolsky's time with the beta showed.

What the web kept is the rule the objectors were defending, one that had never needed saying: a page that says nothing gets the newest behaviour, and a page that wants the past has to ask for it. When the tag was finally let in, the validator would pass exactly one value, the one that tells IE to use the newest engine it has. Keith's complaint in February 2008 was that the only way to opt out of version targeting was to use it. Nearly seven years later the specification admitted the tag on those terms and no others, with great reluctance.

Sources and further reading

  • Compatibility and IE8, Chris Wilson, IEBlog, 2008 (archived)
  • Beyond DOCTYPE: Web Standards, Forward Compatibility, and IE8, Aaron Gustafson, A List Apart, 2008 (archived)
  • From Switches to Targets: A Standardista's Journey, Eric Meyer, A List Apart, 2008 (archived)
  • Targeted, Eric Meyer, 2008 (archived)
  • Internet Explorer 8 and Acid2: A Milestone, Dean Hachamovitch, IEBlog, 2007 (archived)
  • Microsoft's Version Targeting Proposal, Drew McLellan, The Web Standards Project, 2008 (archived)
  • IE8 versioning snowstorm, Karl Dubost, W3C, 2008 (archived)
  • Meta Madness, John Resig, 2008 (archived)
  • In defense of version targeting, Jeffrey Zeldman, 2008 (archived)
  • They Shoot Browsers, Don't They?, Jeremy Keith, A List Apart, 2008 (archived)
  • Version Targeting: Threat or Menace?, Jeffrey Zeldman, A List Apart, 2008 (archived)
  • WaSP Round Table: IE8's Default Version Targeting Behavior, Aaron Gustafson, The Web Standards Project, 2008 (archived)
  • Microsoft's Interoperability Principles and IE8, Dean Hachamovitch, IEBlog, 2008 (archived)
  • Meta-change, Eric Meyer, 2008 (archived)
  • Microsoft reverses version targeting default, Jeffrey Zeldman, 2008 (archived)
  • Rise And Fall Of Version Targeting In Internet Explorer 8, InformationWeek, 2008
  • Internet Explorer 8 Beta 1 for Developers Now Available, IEBlog, 2008 (archived)
  • Martian Headsets, Joel Spolsky, 2008 (archived)
