item.title: left-pad: the eleven lines npm had to un-unpublish
item.description: Azer Koçulu lost the package name kik to a messaging company, asked npm how to delete everything he had published and was sent the command; when he ran it on March 22, 2016, one of his 273 packages was left-pad, and two and a half hours later npm broke its own rule to put it back.
item.content:encoded:
On the afternoon of March 22, 2016, a seventeen-line file that pads strings with spaces disappeared from the npm registry, and for about two and a half hours a large share of the JavaScript world could not install its own tools.

npm ERR! code E404

That line comes from a Travis CI log that a developer with the handle silkentrance pasted into a new issue on a small GitHub repository that afternoon. The issue is still there, titled "npmjs.org tells me that left-pad is not available (404 page)". Further down the same log, npm explains itself:

npm ERR! 404 'left-pad' is not in the npm registry.
npm ERR! 404 You should bug the author to publish it (or use the name yourself!)
npm ERR! 404 It was specified as a dependency of 'line-numbers'

The middle line is advice, and within fifteen minutes somebody had taken the half of it in brackets. The last line names a package that most of the people staring at this error had never knowingly installed.

The legend has four parts: an angry developer, a trademark lawyer, eleven lines of code, a broken internet. The registry's own records and the accounts from that week tell it differently in three places. The author asked to leave and was handed the command to do it. The eleven lines printed in the news stories were not the version the builds were asking for. And the package name the whole fight was about has, as far as the registry shows, never been used by the company that won it.

Seventeen lines by Azer Koçulu

Here is the whole of index.js from left-pad 0.0.3, taken from the tarball the registry serves:

module.exports = leftpad;

function leftpad (str, len, ch) {
  str = String(str);

  var i = -1;

  ch || (ch = ' ');
  len = len - str.length;


  while (++i < len) {
    str = ch + str;
  }

  return str;
}

That is seventeen lines, eleven of them not blank, which is why the Register's headline said 11 and Ars Technica's said 17. Give it 7, 3 and '0' and you get "007".

Azer Koçulu, a developer then living in Oakland, made the first commit on March 14, 2014 and published three small revisions that August. He wrote a great many modules like it. The Verge counted 273 packages under his name, among them rnd, strip and random-color. The repository's history up to the day of the incident is ten commits long. Only one of them is by somebody else: on May 20, 2015, Steve Mao sent a fix titled "make the third argument work", which Koçulu merged and published as 0.0.4.

Mao's fix matters to this story in a small way. In 0.0.3, the line ch || (ch = ' ') treats a numeric zero as no argument at all, so leftpad(17, 5, 0) pads with spaces. Version 0.0.4 replaced it with if (!ch && ch !== 0) ch = ' ';. I ran both tarballs to check:

leftpad(17, 5, 0)
// 0.0.3 => "   17"
// 0.0.4 => "00017"

The code that the Register printed that night, and that most retellings have printed since, is the 0.0.4 version. The builds that failed were asking for 0.0.3.

They were asking for it because of a package called line-numbers, by Simon Lydell, first published in December 2014. Its package.json named its one dependency exactly: "left-pad": "0.0.3", with no caret and no tilde. That was the newest version at the time. Babel's error-printing module, babel-code-frame, depended on line-numbers, and Babel was by then inside most front-end build chains. The Verge noted it was built into React Native as well.

So a module with, as one critic counted that week, eleven stars on GitHub was being fetched about 100,000 times every weekday and about a third as often at weekends, which is the signature of build servers and not of people. The Register quoted npm's figure of 2,486,696 downloads in the previous month. I added up npm's daily counts for February 21 to March 21 and got the same number to the digit.

Kik asks for the name kik

The dispute began with a different package. Koçulu also owned the name kik, and his versions in the registry still carry his description: "Kickstart your new projects with one command". He had first published it on October 31, 2015.

On March 11, 2016, he got an email from Bob Stratton, a patent agent working for Kik Interactive, the Canadian company behind the Kik messaging app. I could not open the full correspondence, which Kik's Mike Roberts later published on Medium, so I'm relying on the long quotations in Sean Gallagher's report for Ars Technica. Stratton said Kik wanted the name for a package it was about to release, and asked Koçulu to rename his. Koçulu declined. Stratton's second message is the one everybody remembers. It opened by saying Kik didn't mean to be unpleasant about this, in a shorter word than "unpleasant", and went on to say that if the project were released, "our trademark lawyers are going to be banging on your door and taking down your accounts and stuff like that". It ended by asking whether the two of them could compromise without involving lawyers. Koçulu answered in the same vocabulary, told Stratton not to email again and, after one more plea, named a price of $30,000.

Stratton then took the matter to npm's support desk, which is the route npm's dispute policy provides. Isaac Schlueter, who created npm and ran the company, made the call and gave the name to Kik. Schlueter's reasoning, as told to Ars, was that someone who types npm install kik "would expect to get something related to Kik." Wikipedia's account dates that decision to March 18.

Koçulu's reply to Schlueter is the hinge of the whole story. He wrote that he wanted everything gone:

I want all my modules to be deleted including my account, along with this package. I don't wanna be a part of NPM anymore. If you don't do it, let me know how do it quickly.

And npm let him know. Koçulu told Ars that the second email he got from npm "was the founder Isaac giving me a one-liner command that deletes all my stuff". Eight years later, in an essay on his own site, he wrote that npm had answered his request with a script that removed all his packages at once, without naming who sent it, and added that he had set no deadline and waited for a reply. The legend has a developer slamming a door. If these accounts and that date are right, he asked how to leave some days before he left, and the command he ran on Tuesday the 22nd came from npm.

To be fair to npm, its own post-mortem says the transfer would have broken nothing. Under the dispute policy, Koçulu's existing kik versions would have stayed installable and Kik would have published under a new major version. Nobody at npm, and by his account not Koçulu either, seems to have asked what else was on the list of 273.

The afternoon left-pad was gone

The registry stamped it all. All times here are Pacific, converted from the registry's UTC.

At 2:27 PM and 15 seconds, left-pad was unpublished by the user azer. That timestamp survives because a commenter pasted the registry's record into the GitHub issue. Koçulu wrote later that he ran the script and left his desk for a few minutes, and that within ten a friend told him he was on Twitter "for some reason". npm says that shortly after 2:30 it began seeing hundreds of failed installs a minute.

At 2:42 PM, fifteen minutes after the deletion, a left-pad 1.0.0 appeared. Cameron Westland had taken the source from GitHub and published it under the vacant name, which the rules of the day allowed anyone to do. The registry's record of that release has since been rewritten under npm's own account, so the attribution rests on Westland's note in the issue thread, which begins: "Yeah I published a 1.0.0 to try to resolve the dependency." It didn't resolve it. line-numbers wanted 0.0.3 and nothing else, and npm's firmest rule was that a version number, once used, could never be published again. A registry record pasted into the same thread shows the package unpublished again at 2:47, this time by Westland's account, and the registry has a 0.0.9 under that account at 2:51. I read those as a second attempt at a version number that would satisfy the pin. It was still not 0.0.3.

The next repair came from Babel. At 3:12 PM, Sebastian McKenzie published babel-code-frame 6.7.3. Its dependency list is the same as the previous version's with one line removed: line-numbers is gone. Babel had cut itself free of the whole chain 45 minutes after the deletion.

By 3:40, Koçulu's explanation, a Medium post called "I've Just Liberated My Modules", had been submitted to Hacker News. Its most quoted sentence is this one:

This situation made me realize that NPM is someone's private land where corporate is more powerful than the people, and I do open source because, Power To The People.

At 4:05 PM npm announced that it would do the thing its own rule forbade. The Register quotes Laurie Voss, npm's CTO, calling the step "un-un-publishing" and saying the company had chosen the needs of the many over the wishes of one author. npm's post-mortem says the original 0.0.3 was re-published from a backup and that the work was finished by 4:55. Westland explained on Hacker News that evening that the request to restore it had been theirs, as the name's new maintainer, and that npm had checked the restored code was exactly the original, so that nothing could be slipped in.

You can still see the seam. The registry's record for left-pad 0.0.3 lists Westland as its publisher and gives it the same timestamp as 0.0.9, to the millisecond: 2:51 PM on March 22, 2016, two hours before npm says the restore was done. The code file inside the tarball is dated August 15, 2014. The record says the licence is WTFPL, and the package.json inside says BSD.

While that was going on, the other names were being picked up by strangers. At 4:52 PM somebody published a kik 1.0.1 whose description is "Damn you Kik". A Hacker News commenter pointed out that names like map, alert and iframe were now free for anyone to fill with any code they liked, to be run on the next npm install. npm's post-mortem says the other 272 packages were adopted by community members, some as forks and some as empty placeholders put there to keep worse people out.

The next day Kik's Mike Roberts published the emails. The Register quoted his apology for "creating any impression that this was anything more than a polite request", and the Verge noted that Kik's own build had broken on Tuesday along with everyone else's. In the GitHub issue, in a comment GitHub dates March 23, Steve Mao asked for the repository, "since I'm the only other author of the module". Koçulu replied that Mao was the new owner.

Why one pinned package stopped Babel

The argument that week was about size. David Haney's essay "NPM & left-pad: Have We Forgotten How To Program?" went up the day after and collected 1,725 points on Hacker News. Haney had found a one-line isArray package with 18 million downloads in a month, and his verdict on anyone who couldn't write such a function in five minutes was that "you don't actually know how to code."

The other side had been put the summer before, when Sindre Sorhus was asked to justify one-line modules and answered that line count has nothing to do with whether code deserves to be a module. I see four forces behind the outage, and I'd argue size is the weakest of them.

The language had no way to pad a string. That is why the function existed at all, in npm and in every codebase that hadn't heard of npm. The TC39 proposal to add one notes that "nearly every app in FirefoxOS had implemented a left pad function". That proposal was already well along. Its README records that the names padStart and padEnd were settled at the committee's November 2015 meeting, four months before anything went missing.

The dependency was pinned and fetched fresh. An exact version in someone else's package.json, several levels below yours, is invisible until it fails, and the weekday download curve shows how many builds were pulling every package from the registry every time. If left-pad had been five thousand lines long it would have failed in the same way.

Deleting was a right. npm let any author remove any version at any time, for what the post-mortem calls "historical reasons", and a name emptied that way went straight back into the pool. The rule against reusing version numbers, which is a good rule, then guaranteed that nobody outside npm could repair the damage.

And there was one namespace, run by one company, which had to decide who deserved a three-letter word. npm insisted the decision was editorial, not legal. Koçulu's point was that it could be made at all.

Where left-pad, kik and unpublish went

The right to unpublish went to npm's support desk. A week after the outage, on March 29, npm announced that a version more than 24 hours old could no longer be removed by its author; you had to write to support, who would refuse if anything depended on it. A fully removed package would be replaced by a placeholder so that the name could not be squatted. The policy as it reads now is looser on time and stricter on everything else: nothing in the registry may depend on the package in any case, and then you have 72 hours from publishing, or longer only if it had under 300 downloads in the last week and has a single owner.

Padding was approved for the language two months later. The committee's list of finished proposals has string padding, championed by Jordan Harband, reaching stage 4 at the May 2016 meeting and it shipped in ES2017 the following year. The notes of that meeting don't mention left-pad at all. So '7'.padStart(3, '0') now does the job with nothing installed.

left-pad outlived its replacement. Mao took over the package and released 1.1.0 on May 1, 2016. The last version, 1.3.0 from April 2018, pads by doubling the fill string and so does in a handful of steps what the original did one character at a time. Every version in the registry now carries the same deprecation notice, "use String.prototype.padStart()". Its traffic has a strange shape. The day after the outage, downloads fell from about 100,000 to 36,971, which I put down to Babel's fix, and through April and May weekdays ran mostly between 20,000 and 35,000. When I checked npm's counter in mid-November 2026, the deprecated package had been downloaded 2,295,504 times in the previous seven days, which is nearly what it managed in the whole month before it vanished.

The name kik was never used. This is the finding I did not expect. On March 23, 2016, the day after the outage, the registry shows npm publishing a "security" placeholder under the name, with a description saying it "is not currently in use" and that npm will "probably give it to you if you want it." Thirteen days later, on the evening of April 4, Pacific time, Kik published its bot library for Node. It went out as @kikinteractive/kik, under the company's own scope, where no dispute had ever been needed. The registry's record for plain kik lists Kik Interactive as the maintainer, Koçulu's old versions, the stranger's protest release, an empty release from an npm staff account and two placeholders. It lists nothing published by Kik.

Koçulu left, first npm and then more. In the days after the outage he gave his repositories to volunteers. In the 2024 essay he says that a few months later he quit his job, left the United States for good and spent a year travelling, and that the part of him that cared about open source "was gone".

The takeaway

left-pad is remembered as a story about small modules, and I think that is the least of what happened. A company wanted a name. A registry that called itself a community resource turned out to have an owner who could reassign names, and an author who had taken "it's your code" at face value asked for the delete command and got it. The builds broke because of one exact version pin and a rule that made the gap impossible to fill. Then npm set aside that rule the same afternoon and wrote a new one within the week. Under the new rule the code you publish stays published, and whether it can come down is for npm to decide. Koçulu had called the registry someone's private land. npm's answer, in effect, was that it is, and that a build system can't work any other way.

The error message at the top of this essay offered two remedies: bug the author, or use the name yourself. Both were tried within fifteen minutes on March 22, and since the following week the second has required a letter to npm support. The name left-pad is still there, deprecated and fetched a couple of million times a week. The name kik is there too, and what it installs is a placeholder.

Sources and further reading

  • "npmjs.org tells me that left-pad is not available (404 page)", issue 4 on the left-pad repository, opened by silkentrance, March 22, 2016 (archived)
  • npm registry record for left-pad (publish times, publishers, tarballs and the deprecation notice) (archived)
  • npm registry record for kik and for @kikinteractive/kik (archived)
  • npm registry records for line-numbers and babel-code-frame (archived)
  • kik, left-pad, and npm, Isaac Z. Schlueter, npm blog, March 23, 2016 (archived)
  • changes to npm's unpublish policy, npm blog, March 29, 2016 (archived)
  • npm Unpublish Policy, npm documentation, current version (archived)
  • left-pad, Azer Koçulu, June 8, 2024 (archived)
  • "I've Just Liberated My Modules", Azer Koçulu, Medium, March 22, 2016 (not linked: I could not open it)
  • "A discussion about the breaking of the Internet", Mike Roberts, Medium, March 23, 2016 (not linked: I could not open it)
  • Rage-quit: Coder unpublished 17 lines of JavaScript and "broke the Internet", Sean Gallagher, Ars Technica, March 25, 2016 (archived)
  • How one developer just broke Node, Babel and thousands of projects in 11 lines of JavaScript, Chris Williams, The Register, March 23, 2016 (archived)
  • How an irate developer briefly broke JavaScript, Paul Miller, The Verge, March 24, 2016 (archived)
  • Hacker News discussion of "I've Just Liberated My Modules", March 22, 2016, with comments by Cameron Westland and Laurie Voss (archived)
  • NPM & left-pad: Have We Forgotten How To Program?, David Haney, March 23, 2016 (archived)
  • "One-line node modules", question to Sindre Sorhus, July 2015 (archived)
  • String.prototype.padStart / padEnd proposal, Kevin Grandon and Jordan Harband, TC39 (archived)
  • Finished proposals, TC39 (archived)
  • TC39 meeting notes, May 25, 2016 (archived)
  • npm left-pad incident, Wikipedia (archived)

item.title: The tracker that got JavaScript an off switch
item.description: In February 1996 a commuter's demo page showed that Netscape 2.0 let any site watch where you browsed next, and three weeks of public argument with the language's author ended in a patch, a $1,000 prize and the first preference to turn JavaScript off.
item.content:encoded:
In February 1996 a web page could follow you around the web and report each address you visited to a stranger, and the one browser that ran such pages had no setting to stop them.

Remember: We're watching...

That is the last line of a page titled "Real Time History Tracking", written by John Robert LoVerso on February 22, 1996. When I fetched it from LoVerso's own site, it sat much as it was left. Its headline reads "JavaScript in Netscape 2.0 shouldn't let me do this, But it does". A few lines above the sign-off is a link labelled "Invoke the tracker", and further up is a sample of what the tracker collected:

Wed Feb 21 23:34:07 EST 1996
REMOTE_ADDR = xxx.xxx.xx.x
REMOTE_HOST = xxxxxxxxx.com
QUERY_STRING = result=3= http://www.yahoo.com/Business_and_Economy/Companies/Apparel/Lingerie/
HTTP_USER_AGENT = Mozilla/2.0 (X11; I; SunOS 5.4 sun4m)  via proxy gateway  CERN-HTTPD/3.0 libwww/2.17

The page explains that this entry "was from a test a friend did for me". So at 11:34 on a Wednesday night, a friend on a Sun workstation opened a Yahoo category page, and a server at LoVerso's office wrote the address down. The friend knew. The point of the page was that the next person would not.

I came to this page expecting JavaScript's first security hole. It wasn't the first, and LoVerso said so at the time. What it was is odder: the report that, as far as I can tell, did most to get JavaScript an off switch, argued over in public for three weeks by a commuter and the language's author.

JavaScript, fresh out of beta

Netscape and Sun announced JavaScript on December 4, 1995. The language was already in people's hands by then under its earlier name, LiveScript, in the public betas of Navigator 2.0. The finished Navigator 2.0 came out around the start of February 1996; Keith Dawson's newsletter Tasty Bits from the Technology Front, dated February 10, reported it "was released last week on all platforms".

Almost nobody could say what the new thing was. The name suggested a small Java, and Sun's Java was the most carefully examined language of the moment. Dawson's issue of February 19 told readers that if they were confused about the difference "you are not alone", and passed on a report that Netscape already regretted the name. It then reprinted a comparison table adapted from Netscape's own tutorial. The two columns differed on every row but the last:

          JavaScript                            Java
 Secure. Cannot write to hard disk.   Secure. Cannot write to hard disk.

The betas had already put that row in doubt. Netscape ran a contest it called the Bugs Bounty, paying $1,000 for a security bug, and JavaScript kept winning it. In beta 2, Scott Weston found a way for a script to send a transcript of a visitor's whole session back to a page's owner; Dawson called the demonstration "massively scary" and noted it was fixed in beta 3. In January, John Tennyson reported a cluster of bugs with a similar effect, including one that let a script list the directories on your disk. Both were awarded the bounty.

Then 2.0 shipped, and on February 13 LoVerso, a researcher at the OSF Research Institute in Cambridge, told Netscape that Tennyson's directory lister still worked in the finished product. His adapted copy of the exploit survives, credited "Originally By" Tennyson. The trick was to submit a form to a file: address in a new window and then read that window's links. The window was asked to be as small as a window can be:

winopts =
  "toolbar=no,location=no,directories=no,status=no,menubar=no,scrollbars=no," +
  "resizable=no,copyhistory=yes," +
  "width=0,height=0"
;

LoVerso's train ride home

On Wednesday, February 21, LoVerso hit a bug by accident. He had a page whose onload handler put up an alert and then called history.back(), and a user at OSF who visited it found the handler would not go away. LoVerso posted to comp.lang.javascript that morning under the subject "Serious Security Bug":

I have seen a case where JavaScript imported from one page is being executed by the Navigator for EVERY subsequent page it renders.

He couldn't make it happen on demand, which makes for a poor exploit. That afternoon, in Netscape's own newsgroup, the language's author Brendan Eich answered a thread titled "Finding out a user's history?". LoVerso later quoted the reply on the tracker page: the copyhistory option had been disabled in beta 6 "to prevent your session history, with potentially secret keys or other URL query strings, from being stolen by malicious hidden scripts."

LoVerso went home by commuter rail. Somewhere on that ride he worked out that he didn't need the unreliable bug at all. A script that stays in memory after you leave its page is a defect. A script that sits in its own window is just a window, and Navigator 2.0 let a script in one window ask another window where it was.

The tracker's own source is the one piece I could not recover. It was served by a program on an OSF machine, and that address no longer answers. What survives is LoVerso's description, which is exact enough. His script opened a second, "(mostly) hidden" window and stayed there. Then, in his words, "it wakes up every second and sees what page you are viewing", and when the address changed it requested a CGI script on his server with the new address in the query string. That request is the log entry near the top of this essay. The page says the demonstration's windows were left large enough to see, and that a real attack could ask for width=1,height=1.

The timestamp on that sample entry is 11:34 the same night. By my reading of the dates, the idea went from a train seat to a working spy in an evening.

A browser with no JavaScript switch

On Friday morning LoVerso sent the story to the RISKS Digest, Peter G. Neumann's moderated forum on the hazards of computers. It ran in volume 17, issue 79 as "Netscape Navigator 2.0 exposes user's browsing history", between a year-2000 bug and a reply from Sun about Java security.

The post is careful about its claims. LoVerso called his tracker "the third (or fourth?) way to steal private data from a user via JavaScript", and claimed only one thing as new: it worked in real time, on the finished 2.0, for as long as its window lived. Addresses carried secrets then as now, so anything a site put in a URL, a password or a session key, went into the log with the rest. He noted that Navigator opened Netscape's own home page at startup, that the page was full of JavaScript, and that a log of where people went next was worth a great deal to an advertiser.

Then came the paragraph that mattered most:

As it stands, with Netscape 2.0 you cannot disable JavaScript. You can disable Java.

LoVerso thought that the wrong way round. Java's design had been pored over by thousands of people. Nobody outside Netscape had seen JavaScript's source, and its specification was whatever Navigator did. You could read any one script with View Source, but nothing told you a page had a script in it, and by the time you looked it had already run.

So people improvised. LoVerso's tracker page asked readers to write to Netscape and request a button. One correspondent in Netscape's developer newsgroup, whose name the surviving copy doesn't give, went further and reported having edited the program itself: "we've patched the binary to not recognize the SCRIPT tag, the onLoad function, and the 'livescript:' URL scheme". On March 7, according to Dawson, the security office of the Naval Research Laboratory advised U.S. military personnel not to use Netscape 2.0 until the problems were fixed. Two days before that, by LoVerso's own tally of the coverage, the story had been on the front page of the San Jose Mercury News.

Netscape's bounty, and Eich's word "minor"

Netscape had in fact answered before RISKS ran the story, and the answer was friendly. Dawson's account, which LoVerso says he was allowed to check before it went out, has Netscape telling LoVerso on Thursday night, the day the tracker page is dated and the evening before the RISKS submission, that he had won a $1,000 bounty. The money was slower. When the San Jose Mercury News reported on March 5 that he had received it, LoVerso noted: "This is not (yet) the case. I've been told I will receive such a prize..." His list of reported problems now records the prize as awarded, and adds: "They also sent me a Mozilla mug."

The second answer came a week later and was neither. On February 29 Eich replied at length to the newsgroup correspondent with the patched binary. The message survives because a subscriber named Alex Kremer reposted it to a JavaScript mailing list the next day under the subject "*THIS* is the official word", although Eich's last lines say it is his opinion and not the company's. Eich ranked the holes:

I consider the directory listing and mail spamming/address-stealing holes serious; the history tracker less so.

The tracker was minor, Eich wrote, "because it is far from invisible" on every system he had tried. That was fair as far as it went: the demonstration was built to be seen. The same message conceded the larger point in one clause. A special release, 2.01, was about to replace 2.0, and it would fix the directory and mail bugs, "plus adding a Preference to disable JavaScript".

The rest of the message is the best record I've found of how JavaScript's security was meant to work, and why the two of them talked past each other. I see three forces at work, two of them in this message.

The first is that the feature and the hole were the same thing. Frames arrived in the same Navigator release as scripting, and a script that could not look into another frame or window could not do much with either. Eich's rule was that a script and the documents it examined "must come from the same server". The directory lister got through because that check had a bug. The tracker, as LoVerso described it, read another window's address with no bug involved. That is why LoVerso complained on his page of press clippings that reporters kept missing the point: the tracker used "a designed in feature of the language".

The second is an honest disagreement about method. The correspondent wanted a written security model, something with the "sense of formalism" Java had. Eich answered that formalism had not saved Java, which had just needed a patch for a hole found by students at Princeton, and that he put more faith in code review and in paying people to publish their attacks. He also sketched what he wanted to build next: "taint" bits on private data, an idea borrowed from Perl, so that a script could read your history but could not send it anywhere.

The third is that Netscape could hardly ship JavaScript switched off, as LoVerso had suggested, because its own site depended on the language. When the off switch arrived, TidBITS noted that with JavaScript disabled, pages that leaned on it, Netscape's included, might load worse than they did in browsers that had never heard of it.

By then the argument had left the mailing lists. That Mercury News story ran on the front page, and the clippings page keeps score of what followed. CMP's NetGuide got LoVerso's name wrong. Educom's Edupage newsletter misread the Mercury News and, in his words, "has just gotten Tennyson a job at OSF", which took three days to correct. PC Week started its story on page 1 on March 11 and printed his web address without his name. Again and again he read that Netscape's patch for the Java hole had fixed JavaScript's bugs. The stories led with stolen e-mail and directory listings, and the tracking that he called "my real discovery" was "often downplayed or left out". The first article he judged to "get everything right" was James Staten's in MacWeek on March 13, nearly three weeks after the RISKS post.

Navigator 2.01, broken in four days

Navigator 2.01 fixed the tracker and added the switch, and four days later LoVerso had the tracker running again. The release began appearing on Netscape's FTP server on March 14, three weeks to the day after the date on the tracker page. Frank Hecker, who worked in pre-sales technical support at Netscape, told the JavaScript list that morning, with a postscript saying the note was not an official announcement. A bulletin from the Energy Department's incident team, reprinted in RISKS, listed five JavaScript problems, two already fixed in 2.0 and the rest fixed by 2.01. The fifth was the logging of every address a browser visited. Whatever Eich thought of the tracker on February 29, the patch covered it.

And there was the switch. Padgett Peterson told RISKS readers where to find it: "you can turn JavaScript off (Options/Security)." LoVerso added an update dated 3/14 to the tracker page, saying the hole was fixed.

The next update on the page is dated 3/18 and says there is a new way that works in 2.01. This time he did use the stuck onload bug from the morning of February 21, because he had found a dependable way to set it off: have the script throw up an unexpected Save File dialog and wait for the user to press Cancel. As he told the www-security list, "you'd press CANCEL, too, if that happened to you!" By March 22 he had two more attacks on 2.01, a rebuilt directory lister and a way to make any form button upload a file from your disk.

What he did next is the part I didn't expect from the person whose page signs off "We're watching". He gave the two worse exploits to Netscape and to nobody else, and held them back for six weeks, partly because they were nasty and partly, he wrote, "because Netscape asked me to". He linked them only on May 1, once Navigator 2.02 was out and had fixed all three. And his March 22 note ends by pointing readers at the thing he had asked for in February: anyone on 2.01 could avoid all three attacks by switching JavaScript off.

Where the tracker's fixes went

The same-server check got a name and became the rule everything else rests on. Netscape's later Client-Side JavaScript Guide opens its security chapter with the same origin policy, and explains it in terms of this exact winter: the restriction "prevents scripts from fetching private information such as directory structures or user session history". By my reading those are Tennyson's bug, then Weston's and LoVerso's. Eich has since described how it came about in two words. The abstract of a talk he gave in 2012, "The Same-Origin Saga", opens: "I created what became known as the browser 'Same-Origin Policy' (SOP) under duress for Netscape 2, 3, and 4 in the mid-nineties." The rule needed many more patches: the W3C's security FAQ, in an entry dated August 1997, describes scripts in invisible windows recording every page a user visits in Navigator 3, Communicator 4 and Internet Explorer 3 and 4, with variants that "reappear at almost monthly intervals".

Eich's taint bits shipped, were withdrawn and left a fossil. The same guide records that data tainting arrived in JavaScript 1.1, the version in Navigator 3.0, where a user had to set an environment variable called NS_ENABLE_TAINT to turn it on, and that "it was removed in JavaScript 1.2". The method scripts used to ask about it outlived the feature. The HTML Standard still specifies navigator.taintEnabled() for browsers in what it calls Gecko compatibility mode, in one sentence: "The taintEnabled() method must return false."

The off switch lasted seventeen years in plain sight. It moved from the Security preferences to a Languages tab in the previews of Navigator 3.0, and its descendant was still a checkbox in Firefox when Alex Limi, of Mozilla's Firefox UX team, filed a bug in March 2013 titled "Remove 'Enable JavaScript' checkbox from Prefs". Limi's essay on the subject argued that most sites that do more than display content now fail "in interesting & mysterious ways" without scripts, so that to ordinary users a browser with the box unticked simply looks broken. Firefox 23, released August 6, 2013, took the checkbox out and reset anyone who had used it to the default. The setting survived in about:config, for people who know to look there.

LoVerso stopped collecting bugs. His list of reported problems has a note that he is no longer gathering JavaScript bugs because his time is going to "other, more important pursuits", a 2002 postscript wondering what he might have found had he kept at it, and a complaint that the file upload bug never earned him a second prize: "I would have preferred another $1000".

The takeaway

The first public fight over the safety of the finished JavaScript was not about a crash or a virus. It was about whether a page you had left could keep watching you, and it was settled in three weeks by a patch, a prize and a preference. The patch tightened the same-server check that later got the name same origin policy. The prize was a thousand dollars and a mug. The preference was an admission that the only safe answer to "what can this script do?" was, for a while, "nothing, if you say so". Eich was right that the 1996 demonstration was easy to spot, and LoVerso was right that spotting it was not the user's job. The web that followed took LoVerso's fear seriously and his remedy less and less, until a browser could remove the switch on the grounds that nobody could afford to use it.

The tracker page is still up, with its dated updates and its 1996 log entry. The "Invoke the tracker" link points at port 8000 of a machine called freebase.osf.org, which did not answer when I tried it. Nothing is watching at that address now. The last line of the page hasn't been changed, and it has turned out to be a fair description of the web.

item.title: The Rhino book: when the bookstore was the curriculum
item.description: From 1996 a book with a Javan rhinoceros on the cover was how you learned JavaScript, and the shelf it sat on explains why web books were thick, yearly and sometimes sold in beta, and where their reference pages went.
item.content:encoded:
For a good many years, the standard way to learn JavaScript was to go to a shop and buy a book with a rhinoceros on the cover, and the book kept a note at the back about the rhinoceros.

The animal on the cover of JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, Fourth Edition is a Javan rhinoceros.

That is the first sentence of the colophon, the page at the very end of an O'Reilly book where the publisher tells you about the animal and the typefaces. It goes on to say that "Fewer than 100 of these animals are still living", that "Edie Freedman designed the cover of this book", and that "The cover image is a 19th-century engraving from the Dover Pictorial Archive." The copyright page at the other end of the same book makes a stranger claim: "the association between the image of a Javan rhinoceros and the topic of JavaScript is a trademark of O'Reilly & Associates, Inc."

Its title is JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, and developers have long called it the Rhino book. It sat on a shelf beside the Camel book and the koala one, and its author, David Flanagan, revised it six times between 1996 and 2020. I knew the nickname and the reputation. What I had not understood until I did the reading was how much of the web's early training ran through a retail product, and how many odd things that fact explains: why the books were so fat, why one of them was sold as a beta, and how the book's author came to work on the free website that took over its reference pages.

Staples and brown covers

O'Reilly did not start as a publisher. A profile the company reprints, "Tim O'Reilly in a Nutshell", says it was founded in 1978 and published its first computer book in 1985, and it has Tim O'Reilly explaining how a technical-writing consultancy drifted into books: in the slow periods, "we started writing manuals for programs we were using that didn't have very good documentation." That clause is the whole business model. The software existed, the vendor's documentation was thin, and somebody could charge for the gap.

The animals came from an outsider. In "A short history of the O'Reilly animals", Edie Freedman recalls that in the mid-1980s the company "was selling short books on Unix topics via mail order", and that these Nutshell Handbooks "were held together by staples, and had plain brown covers." Tim O'Reilly wanted them in real bookstores and did not like the covers a designer had produced. A neighbour who worked there showed them to Freedman, who at the time made slides and video in the world of Digital Equipment Corporation. "I'd never met a Unix programmer or tried to edit a document using vi", Freedman writes.

The usual story is that the Unix command names reminded Freedman of strange animals. Freedman's own account is better. The terms "sounded to me like words that might come out of Dungeons and Dragons". The engravings came second: looking for images, "I came across some odd-looking animal engravings from the 19th century", and they seemed to match. The covers took a whole weekend. Back at the office, "Some of the people at O'Reilly were taken aback: they thought the animals were weird, ugly, and a bit scary." Tim O'Reilly, by Freedman's account, got it immediately.

So before the web existed, the pieces were in place: a publisher whose trade was filling documentation gaps, a cover design you could spot from across a shop, and shops worth crossing. The best of those was Computer Literacy Bookshops in Silicon Valley. The Computer History Museum's record of an oral history with its founders, Dan Doernberg and Rachel Unkefer, says the first store opened in March 1983. In a footnote to the transcript, Doernberg quotes what they told a magazine in 1987: "14,000 titles in our database and 60,000 books in stock." A tenth-anniversary notice in TidBITS quoted Gene Miya on what that did to people: "every one of us who first walked into the place spent $300 in less than a hour of browsing".

A book printed in beta

Flanagan had already written Java in a Nutshell for O'Reilly when he picked his next subject. In a 2020 interview with JavaScript Weekly he remembers telling an engineer from Sun Microsystems, Java's maker, that "I thought JavaScript might become more important in the browser than Java". The engineer "scoffed".

The trouble was that the subject would not hold still. The preface to the second edition tells it plainly:

When Netscape released a final version of Navigator 2.0, I imagined that JavaScript would finally be stable, and that the time was ripe for a book documenting it. Soon after I started writing, a beta release of Netscape 3.0 was announced. It seems like I've been playing catch-up ever since.

O'Reilly's answer was one I did not expect from a print publisher in 1996. In Flanagan's words from the same preface, "we printed a 'beta edition' of this book". He confirmed the label on his own site in 2020: the first edition was published "as the 'beta edition'", in August 1996. Kevin Savetz's Internet book list of that winter records it at 454 pages and $29.95, with a note that it covered the JavaScript of Navigator 2.0 and of the Navigator 3.0 betas, and that "the 3.0 information is current as of the 3.0b4 release." A paper book, in other words, pinned to a beta build number.

The second edition followed in January 1997. Its preface calls it "far superior to the last", "over one hundred pages longer", and is dated November 1996, with visible relief that it "goes to print before the first beta version of Navigator 4.0". Here is the first program in it, Example 1-1:

<HTML>
<BODY>
<SCRIPT LANGUAGE="JavaScript">
document.write("<h2>Table of Factorials</h2>");
for(i = 1, fact = 1; i < 10; i++, fact *= i) {
    document.write(i + "! = " + fact);
    document.write("<br>");
}
</SCRIPT>
</BODY>
</HTML>

It still runs. It is also a tidy record of its year: uppercase tags, a LANGUAGE attribute, undeclared variables and document.write(), which Flanagan later described as "pretty much the main feature of JavaScript at the very beginning, before the DOM." If you wanted the examples without typing them in, the preface sent you to anonymous FTP at ftp.ora.com.

What surprised me most is in the acknowledgments. Brendan Eich "read and provided helpful comments on the beta edition", which you might expect. But Flanagan also thanks three of "the primary developers of Microsoft's version of JavaScript", who "reviewed the Beta edition" too. In 1996 people at the two companies fighting over the browser were both sending comments on the same independent book. My reading is that the book was already doing a job neither vendor's documentation did, which was to describe both.

The shelf fills up

Then the book grew, edition by edition, with the platform. The third came in 1998. The fourth, with a preface dated September 2001, announced a change of method: the focus had moved "from documenting particular JavaScript and browser implementations" to "documenting the standards upon which those implementations are (or ought to be) based", because it was "no longer practical for any one book to attempt to document" every quirk of every browser. The fifth, in 2006, added Ajax and ran to 994 pages by the Internet Archive's catalogue record. The sixth, in 2011, Flanagan himself later called "a 1096 page brick".

It had neighbours. The colophons of the editions on sale in the early 2000s give a koala to HTML & XHTML: The Definitive Guide, a crab spider to Webmaster in a Nutshell, a flamingo to Danny Goodman's Dynamic HTML: The Definitive Reference and salmon to Eric Meyer's Cascading Style Sheets: The Definitive Guide. Freedman reports that the spider drew a complaint from the husband of a reader it terrified. A webmaster with those four and the rhino on the desk owned, more or less, the documentation of their job.

And O'Reilly's was only one colour of spine. Goodman's own list of publishing credits starts its JavaScript line with Danny Goodman's JavaScript Handbook from IDG in 1996, which became the JavaScript Bible and ran to a seventh edition in 2010. Laura Lemay's Teach Yourself Web Publishing with HTML in a Week came out in January 1995, according to a 1997 Salon profile that credits her with 23 titles two years later. Philip Greenspun, writing in 1997 about a visit to a large Barnes & Noble in Manhattan, found a table of Internet books at the front of the computer section, "a massive 'for Dummies' section behind the table", and behind that "an even larger 'how to program HTML' section."

Why the books got so thick

The first force was the software's own pace. Andrew Leonard's Salon piece says that for a computer book "three months from start to finish is not uncommon", and describes a new genre that a literary agent, David Rogelberg, called the "beta book". The technology books editor of Publishers Weekly, Paul Hilts, told Leonard: "These books are out of date before they go to press". And then the part I find most interesting: "But the readers know that. They buy the book as if they are buying a subscription." A new edition every year or two was not a failure of the format. It was the format.

The second force was the shelf itself. Greenspun, who had just written one of these books for Macmillan, reported the trade's belief without much affection: "It is an article of faith in the computer publishing that bigger books sell better. They take up more space on the shelf and readers with a tech problem find a bigger book comforting." This is one author's account, not publisher data, but it fits what you could see. A book was chosen in a few minutes, standing up, from a wall of rivals. Thickness and a bright spine were the only interface it had.

The third was money. Wired reported in 1997 an industry newsletter's figure that sales of trade and professional computer books came to $586 million in 1996, up from $500 million the year before. Salon counted "more than 40 computer book publishers" and quoted Rogelberg on the consequence: "It's cheaper to publish the book and have it fail than to do some market research to see whether it will fail."

The fourth is the one that made a brand matter: most of the results were bad. Douglas Crockford's essay "JavaScript: The World's Most Misunderstood Programming Language" has a section headed "Bad Books", and it does not hedge. "Nearly all of the books about JavaScript are quite awful. They contain errors, poor examples, and promote bad practices." Then: "I have reviewed dozens of JavaScript books, and I can only recommend one", which is Flanagan's. To be fair to the others, Crockford was hard on the winner as well. In a later memoir Crockford calls the Definitive Guide "the only reliable source" and adds that "it was too big", and that "it completely left out closure, which is JavaScript's best part." Still, in a shop with no reviews pinned to the shelf, an animal on a white cover was a working quality signal. It was the nearest thing the aisle had to a ranking algorithm.

How readers coped

These books were expensive, so people read them where they stood. Al Sweigart, who went on to write programming books, describes going to Barnes & Noble after school, "pulling thick $80 tech books off the shelf, reading them in the store for a few hours, then putting them back on the shelf. I did this for years." Sweigart says the employees came to recognise their regular visitor and never made a fuss. I'd guess every large bookshop of the period had a few of these unofficial students, and that some of them now review your pull requests.

You also learned to distrust the page a little. The books had errata lists, and serious readers treated them as part of the text. The FAQ of the Usenet group comp.lang.javascript, in a posting from June 2008 that survives on a forum mirror, says most regulars believe the best book to be the Definitive Guide's fifth edition, and immediately adds: "The errata should be considered a must read along with the book." The best recommendation a newsgroup of experts could give was a book plus its list of known mistakes, and one reply in the same thread disputed even that.

The publisher's own fix for the weight was to put the books on a CD-ROM, a line O'Reilly came to call the CD Bookshelf. An O'Reilly press release from October 1997, reposted at the time to a Boston user group's mailing list, announces WebMaster in a Nutshell Deluxe: one CD-ROM holding five books in HTML, the second edition of the Rhino book among them, sold with a printed copy of WebMaster in a Nutshell for $69.95. HTML on a disc is easy to put on a server, and people did. Tim O'Reilly's 2002 essay "Piracy is Progressive Taxation" says the biggest problem with unpaid copies was not file sharing but "copies of our CD Bookshelf product line being put up on public Web servers, or copied wholesale and offered for sale on eBay." Then it declines to panic: "While these pirated copies are annoying, they hardly destroy our business." The servers that ignored a polite letter, the essay notes, were "typically in countries where the books are not available for sale or are far too expensive for local consumers to buy." The first lesson in that essay is the line people still quote: "Obscurity is a far greater threat to authors and creative artists than piracy."

The legitimate version of the same idea was Safari. A press release of October 1, 2001 announced a joint venture with Pearson and mentioned that the service for individuals had "been available at safari.oreilly.com since February 1, 2001", for $9.99 a month. Hilts had said readers bought computer books like a subscription. Four years later you could buy the subscription and skip the books.

Where the shelf went

The market that built the shelf peaked early. Publishers Weekly's "After the Bust", in September 2002, reports a McGraw-Hill publisher's estimate that the category reached its apex in 2000 and that the number of titles had since fallen by 25 to 30 percent. O'Reilly's Mike Hendrickson, in a 2009 market review that survives as a long quotation on a librarian's blog, wrote that the market "cratered in 2001" and "stabilized in 2004 at about half the size that it was in 2000." The shops went with it. Barnes & Noble's online arm bought Computer Literacy's successor company, Fatbrain, in September 2000, and Doernberg's footnote in the oral history says the original Sunnyvale store stayed open "until Barnes & Noble closed all the stores in I believe 2001."

By 2008 the replacement could say so out loud. Announcing Stack Overflow that April, Jeff Atwood wrote of programming knowledge "hidden away in books that nobody buys any more." Twelve days later, in a post that walks some of that back, Atwood put the case at full strength first: "The internet has rendered programming books obsolete." Atwood's complaint about the survivors would have been familiar to Greenspun: "Programming books sold by weight, not by volume."

Three things from the shelf are still in use, and none of them is where I expected to find it.

The first is the reference section of the Rhino book, which moved to the web, and its author went the same way for a while. Mozilla's developer site began, by Mozilla's own account, in 2005 as a rescue of Netscape's DevEdge documentation, which had vanished from the web under AOL. That is the vendor documentation the books had been competing with since 1996. In 2011, with the sixth edition just out, Flanagan wrote a post about pirated copies of it, and about Google suggesting them to anyone who researched the book. The post is gone from his site, but Mark Bernstein quoted it that April: "I've worked really hard on this book, and I've got to say that this just feels like a kick in the gut." I have no source that ties what happened next to that post, so take the order of events as only that. By the JavaScript Weekly interview, Flanagan had been self-employed "from about 1991 to 2011", mostly writing books; in 2011 he joined Mozilla, and the biography printed with the interview says he has since "worked as a full-stack engineer on MDN". When the seventh edition came out in 2020 it was about 400 pages shorter, and he gave the reason himself: "I've removed the reference section. In 2020 it is faster to look reference information up on MDN than it is to flip through a printed book."

The second is the animal, which escaped into software. Mozilla's history of its Java-based JavaScript engine says: "Rhino gets its name from the animal on the cover of the O'Reilly book about JavaScript." The project started at Netscape in the autumn of 1997, when the book was a year old. A publisher claimed a trademark on the link between an animal and a language, and the language's own makers named an engine after the cover. I can't think of another piece of technical documentation that named part of the thing it documented.

The third is the pirated bookshelf, which has quietly turned into an archive. O'Reilly's site would not show me the old prefaces, and the Internet Archive's scans of the early editions are available only for lending. The 1997 preface and acknowledgments I quote above I read in an unauthorised copy of one of those CD Bookshelves, still being served from a web server two decades on, complete with O'Reilly's copyright notices. I have not linked it. But it is an awkward fact that the copy the publisher wanted taken down is the one a reader can still open, and it is Tim O'Reilly's own lesson about obscurity, applied to his back catalogue.

There is a fourth, smaller one. The "beta edition" of 1996 looked like a stunt. It is now simply how technical books ship: Flanagan's announcement of the seventh edition says "The early release version is available online from the publisher today", with print to follow weeks later.

The takeaway

The bookstore was the curriculum because, for a while, it was the only place where the web's documentation had been edited. Browsers shipped faster than their makers could explain them, the explanations that existed were scattered or wrong, and a publisher with a recognisable cover could sell you a checked, bound, slightly out-of-date account of the whole thing. The thickness, the yearly editions and even the beta label all followed from selling a moving subject through a physical shelf.

What ended it was not that developers stopped reading. The parts of a book that were really a database (the reference pages, the errata, the worked answers) moved to places that could be searched and corrected: MDN, Stack Overflow, a subscription library. What stayed on paper is the part that was always an argument about how to write the language, which is why the seventh edition of the Rhino book spends most of its pages on JavaScript itself and no longer tries to be the manual for the browser. The same rhinoceros is on the cover. Flanagan thinks it looks grumpier these days.

Sources and further reading

  • JavaScript: The Definitive Guide, David Flanagan, O'Reilly: second edition (1997) and fourth edition (2002), read in a CD Bookshelf copy and not linked
  • A short history of the O'Reilly animals, Edie Freedman, O'Reilly, 2013 (archived)

  • Publishing and Media Credits, Danny Goodman (archived)

item.title: #!: the URLs no server ever saw
item.description: From 2010 Twitter and then Gawker put their pages behind twitter.com/#!/name addresses that only JavaScript could read, and the outage and argument that followed sent rendering back to the server.
item.content:encoded:
For a few years around 2011, some of the busiest addresses on the web contained two characters which guaranteed that the server would never learn which page you had asked for.

twitter.com/timbray
twitter.com/#!/timbray

That pair comes from Tim Bray, who wrote in February 2011 of getting "madder and madder" now that the first address "has become" the second. The essay is called Broken Links. Its own URL ends in Hash-Blecch, which tells you the mood.

The two characters were called the hashbang, the name Unix people already used for the #! at the top of a shell script. They were not Twitter's invention. They were half of a deal Google had offered to sites built with Ajax: put #! in your URLs, and our crawler will ask you for the same page under a different, uglier name. This essay is about how that deal came to exist, what happened to a publisher that took it, and why the industry then moved page rendering back to the server it had just left.

The part after the #

The hash sign started as a way to point at a spot inside a page. Jeni Tennison's long essay Hash URIs, the calmest thing written during this argument, traces the definition through the RFCs. In 1994 the thing after the hash was an anchor to scroll to. By 1998, in the text Tennison quotes from RFC 2396, it was "additional reference information to be interpreted by the user agent after the retrieval action has been successfully completed". The current rule is RFC 3986, from January 2005, which says the fragment is "separated from the rest of the URI prior to a dereference" and is handled "solely by the user agent".

In plain terms: the browser keeps it. You can check with any URL parser. This runs in Node:

var u = new URL("http://twitter.com/#!/timbray");
u.pathname  // "/"
u.hash      // "#!/timbray"

I also pointed curl at a local server with that path and fragment. The server logged GET / and nothing more.

For a document, that is a sensible design. For an Ajax application it was the only loose floorboard in the building. Once a page fetched its content with XMLHttpRequest and never reloaded, the address bar stopped changing. The back button left the application altogether, and you could not bookmark or send anyone the screen you were looking at. The Q&A Jesse James Garrett appended to the essay that named Ajax listed the back button among its open questions. The fragment was the one piece of a URL that script could rewrite without triggering a page load, so that is where application state went.

Getting it to work took effort. In September 2005 Brad Neuberg counted five libraries and techniques for "bookmarking and the back button in AJAX applications", Neuberg's own Really Simple History among them. Browsers had no event to tell you the fragment had changed, so libraries looked at location.hash on a timer. The W3C Technical Architecture Group's draft finding Repurposing the Hash Sign for the New Web, which lists a first version from April 2009, gave the appeal ("the characters in the URI bar after the hash can be changed without causing the page to be reloaded") and the cost: "without running JavaScript, the URI has no meaning."

October 2009: Google's offer

A URI with no meaning to anything but a browser is a problem for a company whose product reads the web with something that is not a browser. On October 7, 2009, the Google Webmaster Central blog published A proposal for making AJAX crawlable. It said search engines "traditionally are not able to access any of the content" on Ajax sites, and added a number: "almost 70% of the websites we know about use JavaScript in some form or another."

The proposal had three moving parts. First, a site marks the fragments that represent real, linkable states by starting them with a token. "Based on a review of current URLs on the web, we propose using "!" (an exclamation point) as the token for this." Second, because "URL fragments are never sent with requests to servers", the crawler rewrites the address so the state travels in the query string, under a second token chosen the same way. Third, the site answers that rewritten address with ordinary HTML. The post's own worked example:

https://example.com/dictionary.html#AJAX
https://example.com/dictionary.html#!AJAX
https://example.com/dictionary.html?_escaped_fragment_=AJAX

The first line is what an Ajax site had. The second is what it should publish. The third is what the crawler would fetch, after which the search results would show the second again.

How was the site to produce HTML for a page that existed only after its JavaScript ran? The proposal's answer was: "Use a headless browser that outputs an HTML snapshot on your web server". The server was to run a browser, load its own application in it, and send the crawler the result. Among the stated goals was "Users and search engines see the same content (no cloaking)". I'll come back to both of those.

Mike Davies, whose essay is the centre of the next section, pointed out what Google had been telling people. Its Webmaster Central blog had advised in 2007 that anyone starting from scratch should "build your site's structure and navigation using only HTML" and add Ajax afterwards. The #! scheme was, in Davies's word, a "lifeline" for sites that had already gone the other way. Within a year, a very large site read the workaround as an architecture.

Twitter takes the deal

Twitter relaunched its website in September 2010 as a JavaScript application, known as #newtwitter. Ben Cherry, a front-end engineer on the project, explained the URL change that December:

Many people have noticed that the new Twitter.com brought a small change to the site's URL structure: the introduction of a /#!/ at the front of the path. This is a simple change that most front-end engineers are already familiar with, but with huge performance savings.

Cherry continued that the #! "is there to comply with Google's Ajax crawling specification, so we don't lose out on search engine rankings with the new scheme." Moving from a profile to a tweet no longer threw away the page; script fetched JSON from Twitter's API and drew it.

Tennison tested what the site did with each form of address in early 2011. A logged-in browser asking for the plain URL of a tweet got a 302 redirect to the #! version. Asking for http://twitter.com/?_escaped_fragment_=/JeniT/status/35634274132561921 got a 301 back to the plain one. And curl on the hashbang URL got the home page, with, in Tennison's words, "no idea that the original hash-bang URI was supposed to give me anything different". Twitter had kept its old server-rendered pages and bolted the application on top. The next adopter kept its spare for crawlers only.

Monday, February 7, 2011

Gawker Media rolled out a redesign across its sites, Lifehacker and Gizmodo among them, in early February 2011. The day after it went wrong, Mike Davies published Breaking the Web with hash-bangs. The opening is a fair summary of the incident:

Lifehacker, along with every other Gawker property, experienced a lengthy site-outage on Monday over a misbehaving piece of JavaScript. Gawker sites were reduced to being an empty homepage layout with zero content, functionality, ads, or even legal disclaimer wording.

Davies gives the before and after for one article:

http://lifehacker.com/5753509/hello-world-this-is-the-new-lifehacker
http://lifehacker.com/#!5753509/hello-world-this-is-the-new-lifehacker

and then the line everyone quoted: "So Sunday Lifehacker was a 1 million page site, today it's a one page site with 1 million fragment identifiers." Every URL on every Gawker site now asked the server for the same thing, the home page, and trusted script to do the rest. When the script failed to load, by Davies's account for five hours, there was no rest. Readers arriving from Google got page furniture, and I'd expect View Source showed them little more.

On February 8 The Next Web reported that Google News had not indexed a Gawker story in 24 hours; a Gawker director called it a bug they hoped to fix soon. Davies added a two-line demonstration for people who prefer evidence to adjectives:

$ curl http://lifehacker.com/#!5753509/hello-world- \
  this-is-the-new-lifehacker | grep "Hello"
$

The second prompt, with nothing above it, is the result.

Why sensible people did this

It's easy to tell this as a story about engineers who forgot how URLs work. They hadn't.

It was faster, once you were in. A page of 2010 was mostly header, sidebar and script, repeated on every click. Loading that shell once and swapping the middle saved real time and real bandwidth. Tennison lists it among the advantages: hash URIs "give caching (and therefore performance) boosts", since everybody requests the same wrapper.

They believed they were shipping an application. Four days after the Gawker outage, Cherry published Thoughts on the Hashbang, the best defence anyone wrote. Its argument is that twitter.com "is no longer a collection of Web pages" but "simply an application that you happen to launch by pointing a browser" at it. A desktop program owes you no URLs at all. On that view the hash was a bonus: "The hashbang is in the unfortunate position of being the messenger".

The browsers offered nothing else. The proper fix already existed on paper. HTML5's history.pushState() lets script change the whole path without a reload. MDN's compatibility data puts it in Chrome 5 and Safari 5, both from mid-2010, and in Firefox 4, released in March 2011. Internet Explorer 9 came out the same month without it, and Internet Explorer did not get it until version 10 in October 2012. Cherry says Twitter built the History API integration and would have shipped it "on day one" but for a browser bug they found. For any site with a large Internet Explorer audience, which in 2011 was any site, the fragment was the only mechanism that worked everywhere.

Google had removed the penalty. Before October 2009, a commercial publisher that hid its articles behind fragments would have vanished from search, and nobody would have proposed it twice. The crawling scheme made the choice survivable. I'd argue that is the real effect of the proposal: it was written to rescue existing Ajax sites and it worked as a permission slip for new ones.

The argument, and the workarounds

The week after the outage produced one of the better public arguments the trade has had. Bray's piece put the objection as a contract. A link used to mean: here is a string, send it to a server, get back a representation. Now it meant sending part of the string and "being able to run the code the server sends you". Bray called the Google scheme "a hideous kludge". Jeremy Keith's Going Postel made the robustness point: HTML and CSS skip what they don't understand, while in JavaScript "a simple typo could potentially cause an entire script to fail". Ben Ward's essay "Hash, Bang, Wallop" no longer loads at any address I could find, but Davies quotes an earlier rule of thumb of Ward's: "If site content doesn't load through curl it's broken".

Tennison's conclusion was the one that held up. Hash-bang URIs would "be around for several years", so use them only for browsers that have JavaScript and lack the History API, publish the plain URL as the one people share, and make the _escaped_fragment_ form redirect to it. One warning in that essay has aged well: adopt hash-bangs as your primary URLs and you would be "reliant in perpetuity on Javascript routing" to decode them.

Libraries took the same line and automated it. Backbone 0.5.0, released on July 1, 2011, added pushState as an opt-in. The middle of the start function in its source is the whole history of the problem in nine lines:

// Depending on whether we're using pushState or hashes, and whether
// 'onhashchange' is supported, determine how we check the URL state.
if (this._hasPushState) {
  $(window).bind('popstate', this.checkUrl);
} else if ('onhashchange' in window && !oldIE) {
  $(window).bind('hashchange', this.checkUrl);
} else {
  setInterval(this.checkUrl, this.interval);
}

Read it bottom to top for the chronology. The last branch is 2005: poll the address bar, here every 50 milliseconds, with a hidden iframe a few lines earlier for old Internet Explorer. The middle is the hashchange event, which MDN's data lists in Internet Explorer 8, a 2009 browser. The top is the History API. The browser that was last to pushState was early to the event that made hash routing pleasant. Nobody planned that as a trap, I assume, but it worked like one.

Twitter turns around

In February 2012 Dan Webb, then an engineer at Twitter, tweeted about "undoing twitters hashbang URLs", as Ubergizmo reported. Webb's 2011 essay on the subject, "It's About The Hashbangs", is gone from Webb's site, so I can only name it.

On May 29, 2012, Twitter's engineering blog published "Improving performance on twitter.com", by Webb. The post would not load for me at its current address, and I could not open the Internet Archive's copy linked here either, so I'm quoting it from two reports that reproduced parts of it. NBC News carried the headline claim:

To improve the twitter.com experience for everyone, we've been working to take back control of our front-end performance by moving the rendering to the server. This has allowed us to drop our initial page load times to 1/5th of what they were previously and reduce differences in performance across browsers.

.net magazine quoted the part about URLs:

With hashbang URLs, the browser needs to download an HTML page, download and execute some JavaScript, recognize the hashbang path (which is only visible to the browser), then fetch and render the content for that URL…

Set that beside Cherry's "huge performance savings" from seventeen months earlier. Both were right. The hashbang made the second click fast and the first one slow, and every visit that begins with a link to a single tweet is a first click. Twitter's measure was the time until you could read one tweet, which The Next Web reported as "time to first tweet". The performance people had a new metric and the hashbang failed it.

Google took longer. On October 14, 2015 it published Deprecating our AJAX crawling scheme: "Times have changed", it said, and Googlebot was now "generally able to render and understand your web pages like modern browsers". The advice was progressive enhancement and pushState. A follow-up in December 2017 said that from the second quarter of 2018 Google would stop requesting _escaped_fragment_ URLs and render the #! pages itself.

What survives of the hashbang

The snapshot became the product. Under Google's scheme the server-rendered HTML was a side dish for robots, and the JavaScript application was the meal. Current frameworks serve the snapshot to everyone and then start the application on top of it. React's documentation for hydrateRoot describes attaching "to existing HTML that was already rendered by React in a server environment". The 2015 deprecation notice expected sites to "pre-render pages for performance benefits for users", and said that doing it only for Googlebot "is considered cloaking". The 2009 proposal had promised no cloaking, and then specified a second URL that only crawlers would ever request.

The data in the page source is older than you think. Cherry's 2010 article describes Twitter's Rails server predicting the first API calls the script would make and "sending down the expected response in the initial page source", to seed a client-side cache. I read that as a direct ancestor of the serialized state that server-rendering frameworks embed in a page for hydration. The JavaScript-only Twitter was already server-rendering its data, if not its markup.

A hashbang link cannot be redirected by a server. This is Tennison's "in perpetuity" warning, and it follows from the first code sample in this essay. A moved page can answer its old address with a 301. A page that lived at /#!something never had an address the server could see, so every such link ever pasted into an email or a forum arrives as a request for the home page, and only script shipped on that home page can forward it. When I requested Davies's two Lifehacker addresses, the plain one was redirected with a 301 to a renamed address that answered 410 Gone, and the hashbang one answered 200 with the present-day front page.

The prefix outlived the scheme. AngularJS 1.6.0, released on December 8, 2016, changed the default prefix for its hash URLs "from the empty string "" to the bang "!"", so that mydomain.com/#/a/b/c "will become" mydomain.com/#!/a/b/c, in the words of its changelog. That was fourteen months after Google stopped recommending the convention.

Hash routing never left, and has an honest job. Vue Router still offers a hash mode, and its documentation states the trade in two sentences: because the fragment "is never sent to the server, it doesn't require any special treatment on the server level. It does however have a bad impact in SEO." React Router has createHashRouter. The mode is what you reach for on a static host that cannot be told to serve one file for every path, or, as the Vue docs say, when the app is loaded from a file:// URL. Those are applications in Cherry's sense, with no server to ask.

The takeaway

The hashbang was a reasonable patch on a browser limitation that got mistaken for a design. The limitation was real: until pushState reached every major browser, the fragment was the only part of an address script could change freely. Google's scheme was also a patch, on the crawler's side. Stack the two and you get a site whose every page depends on one script loading, which Gawker demonstrated to a large audience.

What I take from it is that a URL's value comes from how many kinds of client can use it, and that the server is the only party in a position to answer all of them. Twitter's engineers were right that they were building an application, and right that it was faster once it was running. They were also the ones who measured the first load and moved rendering back. The architecture most teams reach for now, a server-rendered page with an application started on top of it, is the compromise both sides of the 2011 argument were asking for. It took browsers shipping one API and about five years of everyone's patience to get there.

Sources and further reading

  • A spider's view of Web 2.0, Google Webmaster Central blog, 2007 (archived)
  • Deprecating our AJAX crawling scheme, Kazushi Nagayama, Google, 2015 (archived)
  • Rendering AJAX-crawling pages, Google, 2017 (archived)
  • Breaking the Web with hash-bangs, Mike Davies, 2011 (archived)
  • Broken Links, Tim Bray, 2011 (archived)
  • Hash URIs, Jeni Tennison, 2011 (archived)
  • Going Postel, Jeremy Keith, 2011 (archived)
  • Thoughts on the Hashbang, Ben Cherry, 2011 (archived)
  • The new Twitter, Ben Cherry, Web Performance Calendar, 2010 (archived)
  • JavaScript and URLs, Chris Shiflett, 2011 (a guide to the whole argument) (archived)
  • "It's About The Hashbangs", Dan Webb, 2011, and "Hash, Bang, Wallop", Ben Ward, 2011 (neither would load; the line of Ward's quoted here is an earlier remark, taken from Davies)
  • Improving performance on twitter.com, Dan Webb, Twitter engineering blog, 2012 (Internet Archive copy; quoted in the essay from the two reports below)
