item.title: Cornify: unicorns on every page
item.description: How a 2009 joke about single-feature startups put glittery unicorns on ESPN and Stack Overflow with one script tag, a bookmarklet and a Konami-code snippet.
item.content:encoded:
On the last day of January 2009, somebody asked Hacker News to review a website whose only feature was putting glittery unicorns on other people's websites, and a little over thirteen months later it won the popular vote at South by Southwest.

cornify_add();

That is the whole programming interface. Each call drops one sparkly unicorn, or one rainbow, at a random spot on top of whatever page you happen to be reading. The site that serves the pictures describes itself as "the #1 unicorn and rainbow service on the internet, and quite possibly in the world," a ranking nobody has challenged.

The launch post went up on January 31, 2009, under the title "Review my website: Cornify", from an account also named Cornify. It read like a startup pitch, which was the joke:

Cornify is all about giving internet users choice of customization. MySpace is a great example of a successful company with a similar vision. Facebook with its Windows 3.1 look - not so much. Cornify provides a service that allows users to cover any website in a beautiful array of unicorn and rainbow imagery - taking back the web one 'corn at a time.

Cornify came in two shapes: a button a site owner could paste into their own page, and a link you could drag to your bookmarks bar and then press on anybody's page. The second was a bookmarklet, a kind of program that had been around for a decade by then, and Cornify may be the most widely seen joke ever told in it. I can't prove that, but I can't think of a rival that made ESPN's home page.

Bookmarks that run code

A bookmarklet is a bookmark whose address starts with javascript: where you would expect http:. Click it and the browser runs the rest of the address as script, inside the page you are already on, with all the rights of that page. Jay Hoffmann's history of the bookmarklet quotes Netscape's own JavaScript guide telling developers that "you can put any statements or function calls after the javascript: URL prefix."

The name came later. Hoffmann dates it to December 1998, when Steve Kangas launched Bookmarklets.com. Kangas's About page is still up, and it states the idea better than anyone has since: "Bookmarklets allow anybody to use JavaScript - on whatever page you choose (not just your own page)." Asked further down whether bookmarklets are the coolest thing since sliced bread, the page answers: "Um, maybe. Sliced bread is pretty cool."

For ten years the form was mostly earnest. Bookmarklets validated your markup, opened every link on a page, and posted the current address to whichever service you were loyal to that year. The whole program had to fit in a URL, so each one did a single job. What they did not have was an installer, a store, a reviewer or a permission dialog. A bookmarklet was a link, and you gave it to someone the way you gave them any other link.

By 2009 site owners had a similar habit. Sharing widgets such as AddThis had taught bloggers that adding a feature meant pasting in one script tag from a company's server and getting a little button in return. The Cornify launch post ends with a credit: "this concept was heavily inspired by AddThis." The Know Your Meme entry, which is user-written, puts it more bluntly: the goal was "to come up with the most ridiculous single-feature web company."

A launch thread in character

The Hacker News thread is the best record of the first day. It collected 61 points and a few dozen comments, most of them playing along. One commenter predicted the thing would "go viral" and advised seeking venture capital at once. The Cornify account answered in the voice it would mostly keep: "No worries, the business model is fully thought through. We're expecting to be profitable in phase 3."

Remember the date. In January 2009 the economy had fallen over, and the thread knows it. A commenter who installed the button wrote, "Who said this is going to be a bad year for IPOs?" I read the thread as a room full of startup people enjoying a parody of their own pitch decks.

The thread also shows the form at work. A few hours in, a commenter posting as tlrobinson wrote a bookmarklet of their own. When someone couldn't get it to run, they posted this tidier version about 22 hours later, with the instruction to "remove the newlines":

javascript:(function(){if(typeof cornify_add==="undefined"){
document.body.appendChild(document.createElement('script')).src=
'http://www.cornify.com/js/cornify.js';}
else{cornify_add()}})();

That is the standard shape of the loader bookmarklet, for programs too big to fit in a URL. It makes a script element, points it at a file on somebody's server, and appends it to the page. The file then runs as if the page's author had put it there. The bookmarklet on Cornify's button page now does the same with more ceremony.

What the script does

The oldest copy of cornify.js I could read is the one committed to GitHub in April 2011, two years after launch. It is 138 lines, and it behaves the way people described in the spring of 2009, so I'll treat it as close to the original. The heart of it is this:

var img = document.createElement('img');
var currentTime = new Date();
var submitTime = currentTime.getTime();
if( cornify_count==15 ) submitTime = 0;
img.setAttribute('src',cornify_url+'getacorn.php?r=' + submitTime + '&url='+document.location.href);

The script has no idea what a unicorn looks like. It builds a div with position: fixed, gives it a random top and left, and puts an image inside whose address is a PHP page on cornify.com. The server picks the picture. The timestamp in r defeats the cache. The other parameter is less cute: url is the address of the page you are on, sent to cornify.com with every unicorn. The joke about being a "service" was true: a server learned where each unicorn landed. My guess is that this is how the counter on the home page, which reads a little over 444 million "unicorns and rainbows provided since 2009", was kept.

Clicking a unicorn makes another unicorn. On hover the image wobbles to a random angle and size, using CSS transforms and a 0.1-second transition. The 2011 source still has the commented-out attempts at other spellings and prefixes around the WebkitTransform line that was kept, an honest record of writing CSS animation in that period.

Then come two surprises. On the fifth click the script appends a stylesheet to the page. The file now served is a single rule:

h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, h6, h1 a, h2 a, h3 a, h4 a, h5 a, h6 a, a, a:link {
	color: #FF00FF;
	font-family: "Comic Sans MS", "Marker Felt";
}

The script then walks every heading on the page and sticks a word in front of it, chosen from a list: Happy, Sparkly, Glittery, Fun, Magical, Lovely, Cute, Charming, Amazing, Wonderful. On the fifteenth click, the picture is centred in the window and the cache-buster is set to zero. The current source calls this one "the grand unicorn." Both tricks were in place by April 10, 2009, when a Hacker News reader wrote that after five clicks "every piece of text gets a very happy modifier" and the Cornify account replied: "Try pressing 15 times for some extra sparkle."

Four days to Wired

On February 4, 2009, four days after launch, Bruce Sterling's Wired blog ran a post titled "Proof why the Cornify button is a great Internet invention". The whole post is a Flickr link, the line "A comprehensive map of all possible human futures," and an instruction: "Now Cornify! See how great that is? Wow!"

The same day, Paul Irish published a jQuery snippet that hid Cornify behind the Konami code, the old Nintendo cheat sequence. I'll come back to it, because it changed where the unicorns could live.

On April 1, Stack Overflow joined in openly. The company's blog recalled a year later that its 2009 April Fools' joke "added a cornify button to every post."

Then, on April 27, Kotaku's Michael McWhertor reported that typing the Konami code and Enter on ESPN.com would "infest the official ESPN web site with mystical ponies," with "a heaping help of Comic Sans," and that every story became "cute," "magical" or "sparkly." That matches the stylesheet and word list the script applies on its fifth call, so my guess is ESPN's wrapper called it several times. David Murphy, in a PCWorld piece carried by ABC News, filed it "right next to Slashdot's 'OMG Ponies' redesign in the Web Pranks Hall of Fame." An update stamped 4:44 p.m. says ESPN had removed it. Irish added a note to the post the same day: "In fact it had been up there for weeks." I found no report that named who at ESPN had done it, or confirmed whose Konami code they had used.

On March 14, 2010, ten days after the IE6 funeral, the SXSW Interactive Web Awards gave Cornify the People's Choice Award. The official results say more than 12,000 people signed up to vote. The Amusement category, which a student reviewer at Texas State had been sure Cornify would take, went to Atlas Obscura.

The include and its wrappers

For site owners, the product was one line, given here as the project's README has it now:

<script type="text/javascript" src="https://www.cornify.com/js/cornify.js"></script>

After that, anything on the page could call cornify_add(). People in the launch thread did so within hours: "I just cornified my blog," "Put it on my site," and, from tlrobinson, "I just added it to my personal website (down at the bottom)."

The include was a building block, and the best-known early thing built on it was Irish's snippet:

var kkeys = [], konami = "38,38,40,40,37,39,37,39,66,65";
$(document).keydown(function(e) {
  kkeys.push( e.keyCode );
  if ( kkeys.toString().indexOf( konami ) >= 0 ){
    $(document).unbind('keydown',arguments.callee);
    $.getScript('http://www.cornify.com/js/cornify.js',function(){
      cornify_add();
      $(document).keydown(cornify_add);
    });
  }
});

It records key codes until the list contains up, up, down, down, left, right, left, right, B, A, and only then fetches the script, with $.getScript. After that, Irish wrote, "every other keystroke will add happiness to the world." Later in 2009, after the ESPN episode, Cornify put the same trigger into cornify.js itself. The object is called cornami, and its comment says it was adapted from Konami-JS, a library George Mandis published on April 28, 2009, citing "the recent attention surrounding ESPN." From then on any site with the plain include had the secret knock too.

The wrappers kept coming. In May 2010 John Hobbs posted Konami Unicorn Blitz to Hacker News: fifty unicorns on the Konami code, with no dependencies, "so people can just drop it right in." Its page credits Eric Ryan Harrison with a jQuery version. The Cornify account turned up to say it looked "very, very inspired by Cornify" and to ask for the artwork. Hobbs said the unicorns came from a MySpace glitter-graphics page. "You have great taste in unicorns," Cornify replied.

That is most of the documented plugin history. I found snippets and one-file libraries, passed around in blog posts and comment threads, and no official jQuery plugin. Irish's later note on the post is modest: "this feature kinda triggered a meme."

Why a joke travelled

It cost nothing to pass on. There was no download and no account. The whole product was a link, and it worked on the page you were already looking at, so the demo and the punchline arrived together.

It used a channel the industry had already built. The paste-this-script-tag habit existed to distribute sharing buttons. A site owner who had pasted three widgets that week needed no instruction to paste a fourth.

Its first audience had production access. This is the force I'd weigh most. Cornify launched on a forum read by people who ran websites, and within three months it was running on Stack Overflow and ESPN.com. Irish's Konami wrapper mattered because it lowered the stakes: an Easter egg nobody sees is easier to ship than a button everybody does.

The tone was airtight. In almost every comment I read, the Cornify account stays in character. In April 2009 it brought a sister product, Hapylink, to Hacker News for review and defended it as "not a url-shortener, but a url-happifier." It also conceded a design flaw: "Most links are actually longer - but they are a lot happier and more like to viewers smile, which is the core focus of Hapylink."

Living with unicorns

The launch thread doubles as the first bug tracker. The earliest report was that unicorns land at random, including on top of the Cornify button. "I almost cried when a unicorn covered up the 'cornify' button and I had to stop," one reader wrote. Another supplied the developer's workaround, which was to skip the button and open Firebug:

for (var i = 0; i < 10000; ++i) { cornify_add() }

The second was that there was no way back. "An 'uncornify' bookmarklet might be nice," a reader suggested, since "sometimes it blocks something important." The 2011 script has no undo short of reloading the page. The current source does include an exit, a "rainbow cupcake button" that removes every unicorn, with a comment that it "should only be used in an emergency, since it's sad."

The third was Internet Explorer 7, where one visitor could not drag the link to the toolbar at all. Two days later the same visitor reported that it worked in Firefox, but that after the tab was closed "the 'music' kept running," and warned that people "in the wild" would be less polite. A fourth reader just wanted "[joke] or something in the title, so those of us short on time can skip it." A prank is only funny to the person who chose it, and ESPN's reaction on April 27 is the corporate form of the same feedback.

And one reader on day one named the real issue, in the middle of a joke review: "I am also a bit ashamed that I executed a stranger's Javascript in my Hacker News context. Who knows what just happened to my cookie?" They read the URL and decided they were safe, "at least for the javascript present the instant I downloaded it."

Where the unicorns went

The defence against it is why it often doesn't work now. That last comment describes the risk exactly. A site that included cornify.js ran whatever cornify.com chose to serve that day, with full access to the page. I've found no sign Cornify ever abused that, but an unapproved script from another host is exactly what Content Security Policy lets a site refuse. When GitHub turned CSP on in April 2013, Joshua Peek's announcement warned that "it may cause issues with some browser extensions and bookmarklets." The spec said bookmarklets should be exempt, Peek wrote, but "none of the browsers get this correct." The current CSP draft still says a policy "SHOULD NOT interfere with the operation of user-agent features like addons, extensions, or bookmarklets." In practice, as far as I understand it, a loader bookmarklet that injects a script from another host is asking for exactly what a strict policy refuses. The web got safer from strangers' scripts, and on those sites the unicorn link went quiet.

The bookmarklet turned into the extension. Hoffmann's history ends with Firefox's add-ons gallery in 2007 and Chrome's extension gallery in 2009, after which "extensions began to overtake bookmarklets in popularity." Cornify's button page still offers the draggable link "for all browsers," and beneath it a Chrome extension and a Firefox one. The Chrome Web Store listing shows version 1.6.2, updated in May 2024, with 10,000 users. A joke that once needed nobody's permission now ships through a store. I think that trade was worth making, and I also think something was lost when "here, drag this" stopped being a way to hand a friend a program.

The parody became a genre, and then a dependency. Know Your Meme lists the imitators: Sharkify, Hoffify, Ninjafy. In March 2011 came Katamari Hack, a bookmarklet that rolls the page you're on into a ball, using the same loader. In June 2010 Newsweek's developers hid zombie headlines behind the Konami code, and The Register cited ESPN's unicorns as the precedent. The original, meanwhile, settled into maintenance. The GitHub history, kept by the account GBKS, whose profile gives the name Christoph Ono and links to the studio credited in Cornify's footer, shows a 2020 commit titled "The most amazing code cleanup and comments" and, that October, a pull request from Wes Bos adding TypeScript typings. A spoof of single-feature startups has outlasted a fair number of them and now has a type definition.

The pitch was a real argument. "Giving internet users choice of customization" was written as a parody of startup prose, with MySpace as the hero and Facebook's "Windows 3.1 look" as the villain. But it is also the bookmarklet's actual claim: that the person at the browser gets a say in what a page looks like after it arrives. I'd argue that claim survives in reader modes, content blockers and the console, and in that one sentence of the CSP draft, which says such features "advance the user's priority over page authors." Cornify made the case in magenta Comic Sans, and I think it was still a serious case.

The takeaway

Cornify was a joke about startups that turned out to be a very good demonstration of the web's loosest mechanism: any link can be a program, and any script tag is an open door to someone else's server. In 2009 that meant a unicorn could get from a forum thread to a sports network's home page in three months, carried by developers who thought it was funny. The same looseness is why browsers and sites spent the next decade adding policies, stores and reviews, and why the bookmarklet is now mostly a curiosity.

I don't think the lesson is that the old way was better. The reader who worried about their cookie was right. But the playful web of those years ran on trust that was mostly repaid, and Cornify is the proof: a stranger's script that has served, by its own count, more than 444 million pictures onto pages its author never saw, and as far as I can find did only what it said it would. The site is still up, the counter is still on the home page, and cornify_add() still produces a unicorn.

Sources and further reading

  • Review my website: Cornify, Hacker News thread, 2009 (archived)
  • About Cornify, cornify.com (archived)
  • Get your Cornify button!, cornify.com (archived)
  • Cornify/Cornify, GitHub repository, 2011 to 2021 (archived)
  • cornify.js as first committed, GitHub, 2011
  • Wait, what's a bookmarklet?, Jay Hoffmann, The History of the Web, 2023 (archived)
  • About Bookmarklets, Steve Kangas, Bookmarklets.com (archived)
  • Cornify, Know Your Meme (archived)
  • Proof why the Cornify button is a great Internet invention, Bruce Sterling, Wired, 2009 (archived)
  • Cornify Konami Easter Egg Plugin With jQuery, Paul Irish, 2009 (archived)
  • Konami-JS - Harness the power of the Konami Code!, George Mandis, 2009 (archived)
  • Reminder: It's April 1st, Stack Overflow Blog, 2010 (archived)
  • The Konami Code Makes ESPN.com Magical!, Michael McWhertor, Kotaku, 2009 (archived)
  • ESPN.com, the Konami Code, and a Whole Lotta' Ponies, David Murphy, PCWorld via ABC News, 2009
  • Ask HN: Review my webapp: hapylink.com, Hacker News thread, 2009 (archived)
  • Cornify: SXSW Web Awards Finalist, Hillary Till, SXTXState, 2010 (archived)
  • Konami Unicorn Blitz, John Hobbs, 2010 (archived)
  • Konami Code for any website - Unicorn Blitz, Hacker News thread, 2010
  • SXSW Interactive 2010 Web Awards Announces Winners, SXSW, 2010 (archived)
  • Content Security Policy, Joshua Peek, The GitHub Blog, 2013 (archived)
  • Content Security Policy Level 3, W3C Working Draft (archived)
  • Cornify - Unicorn and rainbow happiness!!!, Chrome Web Store (archived)
  • Katamari Hack, Alex Leone, David Nufer and David Truong, 2011 (archived)
  • Newsweek: 'Zombies rise from grave, invade US', Cade Metz, The Register, 2010 (archived)

item.title: The blogs and the feed reader: an industry run by correspondence
item.description: From about 2004 to 2013, front-end development argued, reviewed and patched itself across a few personal websites, and Google Reader delivered the whole exchange until Google switched it off.
item.content:encoded:
For about nine years the working knowledge of front-end development lived on a few dozen personal websites, and one tag in the <head> was how it reached you.

<link rel="alternate"
  type="application/rss+xml"
  href="rss-feed">

That is the example from the RSS Advisory Board's autodiscovery specification, wrapped onto three lines. It tells a browser or a feed reader that this page has a machine-readable twin. You never typed it. Your publishing software wrote it, and you saw only its effect: a small orange square that lit up in the address bar.

The tag did a job that sounds minor. It let developers subscribe to each other. Between roughly 2004 and 2013, that turned out to be how the field decided what good JavaScript looked like. In 2004 there was no Stack Overflow and no GitHub, and the nearest thing to cross-browser documentation was one person's website. There were people with a domain, a comment form and a feed, and there was the program you read them in.

Before: bookmarks and reload

Following a website in 2001 meant visiting it. You kept a folder of bookmarks, opened each one and looked for anything new. A site that updated twice a year cost you the same daily visit as one that updated twice a day, so in practice you stopped visiting the slow ones, and the slow ones were often the best.

The fix had existed since the 1990s. Netscape shipped the first version of RSS in March 1999 for its My Netscape portal, according to Wikipedia's history of the format. Netscape then dropped out, and two camps carried the format forward without it. One produced RSS 1.0. The other was Dave Winer, whose RSS 2.0 arrived in 2002 and is the version still published as the specification. A third group, tired of both, started over in 2003 with a format called Atom, which became an IETF proposed standard in 2005.

So by the middle of the decade there were at least three incompatible ways to say "here are my ten newest entries." When David Pierce of The Verge asked Chris Wetherell how Google Reader began, Wetherell's answer was: "a raging battle between feed formats." The formats never merged. The readers simply learned to parse all of them, which is the web's usual way of settling a standards war.

The readers came in two kinds: programs you installed, like NetNewsWire, and websites you logged in to. The best known of the early websites was Bloglines, which launched in 2003 and was sold to the company behind Ask.com in February 2005. The browsers followed. In December 2005 the Internet Explorer and Outlook teams announced they would use the orange icon that a Mozilla designer, Stephen Horlander, had drawn for Firefox, a rare case of Microsoft adopting a competitor's picture on purpose. That detail is in Wikipedia's article on web feeds. By the time the autodiscovery spec was written down in November 2006, it could say that Firefox 2.0 and Internet Explorer 7.0 both lit the icon when they found the tag.

QuirksMode: a one-person lab

The feed was only plumbing. What flowed through it was mostly written by people nobody had hired to write it.

Take Peter-Paul Koch, a freelancer in Amsterdam who signed as ppk. Koch tested what every browser actually did with every DOM method and CSS property, and published the results as tables. Koch's own About page describes the site this way: "This site QuirksMode.org used to be MDN and caniuse rolled into one, and I maintained it by myself, mostly unpaid, from 1999 to around 2014." The same page says that from Safari's release in 2003 until the iPhone in 2007, Apple pointed to QuirksMode for the documentation of JavaScript in "Safari and other browsers." A browser vendor's JavaScript documentation was, by this account, a link to one person's website.

The tables were the reference. The argument happened in articles and on blogs, Koch's own among them: QuirksBlog, whose monthly archives begin in July 2004. That month Koch opened an entry with the sentence "The new buzz word is definitely 'Web Applications'" and complained that nobody had bothered to define the term. Seven months later Jesse James Garrett's essay of February 18, 2005 (a copy survives on an MIT course site) gave the thing a four-letter name. I mention the dates because they show the order of events in this period: the people with blogs were arguing about a technique before it had a name, a book or a conference.

A conversation in function form

Here is what that argument looked like when it worked. In 2004 Koch argued in an article that inline event handlers such as onclick="" did not belong in HTML files. On May 26, Simon Willison answered on a personal weblog, in an entry called "Executing JavaScript on page load". It quotes Koch, links to QuirksMode, credits a function by a third blogger, Scott Andrew, points out that the function "fails silently in IE5/Mac," and then says: "Anyway, I believe I've found a solution. Check this out:"

function addLoadEvent(func) {
  var oldonload = window.onload;
  if (typeof window.onload != 'function') {
    window.onload = func;
  } else {
    window.onload = function() {
      if (oldonload) {
        oldonload();
      }
      func();
    }
  }
}

You probably pasted this. It solves a problem that sounds too small to need solving: two scripts on one page both want to run at load, and window.onload holds only one function, so the second script silently evicts the first. The closure keeps the old handler alive and calls it before the new one.

Now look at the listing as a piece of publishing. It names its browser test matrix in prose. It asks for bug reports. And at the bottom of the page is a note dated May 28, 2006: a reader named Billy Pan had found that the code threw a runtime error in IE 7, his fix was the if (oldonload) line, and Willison had "rolled this fix in to the code shown above." A bug report came in, a patch was accepted and the release was updated, two years after publication, on a personal weblog. This is a pull request, carried out with the tools available.

The next year the same circle made the process explicit. In August 2005 Koch published an entry titled "addEvent() considered harmful," and on September 8 he opened a contest to rewrite the function. Entries were submitted as comments. The judges were Koch, Scott Andrew LePera and Dean Edwards. The prize, in the entry's words, "will consist of eternal and undying fame." On October 18 they named the winner, a 15-line entry from John Resig, and then listed three bugs in it, because that was the house style. What Resig did with the fame is the subject of the jQuery essay.

Ajaxian: the front page

A few dozen blogs is too many to keep in your head, which created a second job: someone to read all of them and tell you which entries mattered.

On March 14, 2005, less than a month after Garrett's essay, Dion Almaer announced a new site on a personal blog: "Ben and I have had great feedback from the presentations that we have given on Ajax, so we created Ajaxian.com, as a place to talk about all things Ajax." Ben was Ben Galbraith. The first topic Almaer mentions is the back button, which tells you how early this was.

Ajaxian became the place where a library release or a clever hack went to be noticed. It wrote up other people's work and ran monthly roundups; the news archive at frontenddogma.com still indexes them, with titles like "Ajaxian Roundup for April 2008: CSS Goodness, Ext Licenses, and the Cloud." By May 2006 Almaer was on the bill of a three-day conference called The Ajax Experience. The same archive lists an October 2008 entry, "Ajaxians Join Mozilla, Creating a Developer Tools Group." Going by that title, a link roundup had turned into a conference circuit and then into jobs at a browser maker.

You can see what a mention was worth in the way authors counted. When Resig reviewed the jQuery 1.3 launch in February 2009, the traffic sources were listed in this order: "we hit Ajaxian, Reddit, Hacker News, and a number of blogs." A few months earlier, offering a site called MiniAjax.com for sale, Resig described its value in the units of the day: "20,900 adds on Delicious," "4,500 – 5,000 Daily Feed Subscribers," "Technorati Authority of 93." Feed subscribers were a line in the sales pitch.

The front page did not get the last word, either. After what Keith calls "the guys from Ajaxian" opened the @media Ajax conference in London in November 2007, Jeremy Keith wrote that evening that "the Ajaxians are missing the core attributes that make the Web so appealing—things like hypertext and markup, to which technologies like JavaScript and Ajax should be subservient." It is the argument about how much of a page should be JavaScript, and the industry is still having it. In 2007 it was being had between two blogs, in public, with permalinks.

Google Reader: the inbox

All of this needed somewhere to land. For most developers, from late 2006 on, that was one browser tab.

The Verge's history has the origin. In late 2004 Jason Shellen, a product manager at Google, asked Wetherell for "just a little thing that would parse Atom" as a demo. Wetherell built a JavaScript app in a night, called it Fusion, and then caught himself using it to read. It grew in 20 percent time. The name was taken away at the last minute, and the replacement was one Wetherell says "none of us liked."

Google Reader launched on October 7, 2005. Wetherell's announcement said the team often got asked "how anyone's supposed to keep up with the firehose of stuff launched from the web's spigot." Then, in Wetherell's words to The Verge: "it bombed. It was terrible." The site fell over on the first day and the interface confused people.

The version you used was the second one. On September 28, 2006, Ben Darnell announced a rebuild with "a clean interface and some JavaScript wizardry," and two features that still define a feed reader: "unread counts and 'mark all as read.'" The same release offered a "shared" icon that put an item on a public page "for your friends to see." Mihai Parparita, one of the engineers, told The Verge that people spent "like an hour a day in Reader." At its peak, the article says, Reader had "just north of 30 million users."

For a working developer the effect was a newspaper that assembled itself. QuirksBlog, Ajaxian, Resig, Willison, Keith and a hundred others arrived in one list, newest first, with a number beside each. The number was the catch. An inbox you did not ask for is still an inbox, and "mark all as read" got used a great deal.

Why a few blogs could run a field

The documentation was missing. Browser makers documented their own browser, when they documented anything, and nobody documented the differences. The differences were the job. Whoever tested them and published the table became the reference by default, and Koch's About page is right to call the result MDN and caniuse in one.

Publishing got cheap and addressable at the same moment. Blog software gave every entry a permanent URL, a comment form and a feed for free. A permanent URL can be cited, and a comment form on it is where the corrections arrive. Add the feed and each correction reaches every subscriber by morning. I'd argue that is most of what peer review is, and it came bundled with the software.

Fame was a real currency. Koch's prize of "eternal and undying fame" was a joke with a business model inside it. Nobody was paid per entry. What a good entry bought was a book contract, a conference invitation or a job. Koch's first book came out in 2007, and by 2008 "Ajaxians" were joining Mozilla. This is my reading of the incentives.

Why the blogs went quiet

Google wanted a social network, and Reader was in the way. The Verge's account is that Reader was put into "maintenance mode" by early 2011 while its engineers were pulled into Google Plus. On October 20, 2011, the Reader team announced that "we'll be retiring things like friending, following and shared link blogs inside of Reader," since those would "soon be available via Google+." On March 13, 2013, the end came as one paragraph in a list of housekeeping items signed by Urs Hölzle: "While the product has a loyal following, over the years usage has declined. So, on July 1, 2013, we will retire Google Reader." The Verge points out that it went up on the day a new pope was elected, and Parparita, who had left Google by then, described the thinking inside the company as: "Okay, the Pope will be the big story of the day. It'll be fine." It was not fine. The Next Web reported Feedly, a rival reader, announcing 500,000 new users in 48 hours.

The blog's jobs were split up among better tools. A 2005 blog entry was a question-and-answer thread, a code host and a link feed all at once. In April 2008 Jeff Atwood announced Stack Overflow, on a blog, with this reasoning: "Blogs are fantastic resources, but as much as I might encourage my fellow programmers to blog, not everyone has the time or inclination to start a blog." GitHub launched the same month, and code that would once have been pasted into an entry went into a repository with an issue tracker. The links, by my reading, went to Twitter, Reddit and Hacker News. Resig's 2009 traffic list already has two of those three sitting beside Ajaxian.

The work was unpaid, and people got tired. Koch's About page is blunt about it: "I ceased working on this site because it was mostly unpaid and I was getting burned out after 15 years." That sentence covers more of the era than one site. A reference library maintained by one person for fifteen years is impressive, and it is also a staffing plan nobody would have signed off on.

It is fair to say Google's stated reason was not false. Feed reading had always been a habit of the people who read a lot, and The Verge notes that the Reader team "struggled to find ways to bring in more casual users." Everyone else was getting their links from a timeline by 2013. Firefox finished the retreat on December 11, 2018, when version 64 noted that "RSS feed preview and live bookmarks are available only via add-ons." The browser that had drawn the orange square no longer read feeds on its own.

Where the readers went

RSS won a different market. The RSS 2.0 specification has an element called <enclosure> that attaches a media file to an item. Its example is an MP3:

<enclosure url="http://www.scripting.com/mp3s/weatherReportSuite.mp3" length="12216320" type="audio/mpeg" />

That one element is the podcast industry. Apple's current requirements for podcasters say feed URLs "must adhere to RSS 2.0 specifications." The format that supposedly died in 2013 is the distribution layer for a whole medium. It just stopped being called a feed.

The newsletter is a feed reader with an editor in it. JavaScript Weekly launched in November 2010, around the time Reader was being wound down to maintenance mode, and its site now counts more than 800 issues. It does Ajaxian's old job, reading everything and passing on what matters, and delivers the result to the one inbox nobody has managed to shut down. It also solves the unread count: one message a week, and no number in the sidebar accusing you of anything.

Reader was the social network Google was looking for. This is the connection I think gets missed. Follow a person, see what they share, comment on it: Reader had sharing in 2006, grew the rest in the years after, and Google retired it all in 2011 to promote a product that did the same thing with less to read. Shellen told The Verge, "I think we built a social product." The article also notes that Kevin Systrom, who had been a product marketing manager on Reader, went on to found Instagram. The feed of things from people you chose to follow did become the dominant interface of the next decade. It was just built elsewhere, and without the open format underneath.

The personal sites outlasted the front page. Every source in this essay had to be opened, and what loaded is its own finding. Willison's 2004 entry is still up, carrying a note that it was "previously hosted at" an older address, and a weblog that has run since 2002 is still running. Koch's 2005 contest is still up. Ajaxian.com, when I tried it, either reset the connection or redirected to TechTarget's home page, and Dean Edwards's site returned a note that the server "is having a nice rest." The aggregator with the audience turned out to be the fragile part. The primary sources were on domains that individuals kept paying for.

The takeaway

From about 2004 to 2013, front-end development was run by correspondence. People published what they had found on their own sites, other people answered on theirs, a couple of aggregators picked the winners, and a feed reader delivered the whole exchange to your desk each morning. Functions like addLoadEvent were specified, reviewed, patched and distributed that way, years before the standards bodies or the code hosts caught up. It worked because publishing was cheap, the browser makers had left the documentation to volunteers, and reputation paid well enough to keep the volunteers writing.

It ended when each job found a better home and the main reading room was closed by a company that wanted its readers elsewhere. The lesson I'd take from it is about what lasts. The platform with thirty million users was gone in eight years. The open format is still carrying every podcast, and the entries written on personal domains are still there to be read. If you want something you write to be findable in twenty years, the evidence favors a plain page at an address you control, with a feed.

  • RSS 2.0 Specification, RSS Advisory Board, version 2.0.11, 2009 (archived)

item.title: JSConf 2009: the community that didn't know it existed
item.description: In April 2009 about 130 people met in a hotel outside Washington for a conference about JavaScript itself. It nearly didn't happen, and its format, its side room and its name spread around the world.
item.content:encoded:
The conference that gave JavaScript developers a community was nearly cancelled for lack of interest, and by the end of its second day it had been promised to another continent.

JSConf 2009 is a conference devoted to the programming language we all love to hate and hate to love, JavaScript.

That is the first sentence of the About page on the JSConf 2009 site, which is still online with its early bird banner intact: $450 if you register by March 11, 2009. The pitch goes on in the same key. "Come to this conference if you love JavaScript, come if you hate it, come if you don't even know how to program." It describes JavaScript as "a language that often gets overlooked." As an advertisement for two days of your time, it is unusually willing to concede the other side's case.

The conference took place on April 24 and 25, 2009, at the Hotel Palomar in Rosslyn, Virginia, which the site's header rounds up to "Washington, DC USA." About 130 people came. Sixteen talks were on the main program, and a side room took whoever else had something to say. Before the year was out there was a JSConf in Berlin, and the name eventually went on events in more than a dozen countries. I'd argue the format of those two days, down to the tours for attendees' partners, is still roughly what a community tech conference looks like.

Ajax had a conference. JavaScript didn't.

It is not that web developers had nowhere to go before 2009. There was The Ajax Experience, with Ajaxian's Ben Galbraith and Dojo's Alex Russell on the bill, first in San Francisco on May 10 to 12, 2006 and then in Boston that October. The libraries had their own gatherings. In September 2007 John Resig announced "the first all-day jQuery mini-conference" for October 27 in Boston, and the next year's announcement reported that "over 100 jQuery developers" had turned up. That second jQuery Camp was scheduled for "the day before The Ajax Experience," which tells you where the centre of gravity was.

So you could attend a conference about a technique, or one about a library. The language underneath them belonged to nobody in particular. Jan Lehnardt, a CouchDB developer who was at the first JSConf, wrote in early May: "Prior to JSConf, there was no conference dedicated to JavaScript developers, heck, even the idea of a JavaScript community was hazy at best." The reason Lehnardt gave was that people wrote JavaScript part-time, "in addition to say, Python, PHP or Ruby."

Kevin Dangoor of Mozilla, writing on the plane home, was more careful about the claim, and I'd go with that version: "It was possibly even the first conference to feature JavaScript as a general scripting language in the same vein as Python or Ruby." Python and Ruby both had conferences run by their own communities. JavaScript ran in every browser and had no meeting of its own, and my best guess at the reason is Lehnardt's: most of the people writing it did not think of it as their language.

A deposit and a sold-out sign

The organizers were Chris Williams and Laura Williams, a married couple. Chris Williams had been to RubyFringe in 2008, a small Ruby conference in Toronto, and came home with an opinion. Lehnardt told the story in a 2015 talk on JSConf's history. Williams had "been to a lot of industry conferences," and having now seen one done right, concluded that a lot of them were not very good. Then Williams asked, over instant messenger, what Lehnardt thought about a JavaScript conference. Lehnardt said it was surely a good idea. The reply: "I'm glad you say this, he says, because I'm organising one."

The site's news page keeps the timeline. The dates and the hotel were announced on January 5, 2009, and registration opened on January 23. The About page promised that the organizers had "no ambition or desire to financially profit from it," and that whatever was not spent on "food, drinks, speakers, and, most importantly, you" would go to charity. The format would be "not barcamp-style and not multi-track style, but somewhere between the two." A speaker announcement in February signed off with "Be here or be static!"

Then the tickets did not sell. In Lehnardt's 2015 telling, a few months in, at three in the morning Berlin time, Williams said they might have to cancel. Lehnardt, trying to cheer up a friend while half asleep, offered: "if JSConf is a success I'll bring it to Europe." Williams remembers it the other way round. The jsconf.com account says "I made a deal with him one night that if we pulled this crazy experiment off, he would have to hold one in Europe." Both agree there was a deal.

A couple of weeks later, the story goes, it was time to tell the venue the event was off and ask for the deposit back, which, in Lehnardt's words, "as it turns out it is backed by their mortgage." So that nobody else would sign up and be let down, Williams changed the website to say sold out, closed ticket sales, and drove to the hotel. Near the end of the 45-minute drive there was an email asking how to get one more ticket. Then another. In total there were enough inquiries to pass break-even, and the Williamses, instead of cancelling, confirmed the conference on the spot.

Williams told a shorter version the following year, in a talk about how the conference got made. Dangoor's notes from it record the lesson: "conference tickets don't sell out until they sell out." People need to feel they are about to miss something. The same notes say Williams put 200 hours into the first JSConf.

Sixteen talks and a side room

The agenda opened on Friday at 9:15 with Francisco Tolmasky of 280 North on Objective-J and Cappuccino, and ended on Saturday afternoon with Peter Higgins on Dojo. In between came, among others, TaffyDB, Appcelerator's desktop apps, CouchDB, a server-side framework called Axiom Stack, XMPP in the browser, Joyent's hosted JavaScript platform, PhoneGap, Stoyan Stefanov of Yahoo on performance, jQuery UI and SproutCore. Resig had the last slot on Friday, listed as "Secret Topic," and used part of it to introduce TestSwarm.

Count the venues for the language in that list: the desktop, the phone, the server, the database. The site's front page promised you would "Write JavaScript for the iPhone, Android, and the Blackberry." Roughly half the program was still about the browser. The other half was about everywhere else, and that half is what the recaps dwell on. Brian LeRoux's PhoneGap talk, by the organizers' account, had a major hand in putting #jsconf on Twitter's trending topics.

The recaps read like people who had not expected to enjoy themselves this much. Stefanov called it "hands down, the best conference I've ever attended," and admitted to changing the slides "on the night before the presentation (and after the first night's party)." Dangoor noted "probably 50% fewer bullet points" than at other tech conferences, which is the kind of praise you can only give in 2009.

The side room turned out to matter as much as the ballroom. The agenda had promised "a side room for lightning talks and hackfests." By April the site was calling it Track B, "our free-form 'unconf' style track," with slots handed out by email, first come first served. Lehnardt reported that "the Track B room was packed both days." Stefanov thought there "wasn't a big difference" between speakers and attendees, "since attendees presented just as good content on the B-track as did the A-track."

One of the Track B talks was Dangoor's. Three months earlier, on January 29, Dangoor had published "What Server Side JavaScript needs", which argued that "JavaScript needs a standard way to include other modules," and started a mailing list called ServerJS. In the side room at JSConf, Dangoor showed what the post-conference write-up calls the group's "biggest milestone to date": one small module, math.js, loaded unchanged into five different server-side JavaScript environments. I don't have that demo file. These are the first two files of the sample code in the Modules/1.0 specification the group published, since superseded by 1.1, which also happens to start with a math.js:

// math.js
exports.add = function() {
    var sum = 0, i = 0, args = arguments, l = args.length;
    while (i < l) {
        sum += args[i++];
    }
    return sum;
};

// increment.js
var add = require('math').add;
exports.increment = function(val) {
    return add(val, 1);
};

The group was renamed CommonJS, and the spec's page lists Node.js among its implementations. require and exports were on show in the side room of a 130-person conference, months before Node.js had its turn on a JSConf stage.

Why JSConf worked

The honest answer includes luck, as the sold-out sign shows. But some of it was structural, and each of these is arguable.

The language had left the browser. Lehnardt's write-up points at "the newly kindled research in speeding up JS runtimes" and at JavaScript having "a life on its own on the server." An Ajax conference was a conference about a browser technique. By 2009 the people doing the most interesting things with JavaScript were running it in places where the word Ajax meant nothing, and they had no event to go to.

Nobody owned it. A jQuery event was jQuery's, and a Dojo event was Dojo's. JavaScript had no company behind it and no foundation, so a conference named after the language was neutral ground. The sponsors page lists Mozilla, Yahoo, Joyent, the agency R/GA and Sun's startup programme. Sponsors' people spoke, but no one company's product was the subject of the event. Dojo, jQuery, SproutCore and Cappuccino shared a single track. My read is that this was the first time many of those people had been in a room where no library was the host.

It was small on purpose. The sponsor pitch offered access to "125 of the best and brightest developers in the world," and Dangoor reported the Palomar's rooms "filled almost to overflowing." With one main track and 130 people, by Lehnardt's account "most people met everyone else."

Hospitality was treated as content. Mozilla's sponsorship went to the food. Friday night was an open bar at the top of Union Station, courtesy of R/GA, and Saturday night was Joyent and Sun's. And there was a "significant other track": the April announcement said "Bring your significant others, we will be planning a track just for them" to see Washington while the conference was on. Laura Williams took spouses, partners and families touring Washington while the conference ran, so the evening events were, as Lehnardt put it, "nicely mixed." Lehnardt added a note to the rest of the industry: "Other conference organizers: DO TAKE NOTICE!"

The talks were given away. Every session was filmed, and the videos went up free on the conference site over the following months, one news item at a time. A conference of 130 could not have defined anything by itself. The recordings and a week of blog posts titled things like "the best conference you couldn't attend" did the rest.

The money was somebody's house. This is the force that is easy to leave out. A year later Williams wrote "Hug a Conference Organizer", which lays out the arithmetic: "roughly 55% of your budget" goes to the venue, a two-day event for 150 people needs "about $50,000" just to secure speakers, food and drink, and break-even without sponsors is "$189 per day per person." The organizer personally guarantees the hotel's room block. A community conference with no company behind it existed because two people were willing to carry that risk.

A franchise with two rules

At the closing announcements on day two, Williams asked Lehnardt to stand, repeated the three-in-the-morning promise to the room, and told the audience that if they thought the conference had been a success, they should let Jan know. Lehnardt's speaker notes record the reaction in a single word, which I'll leave on Speaker Deck.

Lehnardt had, the day before, met Holger Blank and Malte Ubl at the bar. The three of them ran JSConf EU in Berlin on November 7 and 8, 2009. The JSConf 2009 site announced it in August with a line Lehnardt was still repeating six years later: the first conference "proved to be the homecoming of a JavaScript community that didn't know it existed." In Berlin, Ryan Dahl presented a project called Node.js. Ubl's post with the video says "Ryan received standing ovations for his talk and he really deserved it!" That talk is its own story.

The second American JSConf, in April 2010, was pirate themed, "for reasons I still have never asked about," as Charlie Robbins said in a 2015 talk. Its schedule shows what the first year had taught. Track B is now a full column beside Track A, every slot reading "Open Slot. Register Now!" Douglas Crockford opened. Brendan Eich was smuggled in as a surprise. Ted Leung, attending for the first time, wrote that "the conference reminds me of PyCon in its early days," and that it had been put on by "a 10 person staff."

How the name spread is written down on jsconf.com. JSConf calls itself "a very loose federation of developers who share the same general idea about how a technical conference should be held." There are two rules for using the name. "You must have attended an existing JSConf event," and "You must have an existing JSConf organizer as oversight." Each event is run and financed locally. The overseer's main job, the page says, is to be the person outside the planning who can say "It will work out, don't worry," which is the job Lehnardt did in 2009. The same page tells most people not to bother: "most times it is better to run a 'JSConf like' event with a different name."

Plenty did both. The jsconf.com front page lists JSConf events from Budapest to Bengaluru, and a longer "family" that includes NodeConf, CascadiaJS and Web Rebels. By Lehnardt's 2015 count, more than 50 events with "well over 50000 attendees" traced their origin to that ballroom.

Chris and Laura Williams stepped back in 2015, after a farewell event that December called JSConf US Last Call. Its About page explains that after a serious illness in the family, JSConf US "will be on hold for the foreseeable future." JSConf EU called its 2019 event, "our 10th anniversary," the last edition "in its current form." The name outlived both. JSConf US did come back under that name; its 2019 site advertises Carlsbad, California that August. And in October 2025 JSConf North America was held in Maryland, "back under the OpenJS Foundation."

What JSConf handed on

An identity, which is odder than it sounds. Lehnardt described the mood changing after lunch on the first day: "We are slowly starting to realise that we are JavaScript people who do Ruby on the side, Python on the side and PHP on the side." On that account, before 2009 "JavaScript developer" was mostly something a Rails or PHP developer also was. I can't measure that, but I'd argue the job title you see everywhere now needed a room in which people could try it on, and that the conference did less to serve a community than to convince one it existed.

The module system had its outing on the unscheduled track. Every require() in a Node codebase follows the CommonJS convention that was demonstrated in the side room in April 2009, months before Dahl's talk in Berlin. The work was done on a mailing list. The conference's part was to give it an audience, and it did that in the room nobody had curated. JSConf did not invent the open slot. Its own agenda credits the "-camp" style, and Lehnardt's verdict on Track B was "BarCamps rule." What it showed is why a curated conference should keep one: that is where things turn up that a program committee would not have picked, because in April nobody knew they mattered.

The name was governed like open source. The two rules are a fork policy. Anyone can copy the format, and the site encourages it, but the name is protected so that it keeps meaning something. By 2010 the conference's own site was writing it as "JSConf™." Open-source projects handle code and trademarks the same way. It fits that the North American event is now run under the OpenJS Foundation, whose project list includes Node.js. The conference and the runtime its European sibling introduced ended up under one roof.

Its code of conduct was forked too. The 2012 JSConf site carries a code of conduct with a paragraph that starts "JSConf is dedicated to providing a harassment-free conference experience for everyone," followed by a list of who everyone includes. The 2019 site claims JSConf "was one of the first conferences to implement and enforce" one. I can't rank who was first. I can say the text travelled: the page for React.js Conf in January 2015 says its code of conduct "is borrowed from JSConf Code of Conduct." The boilerplate at the bottom of a conference site today was once a decision an organizer had to make.

The fix became the next problem. The "sold out" notice saved the first JSConf, and the lesson Williams drew from it was that people sign up when they fear missing out. Robbins noted in 2015 that JSConf in 2010 "sold out, albeit a bit slower than it does today." Scarcity is what made the event feel like something. I'd argue it is also what made the better-known community conferences hard to get into for anyone not already on the inside. The later JSConf sites show the organizers pushing the other way: the 2019 one advertises scholarships, and the Last Call one a call for speakers "designed to spotlight the new faces and ideas in the community." My reading is that they were working against an effect their own first lesson had created.

The takeaway

The first JSConf was sixteen talks and a side room in a hotel across the river from Washington, attended by about 130 people, paid for at the organizers' personal risk, and saved by a "sold out" notice that was not yet true. What it produced was mostly social. People who used JavaScript on the side of some other job spent two days together and left describing themselves differently. The module convention, the European sequel and the stage Node.js was launched from all followed from that.

Its lasting invention was a way of running the thing: small, single-track with an open room beside it, generous to the point of feeding people properly and looking after their families, recorded and given away, and passed on to anyone who had attended one and could find an earlier organizer to tell them it would work out. Robbins put the principle on a slide in 2015 as "PEOPLE >>> SOFTWARE." Some of the software shown in that ballroom is still in use and a good deal of it is not. The format has outlasted most of it.

Sources and further reading

  • JSConf 2009: A Community's First Gathering, Jan Lehnardt, 2009 (archived)
  • JSConf US Last Call: JSConf History, Jan Lehnardt, slides and speaker notes, 2015 (archived)
  • JSConf 2009: the best conference you couldn't attend!, Kevin Dangoor, 2009 (archived)

item.title: The webmaster: a mailbox that became a job
item.description: "Webmaster" was coined as a mail alias on a style page, grew into the title for whoever ran the whole site, and faded, while the address in the footer link outlived the job.
item.content:encoded:
For about a decade, a website had one person behind it and one address at the bottom of the page where you could reach them. The address has lasted far longer than the job.

Hi Webmaster!
  ...
Can you help?

Those are the greeting and the question from an email sent on March 16, 1995, under the subject "Error 404". The parts I left out are one sentence of explanation, a sign-off and a pasted error: "WWW Alert: Fatal Error 404 No Match Found for", followed by an address on CERN's server. The World Wide Web Consortium still keeps the message in a folder of its history archive called MailArchive/webmaster.

The folder is worth a visit. Its index covers three weeks, from March 14 to April 4, 1995, and lists 405 messages. That is about nineteen a day, arriving in a mailbox that existed because a style guide had suggested it. The subject lines include "help", "Need help!", "test", "Weather", "healing", "Search Frustrations" and a great many "(no subject)".

The word in that greeting became a job title, a magazine survey category, a line in an RFC, the name of a Google product and, eventually, something people stopped calling themselves. This essay follows the word and the address together, because they started as the same thing. "Webmaster" was a mailbox first and an occupation second.

Before: sign your initials

Email had worked out its own version of the problem years earlier. A mail system needs a human who can be told that the mail system is broken, and the address for that human cannot depend on knowing their name. So the name was fixed in advance. As a later RFC put it, the mail standards require "the presence of a <POSTMASTER@domain> mailbox name on all hosts that have an SMTP server."

The early web had no equivalent, and at first it did not think it needed one. W3C keeps a snapshot of CERN's web pages from November 3, 1992, and in it is a page of etiquette for people publishing on the new system. Its first rule is headed "Sign it!":

Make a page for yourself with your mail address and phone number. At the bottom of files for which you are responsible, put a small note -- say just your initials -- and link it to that page.

The page follows its own advice. Here is its last line, exactly as served:

<ADDRESS><A NAME=0 HREF=http://info.cern.ch./hypertext/TBL_Disclaimer.html>Tim BL</A>

That is the original footer contact link, and it points at a person. In 1992 responsibility on the web was per document. Each page had an author, the author had a phone book entry, and if something was wrong you wrote to whoever's initials were at the bottom. The same page tells you to give your server a root page for outsiders and a stable alias like www.dom.edu. It has no word for the person who runs the server, and no address for them either.

A word coined on a style page

The later version of that page, which W3C still serves with a "1992-95" credit at the bottom, has a new section. It is called "An alias for yourself":

You should make a mail alias "webmaster" on the server machine so that people who have problems with your server can mail you about it easily. This is similar to the "postmaster" alias for people who have mail problems with your machine.

And near the top, Tim Berners-Lee added a note that is rare among etymologies, in that the coiner is standing right there: "As a server administrator, or webmaster as they are known (the term having been coined on this page, below) you should make sure this applies to your data."

When exactly? The November 1992 snapshot does not have the section. The later page carries a remark dated "[3/94]". Merriam-Webster gives the first known use of "webmaster" as 1993. So my best guess is 1993, and I can't narrow it further than "after November 1992".

Look at what was actually defined. It was a mail alias, built by analogy with one that already existed, for "people who have problems with your server". It described who should receive complaints. Nothing in it said the recipient should also write the pages, draw the buttons or choose the colours.

In fact the same page argues against it. In the very next section, "Delegating control", Berners-Lee wrote: "Maybe the server administrator has no responsibility at all for the actual content of the data, in which case he or she should just keep the machine running properly." The person who coined the word separated server from content almost in the same breath. The web then spent a few years ignoring the distinction.

The address gets wired in

The other half of the footer link arrived in December 1994. RFC 1738, the URL specification that Berners-Lee co-edited, defined a mailto scheme "used to designate the Internet mailing address of an individual or service." Note the last two words. With the alias and the scheme together, any page could end with a link in this pattern (the domain here is the etiquette page's own example):

<A HREF="mailto:webmaster@dom.edu">

There was a more formal route too. HTML 3.2, published in January 1997, noted that "REV=made is sometimes used to identify the document author, either the author's email address with a mailto URL, or a link to the author's home page." Lynx did something with it. Its user guide still documents a c command to "send a mail message to the owner of the current document", which works when the page's head contains this:

<LINK REV="made" HREF="mailto:user@somedomain.com">

Then the servers picked the idea up. Apache's sample configuration, in the 1.3 branch, has these lines:

#
# ServerAdmin: Your address, where problems with the server should be
# e-mailed.  This address appears on some server-generated pages, such
# as error documents.
#
ServerAdmin you@your.address

That comment undersells it. The 1.3 source builds the Internal Server Error page from a fixed text with the address dropped into the middle: "Please contact the server administrator, [the address] and inform them of the time the error occurred, and anything you might have done that may have caused the error." So at the moment a site failed worst, the server printed the webmaster's email address and suggested the visitor consider their own part in it.

The last step was ratification. In May 1997 D. Crocker of the Internet Mail Consortium published RFC 2142, "Mailbox Names for Common Services, Roles and Functions". It did not claim to invent anything. "Other protocols have defacto standards for well known mailbox names," it says, "such as <USENET@domain> for NNTP (see [RFC977]), and <WEBMASTER@domain> for HTTP". Its table lists WEBMASTER against HTTP, with WWW as a synonym. It also insists that case must not matter, which produces the best sentence in the document: "POSTMASTER, postmaster, Postmaster, PostMaster, and even PoStMaStEr are to be treated the same".

A few years after a suggestion on a style page, the alias was on the standards track.

How an alias became a job

Meanwhile the name on the mailbox had become the name of the person reading it. An undated Princeton Review career profile of the webmaster cites a 1996 survey by Web Week magazine in which "35 percent of respondents reported their official title as 'Webmaster' (either exclusively or in addition to another title), while none reported having that title the previous year."

Jay Hoffmann, who writes The History of the Web, describes the role as it was understood by then: webmasters "were at once the architect and the builder of a website, responsible for every bit of code and content that came through it." Hoffmann's candidate for the first of them is Louise Addis, a librarian at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, who ran the day-to-day operation of the lab's early website. Why did one title swallow the whole site? I count four forces, and none of them was a mistake.

The sites were small. Hoffmann's description of a mid-1990s business site is a front door to the internet, "updated weekly, maybe even less". One person could keep several of those going.

The stack was shallow. A site was a directory of files, a server with one configuration file, and maybe a folder of CGI scripts. All of it fitted in one head. This is my own reading of the period's software, but the Apache file above is a fair exhibit: one setting for who gets told about problems, and it takes a single address.

The institutions were used to it. The web grew up in labs and universities. As Hoffmann puts it, these were places where "it was not uncommon for people to have these pet projects on top of their existing work". A librarian who also ran a web server was normal there.

Nobody knew what else to call it. Organizations wanted a website before they had any idea which department a website belonged to. A webmaster, in Hoffmann's words, "was brought in by a business or a client or an organization when they needed a website and they didn't know who else to call." Hiring one person with a new title was easier than deciding whether the thing was IT, marketing or publishing.

What the mailbox actually got

The alias was meant for "people who have problems with your server". The W3C archive shows what arrived instead, and it is the best job description of a webmaster I have found.

Some of it was exactly what the alias was for. The first message in the archive, from a university in Berlin, is a precise bug report. A geographical listing on W3C's server had grown to 1,118,838 bytes, and the connection gave out after nine minutes: "By that time, we have received the African, Asian and Australian sections and the rest of the world is cut off."

Much of it was not about the server at all. One writer was "desperately looking for a design guide for html documents." One, under the subject "Where I am in here", wrote: "I'm trying to figure out how to get into this network and not having much luck." One message, apart from a name and a signature block, says only: "Hello ! Greetings from Warsaw", from "a WWW user". To a newcomer, the webmaster of the web's home site was the front desk of the entire internet.

Software authors noticed the pattern. Apache's documentation for ServerAdmin still advises: "It may be worth setting up a dedicated address for this", and gives the reason with some feeling: "users do not always mention that they are talking about the server!"

Then came the mail nobody had asked for. RFC 2142 had seen it coming. Its entire security section is one sentence: "Denial of service attacks (flooding a mailbox with junk) will be easier after this document becomes a standard, since more systems will support the same set of mailbox names." An address that everyone can guess, printed in a link that any program can read, is a gift to anyone compiling a mailing list.

Webmasters coped in two ways. The first was to stop printing the address and let a script build it in the browser, on the theory that a harvesting program reads HTML and does not run JavaScript. This is a typical version, written to run as shown and not taken from any one site:

<script type="text/javascript">
var u = "webmaster";
var h = "example" + ".com";
document.write('<a href="mai' +
  'lto:' + u + '@' + h + '">' +
  u + '@' + h + '<\/a>');
</script>

Wikipedia's article on address munging records the trick and its limit: newer harvesting programs can often run the script themselves.

The second was to replace the link with a form. The standard tool was FormMail, a Perl script from Matt's Script Archive that turned any HTML form into an email. Its page calls it "quite possibily the most used CGI program on the internet, having been downloaded over 2,000,000 times since 1997." View the source of that page and you find a notice, now commented out, dated April 19, 2002: "Several important spam-related security holes have been fixed". The script installed to keep the webmaster out of spammers' lists had spam problems of its own.

Why the title wore out

Hoffmann gives two reasons the role faded, and I think both are right. First, in Hoffmann's words: "Things got too hard for one person to manage." Ambitious sites were now built by teams of art directors, editors, developers and writers, and Hoffmann says of one such site, Word magazine, that it was "well beyond the scope of what one person could reasonably accomplish on their own." Second, things got too easy: visual editors, content management systems and hosted services each took over one of the webmaster's chores, until, in Hoffmann's phrase, "one by one the jobs of the webmaster were peeled away and outsourced to some tool."

The title hung on for a long time at Google. Jens Oliver Meiert writes that on joining Google in 2008, "I joined the 'Webmaster Team,' and we were on Google's webmaster job ladder." The product for site owners was called Google Webmaster Tools until a post on May 20, 2015 announced that it would become Search Console. The announcement was polite about it: "It turns out that the traditional idea of the 'webmaster' reflects only some of you." The users, Google had found, were "hobbyists, small business owners, SEO experts, marketers, programmers, designers, app developers, and, of course, webmasters as well."

Five years later the courtesy was dropped. On November 11, 2020, Google Webmasters Central became Google Search Central, and the post said plainly that "the term is becoming archaic". A user study had shown that "very few web professionals identify themselves as webmasters anymore." The Princeton Review profile had allowed for it. Its outlook for the career warned that "what it means to be a Webmaster today may completely change over the next few years and may even become obsolete."

Who inherited the mailbox

The address became a key. This is the part I did not expect. When a certificate authority issues a TLS certificate, it has to check that the applicant controls the domain. The CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements list the permitted methods, and one of them, section 3.2.2.4.4, is to send a random value by email to an address made from "'admin', 'administrator', 'webmaster', 'hostmaster', or 'postmaster'" at the domain and wait for a reply. Whoever reads webmaster@ can be treated as the owner of the site.

That has gone wrong in the way you would predict. In March 2015 Microsoft disclosed an improperly issued certificate for the domain live.fi: "An email account was able to be registered for the live.fi domain using a privileged username, which was subsequently used to request an unauthorized certificate for that domain." The advisory does not say which username it was. Whichever it was, a list of mailbox names that began as a courtesy to people with problems had become a list of credentials. The same document now gives it an end date: the method "SHOULD NOT" be used from March 15, 2026, and from March 15, 2028 a certificate authority "MUST NOT rely on this method".

Every specialty rebuilt the mailbox. When the job split, each piece needed its own way to be reached. RFC 9116, from April 2022, defines security.txt, a file at a well-known path that says who to contact about a vulnerability. It cites RFC 2142, which also reserved a SECURITY@domain mailbox, and its complaint about that convention is that it "provides only a single, email-based channel of communication per domain". It even inherits the old worry, in a section headed "Spam and Spurious Reports". I'd argue security.txt is the 1993 alias, rebuilt for one of the webmaster's descendants.

The defaults still assume one person. Apache's sample virtual host in the current development tree still reads ServerAdmin webmaster@dummy-host.example.com, and the error text still asks you to contact "the server administrator" and describe "the actions you performed just before this error." The software still imagines a single reachable human who owns the machine. Production sites replaced that human with an on-call rotation, which is my comparison and not Apache's, and the visitor's half of the link disappeared in the trade.

The generalist keeps coming back. Meiert's post, written in 2026, argues that AI tools are "allowing a single person to once again manage the entire stack", and that the webmaster may be "leveling up" instead of dead. That is a forecast, and I'd treat it as one. But notice which half of the old role the argument revives. It is the breadth: one person across design, code and servers. The 1993 definition was the other half, the person who answers for the site. Meiert's piece does get to it: "the webmaster orchestrates and takes the responsibility".

The takeaway

The webmaster was an address before it was a job. Berners-Lee's page asked for a mailbox so that a stranger with a problem could reach someone responsible, and it said in the next section that this someone need not be the person who wrote the content. For a few years the sites were small enough that it was the same person anyway, and the industry mistook a coincidence of scale for a profession. When the sites grew, the profession came apart along the line the style page had already drawn.

The breadth went to "full-stack" and now, perhaps, to one person with good tools. The work went to teams. What mostly did not survive is the footer link's promise: that a visitor who found something broken could tell a human, in one click, and that the human could fix it. The address itself is still honoured by mail systems, sample configs and, until 2028, certificate authorities. It is the most durable thing the webmaster built, and on most sites nobody is reading it.

Sources and further reading

  • Etiquette, Tim Berners-Lee, CERN, snapshot of November 3, 1992 (archived)
  • Web Etiquette, in the Style Guide for Online Hypertext, Tim Berners-Lee, 1992 to 1995 (archived)
  • The webmaster mail archive, March 14 to April 4, 1995, W3C history archive (archived)
  • "Error 404", message to the webmaster mailbox, March 16, 1995 (archived)
  • "TimeOut", message to the webmaster mailbox, March 14, 1995 (archived)
  • webmaster, Merriam-Webster dictionary (archived)
  • RFC 1738: Uniform Resource Locators (URL), T. Berners-Lee, L. Masinter and M. McCahill, 1994 (archived)
  • HTML 3.2 Reference Specification, Dave Raggett, W3C, 1997 (archived)
  • Lynx Users Guide, the Lynx project (archived)
  • httpd.conf-dist, Apache HTTP Server 1.3 branch, Apache Software Foundation (archived)
  • http_protocol.c, Apache HTTP Server 1.3 branch, Apache Software Foundation
  • ServerAdmin directive, Apache HTTP Server 2.4 documentation, Apache Software Foundation (archived)
  • httpd-vhosts.conf.in, Apache HTTP Server trunk, Apache Software Foundation (archived)
  • http_protocol.c, Apache HTTP Server trunk, Apache Software Foundation (archived)
  • RFC 2142: Mailbox Names for Common Services, Roles and Functions, D. Crocker, 1997 (archived)
  • A Day in the Life of a Webmaster, The Princeton Review (archived)
  • What Happened to the Webmaster, Jay Hoffmann, The History of the Web, 2020 (archived)
  • Address munging, Wikipedia (archived)
  • FormMail, Matt Wright, Matt's Script Archive (archived)
  • Maybe the "Webmaster" Isn't Dead After All, Jens Oliver Meiert, 2026 (archived)
  • Announcing Google Search Console - the new Webmaster Tools, Michael Fink, Google, 2015 (archived)
  • Goodbye Google Webmasters, hello Google Search Central, Lizzi Sassman, Google, 2020 (archived)
